events.title: Why a Starbucks takeover of Chipotle would — and wouldn't — make sense for both companies
events.summary: Starbucks has been working with advisers on a takeover proposal of Chipotle Mexican Grill in recent months, the Financial Times reported. If the deal happens, it would combine two of the nation's largest restaurant chains. But the potential takeover comes with pros and cons for investors of both companies. Starbucks has reportedly explored buying Chipotle Mexican Grill , but investors are split on whether the megadeal would make sense for both companies. The coffee giant has been working with advisers on a takeover proposal of the fast-casual chain in recent months, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. If Starbucks bought Chipotle, it would combine two of the largest U.S. restaurant chains. With about $31 billion in annual domestic sales, Starbucks is the second-biggest U.S. chain by sales. Chipotle sits in the number seven spot, with more than $11 billion in annual system-wide sales in its home market. The report sent Chipotle stock up about 7% in afternoon trading, while shares of Starbucks fell roughly 4%. It is not unusual for deal rumors to lower the potential acquirer's value and increase the target's share price, but investor reactions show that a prospective takeover comes with pros and cons for each side of the deal. To be sure, it is unclear if Starbucks will even pursue the takeover. D.A. Davidson analyst Matt Curtis wrote in a note to clients on Thursday that he views the odds of a deal being completed as "relatively low" — about 20%. A Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC that the company does not comment on rumors and speculation. Chipotle did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol knows more than a thing or two about Chipotle. Before joining the coffee company in 2024, he was chief executive of Chipotle for more than six years. He led a turnaround of the burrito chain, helping it bounce back from a series of foodborne illness outbreaks that had turned into a full-blown crisis for the company. In the wake of Niccol's departure, traffic to Chipotle restaurants fell in 2025, as budget-conscious consumers visited its restaurants less often. These days, the chain looks like it is starting to get back on track, with signs of "encouraging progress," Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said on the company's earnings conference call in late July. Still, its shaky 2025 means that the stock is trading at a 20% discount from a year ago, even with Thursday's big move. And since Niccol left, shares have lost about 40% of their value. Chipotle would be a splashy acquisition for Niccol. More than that, it could create a new restaurant conglomerate, following in the footsteps of Yum Brands , Restaurant Brands International and Roark Capital-backed Inspire Brands. Multi-brand restaurant companies are more diversified, which can be more attractive to investors. While Starbucks is still a much larger chain than Chipotle, the difference in their categories means that one's poor performance could be offset by growth at the other. Moreover, Starbucks could help Chipotle grow more quickly in international markets; the burrito chain only has about 100 locations outside of the U.S., while Starbucks has about 23,000. Other restaurant companies have set a blueprint for that strategy: Yum has leaned on its international experience from KFC and Pizza Hut to launch Taco Bell outside of the U.S. And Restaurant Brands has leaned on Burger King's international expertise to grow Popeyes' international footprint. With any strategic acquisition, investors hope for synergies that justify the price tag and explain why the deal makes sense. A coffee shop and a burrito restaurant do not have much overlap in ingredients, but there are other potential benefits for both companies and their investors. Combining Starbucks and Chipotle would open up potential cost cuts, like layoffs for some now-redundant corporate roles. The two chains also have significant overlap in their U.S. real estate footprints. Roughly 90% of Chipotle restaurants are within one mile of a Starbucks cafe, according to a research note from Stephens analyst Jim Salera published on Thursday. Both companies could benefit from shared real estate development and even operating efficiencies as a result. But real estate is not the only area where they overlap. Many Starbucks customers also frequent Chipotle restaurants. As one entity, they could leverage that overlap through a combined rewards program, Salera suggested. Unlike many big restaurant players, both Chipotle and Starbucks operate most of their U.S. locations, although Starbucks also has thousands of licensed cafes in its home market. That marks a difference from Chipotle's last strategic owner — McDonald's . The burger giant, which franchises the vast majority of its U.S. restaurants, made a majority investment in the upstart Mexican-inspired chain in 1998. But by 2006, McDonald's divested its ownership.

events.title: ‘War lives in me’: Gaza playwright Ali Abu Yasin wins English PEN award
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Ali Abu Yasin, honoured for his artistic resilience, has endured Israeli bombardment, displacement and personal loss over the past three years. London, United Kingdom – Ali Abu Yassin, a playwright from Gaza who continued writing even as Israel’s genocidal campaign devastated the world around him, has won a prestigious award in London. “This prize is great not only for me, but for Gaza, Palestine, and all the Palestinian people,” Ali Abu Yasin, who was named on Thursday as “Writer of Courage 2026” by the literary group English PEN, told Al Jazeera. list 1 of 4 ‘Not backing down’: The Britons pushed towards Palestine by Gaza genocide list 2 of 4 How genocide in Gaza followed Bosnia’s painful pattern list 3 of 4 Gaza child’s autoimmune condition triggered amid Israel’s war list 4 of 4 Global protests mark October 7 attack with calls for Gaza ceasefire The 62-year-old began writing plays and mastering the oud as a teenager in al-Shati refugee camp in Gaza, one of the largest in the Strip and a target of recent attacks. “It’s how I was born, I’ve wanted to express myself using art since my childhood,” he told Al Jazeera. After the war began in October, 2023, Abu Yasin stopped writing plays and instead wrote about life under Israeli bombardment. Abu Yasin said for the first two years, he wrote about the situation in Gaza as Palestinians fled and feared for their lives. “There was no theatre; it was impossible to have a theatre because Gaza was being destroyed,” the writer said, shaking his head. Since 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza and the majority of survivors have been displaced several times over. Abu Yasin works with actors who now rehearse their lines in makeshift tents, against the sound of gunfire. “I was near death four, five times. I saw people around me die. We lived by chance, and those who died, died by chance,” Abu Yasin told Al Jazeera. “My son was trapped under rubble; my house was bombed. So, during those two years, I was trying just to provide some safety to my family. To protect them from famine. And to document what was happening, so the world can hear my voice before I die.” After a break, he wrote several screenplays that he hid and carried with him throughout displacement. In 2004, Abu Yasin began working with the Said Al-Mishal Theatre, a hub for Palestinian culture in Gaza City that was levelled in a 2018 Israeli bombing. Leading playwrights and theatre directors described the attack as “obliteration of this symbol of Palestinian culture and identity” in a letter to The Guardian newspaper. In 2008, Abu Yasin began writing the Gaza Monologues, a series illustrating life in Gaza, both moments of joy and of pain. A few weeks ago, Abu Yasin left Gaza with the support of an artist residency programme in France. “I didn’t actually leave the war. The war lives in me, Gaza lives in me,” he said. He has found himself conserving small amounts of water and minimising waste, habits he developed by living through the humanitarian crisis. The award ceremony aligns with his trip to France, allowing him to attend in person largely by fortunate coincidence. For English PEN, the privilege of an in-person ceremony at the British Library is not taken for granted. “For many years, writers living in Gaza have been among those with the most limited freedom of movement in the world. We recognise this and the direct impact it has on their freedom of expression,” an English PEN spokesperson told Al Jazeera. Abu Yasin’s recent play, 50 Minutes , was shown in Gaza and tells the story of genocide and mourning. Actors rehearsed in a makeshift tent in a car park, many of them without any previous theatre experience. Abu Yasin was nominated by the British academic and cultural critic Jacqueline Rose, who won the 2026 PEN Pinter Prize. The Writer of Courage “is awarded to an author who is active in defence of freedom of expression, often at great risk to their own safety and liberty, and shares the PEN Pinter Prize with the winner,” says English PEN. The organisation is the United Kingdom branch of PEN International, a global association of writers dedicated to “championing freedom of expression and literary advocacy worldwide”. PEN America, its United States counterpart, came under fire in recent years as some alleged it did not support Palestinian writers. PEN America faced a boycott, leading to the resignation of its president in 2025. English PEN, which operates independently from the US group, joined PEN International in calling for an arms embargo on Israel and condemning the killing of Palestinian writers. Rose described his work as “a call for justice, a cry of outrage and a spiritual quest” in a press release. “He has been the consistent chronicler of the harshness and cruelty of Palestinian existence, and the mentor of young people struggling to pluck meaning from the debris of their lives.

events.title: A timeline of former Prince Andrew's ties to Jeffrey Epstein, from the Virginia Giuffre lawsuit to his arrest in 2026
events.summary: Prince Andrew in December 2023. Adrian DENNIS / AFP via Getty Images Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office. On Thursday, a judge said that the search warrants used to search his homes were unlawful. The arrest followed years of public scrutiny over Mountbatten-Windsor's ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The investigation into Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor received a setback. Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, was arrested by Thames Valley Police , the local force for southeast England, at a royal home on suspicion of misconduct in public office related to his ties to Jeffrey Epstein in February 2026. On Thursday, a judge said that search warrants issued at the time of his arrest were unlawful. Still, the Thames Valley Police's investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor's ties to Epstein continues. Mountbatten-Windsor has repeatedly denied any involvement with Epstein's sex-trafficking crimes. However, his relationship with Epstein has been under scrutiny for over a decade, as Virginia Giuffre named him in a lawsuit she filed against Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell in 2015. That scrutiny only intensified after the release of documents in the Epstein files in early 2026. According to emails released, the former prince appeared to forward reports related to his work as UK trade envoy to Epstein in 2010 and 2011. King Charles said in a statement at the time of the arrest that "the law must take its course" and that the authorities had the royal family's "full and wholehearted support and co-operation." Here's a timeline of Mountbatten-Windsor's connection to Epstein. 1999: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Jeffrey Epstein reportedly met through Ghislaine Maxwell. Melania Trump, Prince Andrew, Gwendolyn Beck, and Jeffrey Epstein at a party at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach in 2000. Davidoff Studios/Getty Images As the BBC reported , Ghislaine Maxwell introduced Epstein to Mountbatten-Windsor in 1999. The trio remained friends throughout the early 2000s, with Epstein and Maxwell attending parties at Windsor Castle and Sandringham. The three were also photographed together at events, including a 2000 party at Mar-a-Lago with Donald and Melania Trump and the 2000 Royal Ascot. Epstein and Maxwell were also photographed at Princess Beatrice's 18th birthday party in July 2006, the BBC reported . In 2008, Epstein pleaded guilty to solicitation of prostitution and solicitation of prostitution with a minor under the age of 18, and was sentenced to 18 months. Mountbatten-Windsor visited Epstein in New York in December 2010, just four months after Epstein's release. Mountbatten-Windsor said it was a "mistake and an error" to visit Epstein after he was convicted of the sex crime in a statement released by Buckingham Palace in August 2019. April 2015: Virginia Giuffre sued Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell for defamation, naming Mountbatten-Windsor in the suit. Prince Andrew and Virginia Giuffre, then known as Virginia Roberts, along with Ghislaine Maxwell. This photo was included in an affidavit where Giuffre claimed Prince Andrew directed her to have sex with him. Florida Southern District Court In 2015, Virginia Giuffre brought a defamation case against Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell , alleging that the pair had sex-trafficked her starting in 2000, when she was known as Virginia Roberts. Giuffre alleged that Epstein forced her to have sex with Mountbatten-Windsor in his New York mansion, in London, and on Epstein's private island in the US Virgin Islands in 2001 when she was 17.  However, the allegation was thrown out and struck from the record by a judge, who said it was "immaterial and impertinent to the central claim" in the case at the time. August 2019: Giuffre's allegations were made public when documents from the 2015 case were unsealed. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor at he funeral of Britain's Prince Philip in April 2021. Chris Jackson/Pool via Reuters Further details about Giuffre's allegations against Mountbatten-Windsor were made public in 2019, after documents from the 2015 defamation case were unsealed . In the documents related to sex-trafficking charges against Epstein, witness Johanna Sjoberg told investigators about a sexual incident that she said happened, and involved herself, Maxwell, Mountbatten-Windsor, Giuffre, and a puppet of the prince. "Andrew and Virginia sat on the couch, and they put the puppet ... on her lap," Sjoberg was quoted as saying in the documents. "I sat on Andrew's lap, I believe on my own volition, and they took the puppet's hands and put it on Virginia's breast, and so Andrew put his on mine." Buckingham Palace denied Mountbatten-Windsor's alleged involvement with Giuffre in a statement at the time. "It is emphatically denied that The Duke of York had any form of sexual contact or relationship with Virginia Roberts," the palace's statement read. "Any claim to the contrary is false and without foundation." August 2019: Giuffre said Mountbatten-Windsor "knows exactly what he's done" after the royal denied involvement in Epstein's sex-trafficking operation. Prince Andrew, left, and Jeffrey Epstein, right. AP/Sang Tan, Patrick McMullan via Getty Images Mountbatten-Windsor made a statement after Epstein was found dead in his Manhattan jail cell on August 10, 2019, saying he sympathized "with everyone who has been affected and wants some form of closure." Mountbatten-Windsor added that during the time he knew Epstein, he did not witness or "suspect any behavior of the sort that subsequently led to his arrest and conviction." Giuffre responded with a statement of her own. Speaking to reporters outside a Manhattan court at the time, she said the prince "knows exactly what he's done, and I hope he comes clean about it." November 2019: The then-prince stepped down from his royal duties days after a disastrous BBC "Newsnight" interview. BBC News/YouTube Discussing the allegations in a BBC "Newsnight" interview with host Emily Maitlis on November 16, 2019, Mountbatten-Windsor suggested that a photo appearing to show him with his hand around Giuffre's waist  was fake. He also said during the interview that on the night Giuffre alleged they had dinner, partied at a club in London called Tramp, and later had sex, that he was at home with his daughters, Beatrice and Eugenie. The interview was perceived negatively and labeled a "car crash" by much of the British media. Following the interview, a string of charities, businesses, and universities cut ties with Mountbatten-Windsor , and on November 20, 2019, the duke announced he would step back from his royal duties. events.title: Trump Administration Cuts Off Access to a Major Immigration Program for Workers at Microsoft and Adobe
events.summary: The Trump administration will no longer allow Microsoft and other tech companies to participate in a program that allows H-1B visa holders to apply for green cards, one of the most common pathways for skilled foreign workers seeking permanent residency in the United States. In addition to Microsoft, administration officials said on Thursday that software giant Adobe and IT companies including Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata will be suspended from the PERM program, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification program. PERM is a key step for H-1B visa holders to gain permanent residency, requiring employers to prove that there are no American workers who would be suitable for the applicant's permanent job opportunity. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said that the agency is investigating whether these companies committed fraud, undercutting American workers by hiring foreign employees. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, singled out Microsoft. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said during a press conference. In a statement provided by Microsoft representative Kaitlin Haskins, the company said it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," adding that it develops its workforce by "strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world." Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment. The suspension marks a victory for tech workers who have complained about unfairly losing out on jobs to immigrant workers. Jobs Now, an advocacy group composed of US citizens working in big tech, celebrated Vance’s announcement on its X account with a video of dancing crabs. The group publicizes otherwise difficult-to-find PERM job postings and says it helped Americans apply to nearly 500,000 jobs across 7,000 employers between last January and this past July. The organization and its members have also filed complaints against tech companies about alleged abuse of the PERM system, and have called for a number of changes to the employment immigration system. “Every job in America should be offered to an American first, no exceptions,” the group told WIRED in an unsigned statement. This isn't the first time tech companies have been targeted over PERM. Earlier this year, OpenAI and a company it acquired agreed to settle accusations from the Trump administration about violating rules for the program. Apple reached a similar deal in 2023. The administration's disparagement of H-1B visas—one of the most common work visas in the US—has sent waves of panic through Silicon Valley since Trump's reelection. Tech companies are some of the H1-B program's biggest users: So far in the fiscal year 2026 , the top three employers with the most visas approved are Amazon, Tata, and Infosys. Microsoft is No. 5, with 3,688 visas approved in 2026; in 2025, 6,258 visas were approved. According to the company, 80 percent of last year's visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees, not to hire new people. "The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our US workforce," Microsoft’s statement said. It's unclear if Thursday’s announcement would affect the ability of employees at these companies to apply for H1-B visas themselves. The Office of the Vice President and the Department of Labor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for clarity on if the suspension would impact those seeking H-1B visas. "It's one thing if you want to bring in someone like Elon Musk" who aims to "build something great in America," Vance said on Thursday. He equated the current state of the H-1B program to bringing "indentured servants" into the US, taking jobs away from American workers. (Musk, who was born in South Africa, came to the US via Canada to pursue a bachelor's degree at the University of Pennsylvania.) The announcement came shortly before Trump was set to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. When asked about the upcoming event, Vance said, "We’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.” Vance also said that the administration is investigating nine universities to see if they might be committing fraud with the J-1 visa program, which allows international candidates to study and conduct research in the US.

events.title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
events.summary: Jorge Moreno (left) says "vulture funds" are hiking up rents, while Pierina Nicuray points out that there is "a lack of homes" in Spain Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis , she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause. "It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes." She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb." Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees. "There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own. "They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home." His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government. On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate". Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month. Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay. Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday . Protesters at Pueta del Sol have been paying tributes to Maricarmen Abascal Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market. Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years. When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent. "When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security." Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista. In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%. Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern. A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market. Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes. Carmen Pérez says high rental costs have affected her health However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation. He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies. Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain. "When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years." The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes. The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million. There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs. Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.

events.title: Philippines ex-President Duterte fit to stand trial, ICC rules
events.summary: The former president is able to understand the charges and follow the proceedings, panel of experts find. Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have found former Philippine President Rodrigo ⁠Duterte fit to stand trial and able to face charges of crimes against humanity related to the so-called “ war on drugs ” he waged while in office. The ex-leader is accused of murder and attempted murder for his alleged involvement in dozens of killings. He denies the charges, but faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment if convicted. list 1 of 3 Chinese ship rams Philippines gov’t vessel in South China Sea: Coastguard list 2 of 3 Video: Students flee deadly school shooting in the Philippines list 3 of 3 Powerful El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths, scientists say The court in The Hague said on Thursday that independent medical experts had examined the 81-year-old’s health and concluded he was mentally fit to understand evidence and discuss his defence with his lawyers. “The chamber was satisfied that the accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings,” the court said. His legal team had previously attempted to get the case thrown out on medical grounds, arguing that serious memory loss had left him unable to absorb new information or reliably recall the past. The trial is scheduled to open on November 30. Duterte, who served as president from 2016 to 2022, was arrested in the Philippines in March 2025 and sent to the ICC’s headquarters in The Hague following a lengthy ICC investigation. Last month, he appeared in person for the first time at the ICC. Duterte denies the charges against him, saying he only ordered police to act in self-defence as part of his anti-drugs offensive. Judges also denied a request for him to be released from custody. Estimates of the death toll in the crackdown on drugs during his presidential term vary, from the more than 6,000 reported by the national police to up to 30,000 claimed by human rights groups. Prosecutors say that police and government hit squads carried out dozens of killings at his orders, motivated by the promise of money or to avoid becoming targets themselves. Throughout his presidency, Duterte enjoyed a high approval rating from the public, allowing him to push for his brutal anti-drugs agenda. He became the first Asian ex-leader to be arrested by the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world’s worst crimes, such as war crimes and crimes against humanity.

events.title: Veterans sue government over 'mass and routine' medical data sharing
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Veterans sue Australian government over sharing of medical data Alan Ashmore said he was "staggered" by the volume of information transmitted to UniSA. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) A new class action alleges the federal government breached privacy laws by disclosing thousands of ex-ADF members' medical records to an Australian university. The MATES healthcare program was shut down by the Veterans' Affairs Minister in 2024. The case will be heard in the Victorian Supreme Court and the Department of Veterans' Affairs declined to comment while proceedings are underway. A class action has been launched against the federal government over allegations of "mass and routine sharing" of veterans' medical records over 20 years. On Wednesday, Gordon Legal served the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) with a privacy breach claim, following a two-year investigation into a health program which accessed thousands of Australian military veterans' data. Medicines Advice and Therapeutics Education Services (MATES) was administered by the now-defunct University of South Australia (UniSA) under contract from 2004 to 2024, when the Veterans' Affairs Minister shut it down after an ethics review. Gordon Legal partner Seb O'Meara, who worked on the Robodebt class action settlement, said anyone who used a DVA healthcare card while MATES operated — around 300,000, including bereaved spouses – could register for the lawsuit. Lawyers for the plaintiff will alleged most veterans were "not aware of the MATES program" and "did not provide consent … for the disclosure of their personal information". The firm will seek damages for breach of confidence in the Victorian Supreme Court. Gordon Legal estimated more than 300,000 veterans and family members with DVA healthcare cards had been auto-enrolled in MATES. ( AAP: Tracey Nearmy ) Case about 'what government can do with our information' DVA's website said MATES was about "preventing adverse health outcomes, such as hospitalisations or unwanted side effects, for veterans who take multiple medications". Their DVA healthcare card payments — equivalent to Medicare data — were periodically sent to UniSA, including their name, address, accepted medical conditions and treatments. The patient's identity was initially obscured, but if health risks were found, "a restricted and small number" of staff identified them and contacted their GP. "In these instances, the data accessed was limited to the veteran's name, address and targeted patient feedback … this may have included prescribed medicines, prescriber details and potential risk factors," the website said. Mr O'Meara said the legal issue was that DVA enrolled participants without seeking their informed consent about who would see their personal information and where it would be stored. Seb O'Meara said at least 6,000 people have expressed interest in joining the class action. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) "At the heart of this case is what our own government can do with our personal information, and in particular … of a reasonably vulnerable cohort of people," Mr O'Meara said. "A lot of these people have pretty complex medical histories. "They include complex psychiatric and psychological conditions, and for many of them, learning of the disclosure … has caused them pretty significant distress." A DVA spokesperson said it was aware of the class action but it would "not be appropriate to comment" while the matter is before the courts. "Throughout its operation, the program was conducted under ethics approvals and formal contractual arrangements, including data security requirements," they said. "As this matter is the subject of active legal proceedings, it would not be appropriate to comment further on questions relating to program governance, consent arrangements, data handling processes, or allegations made by parties." DVA previously said MATES prevented 930 hospitalisations and 140 deaths. Adelaide University, an institution created during a merger between UniSA and University of Adelaide, declined to comment. Vietnam War veteran Alan Ashmore, who has "significant health issues" stemming from deployment, is among at least 6,000 who have expressed interest in joining the action. Mr Ashmore, of Melbourne, is helping others use Freedom of Information to access their MATES files, following a recent swell of interest. Alan Ashmore was sent to Vietnam as part of his national service. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) He was "staggered" to discover his own contained 25 pages, including health conditions and prescribed medications.

events.title: 'Got to be more careful': Paxton leaks prompt Republican handwringing
events.summary: The News Three is a trend, and the leaks about Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton’s campaign have more than hit that threshold. On Thursday the Texas Tribune published audio of Paxton saying the US needs to “suck it up” and cut federal programs, more drips from the same fundraiser that elicited Paxton’s complaints about gas prices , lack of control over his own campaign, and the Republican midterm convention depressing his numbers. “Paxton has always relied on his base and a strong statewide ticket to carry him across the finish line. He’s never played anywhere near this level and doesn’t understand the magnitude of effort being expended on his behalf to try to win this race,” Steven Law, former leader of the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC, told Semafor. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, said of Paxton: “Got to be more careful when you run with the big dogs.” Republicans don’t see any of Paxton’s remarks as politically fatal to Paxton’s campaign, but the leaks are not helpful — they only contribute to perceptions of GOP disarray in a tight Senate race. National Republican Senatorial Campaign spokesperson Joanna Rodriguez told Semafor that Republicans need to “put your jersey on and fight with us or go sit in the stands enjoying tofu with the Talafreakos.” Know More Polls this week have continued to show Democratic nominee James Talarico with a slight lead or tied with Paxton, a harrowing result for the GOP in the home state of the modern Republican Party. President Donald Trump rallied with Paxton on Wednesday night, then offered Paxton up for a debate with Talarico — prompting the Democrat to quickly agree and say: “I agree. Ball’s in your court, Ken.” Republicans saw all this coming from a mile away, of course, spending huge sums to help Cornyn defeat Paxton in the primary, reasoning that the general election would be a relative layup for Cornyn. But that didn’t happen, Trump endorsed Paxton, and now Republicans say they need to act like the entire majority is on the line in Texas — because it very well might be. “There are only two teams fighting for Texas’ future: the one with vegans and radicals who want to ban meat, reopen our borders, and transition your kids or the Republican team with a proven record fighting everything the other stands for,” Rodriguez said.

events.title: Mikey Madison plays a Facebook whistleblower in 'The Social Reckoning.' Here's where the real Frances Haugen is now.
events.summary: Jeremy Allen White and Mikey Madison in "The Social Reckoning." Sony Mikey Madison plays Frances Haugen in Aaron Sorkin's new film "The Social Reckoning." In real life, Haugen is a former Facebook product manager-turned-whistleblower. Haugen testified before Congress in 2021 that Facebook was knowingly causing harm. Much like its acclaimed predecessor, Aaron Sorkin's new film "The Social Reckoning" examines and dramatizes the real people in Mark Zuckerberg's orbit . Billed as a companion piece to the 2010 hit film "The Social Network," which told the story of Facebook's early-aughts founding and rapid climb to a multibillion-dollar valuation, "The Social Reckoning" stars Jeremy Strong as a grown-up Zuckerberg in the throes of wealth, power, and scandal. "The Social Reckoning" also stars Oscar winner Mikey Madison as Frances Haugen , better known as the "Facebook whistleblower." Starting in September 2021, The Wall Street Journal published " The Facebook Files ," an investigative series made possible by Haugen, a data scientist and former product manager on Facebook's civic integrity team. Haugen leaked tens of thousands of internal documents after leaving the company, sharing many with reporter Jeff Horwitz (played by Jeremy Allen White) to expose its harmful policies and prompt change at the company. Here's everything to know about the real-life woman who inspired Madison's character. Frances Haugen began her career at Google in 2006 Aaron Sorkin and Mikey Madison on the set of "The Social Reckoning." Sony Born and raised in Iowa, Haugen studied computer engineering and later earned a master's degree in business from Harvard. In her 2023 memoir, "The Power of One," Haugen writes that when she arrived in Silicon Valley in 2006, it was very much a boys club. She felt like an outlier. "Blonde women were on the sales team or were marketers," Haugen writes. "They did not code — but I did." On that note: Sorkin told Business Insider's Jason Guerrasio that Madison was keen to dye her hair blonde, but he dissuaded her from the idea. (They did, however, agree to give Madison a shorter haircut.) "I didn't want her worried about that in the performance," Sorkin said. "I always worry, like for instance, if I cast a British actor and they need to do an American accent, is that going to be your concern every moment of every day? Are you going to be able to do what I need you to do in terms of getting into the text if all you're thinking about is the American accent?" In "The Social Reckoning," Haugen is shown dealing with dismissive comments from male colleagues, like one who tells her to join a dating app because she would "benefit from loosening up." Haugen spent the first eight years of her career working in various positions at Google. She resigned from the company in 2014, largely due to health issues. She was diagnosed with celiac disease and later with non-occlusive temperature-sensitive vasoconstrictive disorder, a rare condition that causes chronic pain and inflammation in cold temperatures. Haugen was hired by Facebook in 2019 to work on the civic integrity team After Haugen's health improved, she worked at other major tech companies, including Yelp and Pinterest, before being recruited by Facebook in 2019. She has said she agreed to work at Facebook on the condition that her role would be in detecting and combating misinformation on the platform, motivated by a former friend who'd become obsessed with conspiracy theories. "It's one thing to study misinformation, it's another to lose someone to it," she told The Wall Street Journal . "A lot of people who work on these products only see the positive side of things." Haugen was assigned to monitor Facebook's impact on international elections and protect against election interference, and later said she was shocked by the "horrifying magnitude of the danger that we were facing." Haugen said her breaking point was when the civic integrity team was dissolved in the wake of the 2020 presidential election , and she quit in May 2021 — but not before secretly copying about 22,000 internal documents, many of which she shared with Horwitz and federal law enforcement. (At the time, Facebook said the civic integrity team wasn't dissolved, but "integrated into a larger Central Integrity team.") Haugen, then 37, sought federal whistleblower protection with the Securities and Exchange Commission. She then publicly revealed her identity during a "60 Minutes" interview with Scott Pelley. "When they got rid of civic integrity, it was the moment where I was like, I don't trust that they're willing to actually invest what needs to be invested to keep Facebook from being dangerous," Haugen told Pelley. Haugen said the root of Facebook's problems is how it optimizes for engagement: Posts that contain divisive language and misinformation are more likely to elicit likes, comments, and shares, so the algorithm amplifies them . "Facebook has realized that if they change the algorithm to be safer, people will spend less time on the site, they'll click on less ads," she said. "Facebook makes more money when you consume more content." Haugen added that, in her view, Facebook routinely prioritizes "profit over safety." The documents obtained by Haugen included a range of internal reports and studies showing, in part, that Facebook's algorithm had encouraged political parties around the world to embrace extremist ideas; that drug traffickers and human traffickers openly used Facebook's services; and that Instagram, acquired by Facebook in 2012, increased rates of depression and eating disorders among its users, especially teenage girls , more so than other social media apps. Haugen testified before Congress in October 2021 Frances Haugen testified before Congress in 2021. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Haugen testified before the Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection that Facebook not only causes harm but does so knowingly , while hiding its research from the public. In her opening remarks, Haugen said that Facebook is used to "deepen divides, destabilize democracies, and make young girls and women feel bad about their bodies." Haugen also stressed the need for government regulation , telling the lawmakers, "There is no one currently holding Mark accountable but himself." "When we realized tobacco companies were hiding the harms it caused, the government took action. When we figured out cars were safer with seat belts, the government took action. And today, the government is taking action against companies that hid evidence on opioids," she said in her written testimony . "I implore you to do the same here." Haugen's testimony received bipartisan support, and Sen. Ed Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts, called Haugen "A 21st-century American hero." Zuckerberg said in a statement that Haugen presented a "false narrative" about the company. Where is Haugen now? Frances Haugen photographed in Australia

events.title: Oil prices jump as Iran steps up tanker attacks, hurricane threatens U.S. Gulf production
events.summary: Iran is ramping up tanker attacks while Houthi militants fired ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh. Oil prices came off their session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. Oil companies shut in about 500,000 barrels per day or 25% of production in the Gulf of Mexico in response to Hurricane Isaias. Crude oil prices rose sharply Thursday, as Iran ramped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and Hurricane Isaias threatened U.S. offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, gained 4% to close at $104.28 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 3.6% to settle at $91.49 per barrel. Nine tankers have come under attack in and around Hormuz over the past week, jeopardizing the recent recovery in crude oil flows through the strait Oil prices backed off session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. NBC News, citing unnamed sources, reported earlier that Trump and his national security team were considering renewing strikes in the coming weeks. Some 9.5 million barrels per day exited Hormuz during the week ended Tuesday, about 30% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to Kpler data. Crude flows from the Middle East, including pipeline workarounds, stood at 16.4 million bpd which is nearly equivalent to prewar levels. In the Gulf of Mexico, oil companies have shut in about 500,000 bpd, or 25% of offshore production in the region, as Hurricane Isaias churns toward the coasts of Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida panhandle. Tensions are sharply escalating in the Middle East. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen fired missiles at airports in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and the city of Abha on Tuesday and Wednesday. Three people died and 36 were injured, according to the state-owned media outlet Al Arabiya. The Saudis intercepted another volley of ballistic missiles fired Thursday at Riyadh and Khamis Mushait, a spokesperson for the kingdom's military said. "While flows from the region have largely normalized, the need for US navy escorts, increased costs and logistical frictions and constant risk of being attacked call into question the longer-term feasibility of the flows," said Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities. "This ultimately warrants a sticky risk premium to remain in pricing," McKay told clients in a Thursday note.

events.title: Exclusive: Anthropic's plan to protect critical infrastructure
events.summary: Anthropic is launching a new cybersecurity initiative designed to bring its most powerful AI models and engineers to companies protecting power grids, water utilities and other critical infrastructure, the company first shared with Axios. Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are struggling to secure aging, complex systems as AI threatens to make cyberattacks faster and cheaper to execute. Driving the news: Under its new Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, Anthropic will provide its frontier AI models, on-site engineers and threat research to companies already responsible for securing critical infrastructure systems. Participating companies will use these resources to identify and fix vulnerabilities in their customers' systems. The program's founding partners include Accenture, Booz Allen Hamilton, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC and Rockwell Automation. Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same. Zoom in: Anthropic is also launching a free AI-powered vulnerability scanning service for open-source software projects, called OSS Scanner. Participating projects will receive periodic scans from Claude, along with automated reports detailing vulnerabilities, how they could be exploited and suggested fixes. The reports won't undergo human review before being sent to software maintainers, meaning some findings could be inaccurate. The big picture: Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI developers are looking for ways to put their most powerful models in the hands of cyber defenders as hackers gain access to similar capabilities . Anthropic's new initiative builds on lessons from Project Glasswing, which gave vetted organizations access to its most capable AI models to identify security vulnerabilities. The company said the project demonstrated how quickly AI can uncover vulnerabilities, but also how difficult it remains to verify and fix them. Yes, but: It's unclear how participating companies will safely test and deploy fixes without disrupting utilities' operations, one of the biggest challenges in securing critical infrastructure. Anthropic also didn't specify whether partners will receive free model access or who will cover the computing costs associated with using its AI tools. events.title: U.S. suspends Microsoft, Adobe from green card labor program in foreign worker crackdown
events.summary: The U.S. Labor Department announced it would suspend Microsoft and Adobe from its Permanent Labor Certification. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro and HCL were also suspended from the program. The U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft and Adobe from its Permanent Labor Certification program on Thursday, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said, as the Trump administration continues to take aim at immigration and foreign hiring programs ahead of November's midterm elections. Sonderling said the Labor Department won't accept or process any new applications under the program for a host of companies, including Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro and HCL. The secretary said Adobe and Microsoft were also suspended "due to multiple active federal investigations." "Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers," Sonderling said. Vice President JD Vance criticized Microsoft specifically, pointing to the firm's 6,000 layoffs in 2025. Vance claimed that the company "replaced" those workers with people on H-1B visas. "So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first," Vance said. Microsoft responded to Vance's claims and defended its hiring practices in a statement Thursday, saying "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." "Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees," the company said. President Donald Trump is set to award the National Medal of Science to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other leading technology CEOs on Thursday at the same summit where the suspension announcement was made. Nadella is from India and moved to the U.S. in 1988. He joined Microsoft in 1992. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su are also being honored at Thursday's medal ceremony. Each of the leaders immigrated to the U.S. Musk was born in South Africa and Su and Huang were born in Taiwan. "It's one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk," Vance said. "I think 99% of American citizens look at somebody like Elon Musk or Lisa Su, the CEO of AMD, and they say, obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that." Tech giants like Microsoft, Google , Amazon and Apple have been among the top sponsors of H-1B visas for decades. This year, Amazon had the highest number of petitions at 35,426 workers, followed by Cognizant and EY, according to 2026 data from Levels.fyi . Microsoft was a close fourth at 21,706 petitions for 2026, with a median base salary of $180,710. Microsoft said that petitions were only filed for workers "who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and said Microsoft's wages for H-1B workers were among the highest of all H-1B filings. CNBC has reached out to Adobe for comment. events.title: Vance says the US is suspending permanent visa residency program for Microsoft
events.summary: Vance announced the visa changes at a press conference Thursday. Alex Wong/Getty Images The Trump administration says it's suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal program used to sponsor foreign workers. JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” the VP said. The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal program that companies use to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said Thursday during a press conference. Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM. The program is an initial step that employers generally must complete before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card, requiring them to show that no qualified and available US workers could fill the role. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. The announcement came just over a week after Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella sat two seats away from Vance at President Donald Trump's White House "Super Intelligence" luncheon, a gathering of tech executives focused on AI. A Microsoft spokesperson pointed Business Insider to a blog post the company published Thursday, which said “the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans.” Microsoft wrote that roughly 80% of the about 6,000 H-1B visa applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees, rather than to hire new people. It said the remaining applications were for people already legally in the US and amounted to 1% of its US workforce. Adobe did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the administration was also suspending Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini from the program. The IT companies are among the largest users of PERM and other employment-based immigration pathways in the US. Vance also said the administration would investigate nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, and Stanford, over allegations that they used J-1 exchange visas to undercut American wages. Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. The announcement is the latest escalation for the administration against companies that rely on highly skilled foreign workers, particularly through the H-1B visa system . Microsoft is one of the biggest employers of H-1B workers in the US. It was not immediately clear how long the suspension would last or what it would mean for Microsoft employees whose permanent-residency cases are already pending. The process is already slow: The Labor Department says PERM applications took an average of 336 calendar days to process in August. Correction: October 8, 2026 — An earlier version of this story misstated who announced Adobe's suspension. It was Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Facebook whistleblower behind ‘The Social Reckoning’ says Zuckerberg is ‘playing with fire’ on AI
events.summary: Welcome to Eye on AI. Beatrice Nolan here. In today’s issue: The Facebook whistleblower on Meta’s AI bet. OpenAI’s human rights lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night.’ Fired OpenAI safety staffers urge company to protect AI monitoring. And voters increasingly see AI as a threat to American workers. First, a quick note: Fortune Brainstorm AI returns to San Francisco Dec. 7–8 to convene technologists, entrepreneurs, Fortune Global 500 executives, investors, policymakers, and the brilliant minds in between to interrogate the most pressing questions about AI. We will explore how organizations are deploying and scaling AI in their industries. Come join me there. Apply to attend now This week, director Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning, a follow-up to The Social Network , opens in U.S. cinemas. The 2010 film was about how Facebook was founded. This one is about the company’s moment of reckoning: whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision in 2021 to walk out of the company with tens of thousands of pages of internal documents. Haugen, played by Mikey Madison in the new film, was a product manager on Facebook’s civic integrity team. She gave the documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by Jeremy Allen White, and they later became the basis of an investigative, award-winning series of stories that the Journal called The Facebook Files . Among other things, the series revealed that the company’s own researchers had found Instagram made body image issues worse for some teenage girls. Haugen filed whistleblower complaints with the SEC and testified before the Senate, and her disclosures have since helped drive a wave of lawsuits against social media companies. I spoke with Haugen this week about how Facebook (now called Meta, of course) has changed since she walked out, what she makes of Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s AI push, and what she wants employees at the leading labs to take from the film. “My hope for the movie is that people, especially at the frontier AI labs, see themselves in the Frances Haugen character. If they see something, feel like they can say something,” Haugen told Fortune . But, in a moment where the AI industry is filled with existential anxiety, and even its leaders are calling for brakes, Haugen isn’t advocating for a pause in AI development. “We have never done a prohibition where we could properly check,” she said. “Slowing down just means whoever doesn’t want to slow down wins.” Instead, she’s backing a different part of Dario Amodei’s recent plan : independent auditors. Amodei proposed that frontier labs give third-party evaluators ongoing, “employee-like access” to check safety practices and report incidents, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said his company would do the same. Haugen says the best mitigation to AI harms is for this kind of auditing to be required by law across the industry, the way outside auditors are entitled to review the books at banks. AI companies already publish far more research into their products than Facebook ever did, she said, but she questions whether what they publish reflects what’s actually happening inside. As for Meta, Haugen views Zuckerberg’s recent AI efforts as “playing with fire,” driven by his desire for a positive legacy. She also doesn’t think the company has changed since she blew the whistle. “I have not seen a culture change that shows that they have…turned a new leaf,” she said. Meta is still behind leading labs like Anthropic and OpenAI—and Zuckerberg has been prominent in pushing back on regulatory efforts. “He wants to catch up, so he wants there to be no constraints until he’s at least at the same table as the big boys,” she said of Zuckerberg’s anti-regulation stance, “not just pretending to be where the big boys are.” ( Fortune contacted Meta for comment on Haugen’s claims but the company did not reply before press time.) AI content moderation How Meta moderated harmful content on its platform was a big part of Haugen’s 2021 disclosures. Some of the internal documents she took suggested Facebook acted on as little as 3% to 5% of hate speech on the platform, and she has previously said the company’s decision to dissolve her civic integrity team after the 2020 election helped push her to come forward. Last year, Meta shifted its automated content moderation toward high-severity violations and replaced some its U.S. third-party fact-checking program with an X-style Community Notes system. This year it has gone further. In March, it said it would rely less on outside vendors and human contractors for enforcement, and in June the Financial Times reported that AI models had already taken over about half of human review requests. Haugen expects better models to make fewer mistakes and catch more harmful content, but not all of it. When she left, the company was catching about 5% of harmful content, she said. But she predicts that even very advanced AI might only reach 10% to 20%, because language is so nuanced. “The real solution is designing the systems from the ground up to be safer, not just trying to clean them up in the end,” she said. With that, here’s more AI news. Beatrice Nolan beatrice.nolan@fortune.com @beafreyanolan This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.summary: Jev, an AI model built for quick decisions, went viral among AI developers and Silicon Valley cognoscenti when the startup TypeSafe AI released it in September. These early adopters were quick to experiment with the AI model, which could perform all kinds of classification decisions—like sorting online customers into buckets based on certain data points or categorizing documents—at a fraction of the cost of many leading AI models. Programmers showed it sorting email, spotting writing mistakes and even playing games. Within a day of arriving on Vercel’s AI Gateway, a service for accessing different models, nearly 13% of its paid teams had tried Jev. Vercel said Jev reached more than twice as many paid teams in its first 24 hours as any previous model launch. Perhaps the clearest sign that TypeSafe was on to something: on Oct. 6, just three weeks after Jev’s launch, OpenAI rolled out a competing product, called Decisions API . These services are competing to make AI practical for the thousands of routine judgments businesses might want to automate each day. At that volume, small differences in cost, speed and error rates can change whether automating a task is worthwhile. TypeSafe trained Jev specifically for this work. OpenAI’s Decisions API uses GPT-6 Luna, an existing model in its lineup. An AI model that skips the prose TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida told Fortune he began thinking about Jev after helping develop the technology behind ChatGPT at OpenAI. Almeida saw a gap between models’ ability to answer people’s questions and their usefulness in automating routine work. Almeida said he wanted to address AI’s “massive over-promise under-deliver issue” and avert an “AI winter.” “Building a company just happened to be the most effective way to do that,” he said. Before joining OpenAI in 2020, Almeida took a year and a half off to travel, meditate and play games. He says he reached “top-2 in Hearthstone,” the digital collectible card game, an accomplishment he joked might have been harder than building Jev. Almeida has said he had tried to work backward from a future in which AI had transformed the economy. In that future, would most requests to models come from people, or from code running automatically? He concluded that the vast majority would come from code. A customer-service program, for example, could ask a model whether an incoming message concerns a billing issue or a technical problem, then use the answer to route it to the appropriate team. Developers could set a threshold for the model’s confidence about its routing decision. Above that threshold, the message would be routed automatically to billing or technical support. Below it, and it would be flagged for a human to check.. This sort of classification task is something that rudimentary AI, or machine learning systems, have handled for decades. Computer science students are often taught to build these classifiers in machine learning courses. Email services have long used these simple models to filter spam. A model can estimate how likely a message is to be spam, and the software can move it to the junk folder when that estimate crosses a threshold set by its developers. The problem with these simple models is that they tend to be relatively inflexible, without much understanding of a document’s text, and they require some technical know-how to create. In some ways, large language models (LLMs), which are what today’s best known AI systems are based on, represented an improvement on these simple classification systems. LLMs can perform classification tasks too, sorting customer-service messages based on written descriptions of categories such as billing questions or technical problems. They have a much deeper understanding of the text they are processing, so can make finer-tuned decisions. Developers can also change the LLM’s instructions to use the same model for other jobs. So that makes these systems more flexible than the old classification models. But LLMs take more computing power to process these decisions, which makes them both more expensive and slower than the old, simple machine learning classifiers. When the LLM has to handle thousands of these requests throughout the day, the cost and delay of each call add up. TypeSafe says Jev is designed to handle these judgments faster and more cheaply than general-purpose language models, but with the same ability to set up the classifier through easy, natural language instructions that LLMs offer. Developers describe what they want Jev to evaluate, and Jev returns choices, scores or probabilities their software can use. The company says it produces those outputs together, avoiding the time spent generating an answer piece by piece. Developers still have to establish whether its judgments are accurate enough for their particular task. Almeida initially thought making the models behind Jev reliable would take him a week. Instead, TypeSafe spent two years developing Jev. “Making the models reliable was so much harder than expected,” he told Fortune .  What developers love about Jev Niels Mouthaan, the independent developer behind the Daily time-tracking app, told Fortune he tested Jev in a spelling and grammar prototype that gave users feedback as they typed. Users expect “close-to-instant feedback while typing,” he said. He was impressed by Jev’s speed and saw promise in using it to flag errors, with a language model suggesting corrections only where needed. TypeSafe calls Jev a “System One” model, borrowing the term for fast judgments from psychologist Daniel Kahneman. After experimenting with Jev, Ashutosh Mathore, a founder of environmental compliance software startup Atlensa, told Fortune its speed made him reconsider “where we may be using LLMs out of habit even when the task is not really a language problem.” Jev is named for economist William Stanley Jevons , Almeida wrote in TypeSafe’s launch post. Jevons argued that more efficient steam engines would, somewhat counterintuitively, increase overall coal consumption by making coal-powered work cheaper. The lower cost of coal-power would increase demand, leading people to use it for more things. Applied to AI, the idea is that lower costs could make many more tasks worth automating. Paolo Rosson, head of applied AI at bookkeeping software company Dext, said that the problem with LLMs is that “you pay for a full written answer when all you need is a label.” In a personal project screening proposed software changes, he has used Jev to reduce how often routine changes go through a larger model. He estimated the cost of Jev’s model calls at seven cents per 1,000 changes. He also spent considerable time deciding which probability estimates should trigger human review, depending on “how much risk you’re ok with,” he told Fortune . events.title: I always thought I'd settle down in Canada. Living in Japan for a year changed my mind.
events.summary: Living in Japan changed my plans for the future. Alessa Hickman After spending most of my life in Ottawa, I moved to Japan expecting to head home after one year. Living abroad showed me how much I value spontaneity, travel, and a life that feels like my own. Now, I'm heading back to Canada with a different perspective on what I want from my future. I was born and raised in Ottawa, and aside from a handful of vacations abroad and summer road trips to nearby Canadian cities , it's where I spent almost all of my time. Most of my family lives there, and the relatives who don't are only a few hours away. Growing up, the path modeled to me was pretty straightforward: Stay close to home, take vacations when you can, and build your life nearby. As I got older, though, I felt a growing need to see what else was out there. I was also feeling the pressure of rising costs in Canada , and my apartment lease was ending, so the timing felt right for a change. I'd visited Japan a couple of years earlier and loved it, so when I found out about the yearlong Working Holiday Visa program, it felt like the perfect fit. I assumed that once the year was up, I'd just come back home and sign another lease nearby. However, after my first night out in Tokyo, I was already looking into how I could stay away longer. Living in Japan has been better than I ever imagined I've missed Canada at times, but Japan has felt like home in a way I didn't expect. Alessa Hickman For most of my life, I've craved adventure. I grew up hiking, taking little road trips with my mom, and looking for any excuse to get out of the city for a day. I've always loved novelty, and living in Japan has given me so much of it. Since moving here, I've lived in multiple places, including Tokyo and Osaka . I've traveled to over a dozen more cities and towns, tried countless new restaurants, and met people from all over the world. It feels like there's constantly something new to see or explore. The train system here makes it so easy to lean into that spontaneous side of myself. I love being able to visit a new city on a whim, whereas in Ottawa, doing the same thing would usually require a little more planning and a lot more money. The more I've experienced this kind of lifestyle, the harder it is to imagine giving it up. I don't necessarily want to spend my life in one place just because it's where I'm from, and now, I know a future filled with new places and experiences is available to me. I'm going home, but I'm not done exploring Now, I know I want to see more of the world. Alessa Hickman Going back to Canada is the next logical, short-term step for me. My visa's coming to an end, and making a permanent move abroad would take a lot more planning and paperwork. This doesn't mean I'm done exploring the rest of the world, though. After I leave Japan in a couple of months, I'm planning to spend some time in Southeast Asia — and if I can, I might squeeze in a couple more stops on my way home. Once I'm back in Canada, I'm sure I'll jump into planning another trip, or maybe I'll start looking into another yearlong visa. I can see myself living abroad again, or at least spending more time traveling internationally, whether that's in Japan or somewhere completely new. For now, though, I don't plan to settle back into life in Ottawa the way I once thought I would. While I'm in this up-in-the-air phase, I'd love to move (or drive!) across Canada and see where life takes me from there. I'm looking forward to exploring more of my home country. Since moving to Japan, I feel like I've changed, too — and I've reflected on how little of Canada I've actually seen. I'm excited to experience my home with a new perspective. I'm still in my 20s, so I feel lucky to have the freedom to keep figuring things out as I go. And living in Japan didn't give me all the answers, either. If anything, it gave me more questions. As I head home, I'm taking everything I've learned and felt this year in Japan with me — and I'm so excited to see where I'll go next. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Judge seems poised to reinforce block of Trump's White House media ban
events.summary: President Donald Trump speaks to the news media, including CNN news anchor Kaitlin Collins. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images A federal judge appeared inclined to extend his block on Trump's ban on three media outlets from the White House. The judge said on Thursday that one of the administration's arguments is contradicted by the president's own words. "That's an uphill climb," the judge said of the DOJ's effort to defend the ban on national security grounds. A federal judge appeared inclined to extend his block on President Donald Trump's ban on three media outlets from the White House. The administration's argument that the ban was based on national security concerns is contradicted by the president's own words, US District Judge Timothy Kelly said during a hearing Thursday. "That's an uphill climb," Kelly said of the Justice Department's effort to defend the ban on national security grounds, noting Trump's claim that his ban was based on his disapproval of the outlets' coverage. Kelly is weighing whether to grant a lengthier block of Trump's move to ban POLITICO, CNN, and MS NOW from the White House. The Trump-appointed judge already lifted the ban last month, issuing a two-week restraining order , which he extended through Tuesday, that enabled the three organizations to regain access to the West Wing. But he now appears to be leaning toward a more durable injunction that would maintain the outlets' access during what could be months of litigation. Kelly's original ruling found that the ban likely violated the news outlets' due process rights, since the White House restricted access without any notice and without setting out any identifiable standards for news organizations to follow to maintain their credentials. "That's probably the biggest hurdle you all have," Kelly told the government during a hearing that drew a swath of media executives, reporters and First Amendment attorneys to the federal courthouse in Washington, D.C., leading Kelly to remark on the vastly outnumbered Justice Department attorney assigned to the case. In what has been a recurring theme in court battles across the country, Kelly pointed out that Trump's own comments — declaring repeatedly in interviews and on social media that he banned the outlets for writing "negative" stories about him — conflicted with the Justice Department's later efforts to claim the ban was a response to the outlets' publication of sensitive national security information. A lawyer for the news organizations, Theodore Boutrous Jr., urged Kelly to reject Trump's ban for a second reason: a violation of news organizations' First Amendment rights and an effort to chill the free press. Boutrous argued that a recent interview Trump gave to Time magazine "amounts to a confession" from the president that he revoked the journalists' press passes because he considered their stories to be too negative. "That interview really is the coup de grace," Boutrous said. He also pointed to a recent comment from Attorney General Todd Blanche that Trump banned the outlets from the White House due to their "one-sided reporting." Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik argued that the Trump administration had, in fact, provided due process to the news outlets — after Trump's ban went into effect. He cited unsigned letters from the White House press office delivered in the days after the lawsuit was filed, identifying a handful of stories the administration viewed as "misinformation" or "national security" risks. Velchik argued that the outlets "defaulted" by failing to respond to those letters. He also repeatedly attributed the letters to Trump himself, even though they were unsigned and Trump never referred to them publicly. Boutrous, calling this after-the-fact effort a "sham process," underscored the absence of any indication Trump had signed off on — or even had any awareness of — the letters. Velchik also repeatedly argued that the courts should give the president more leeway than might apply in other contexts, where decisions about reporters' access are made by federal agencies. "The White House is a sacred place," Velchik said. Kelly asked whether the president could ban a news organization from the White House based on stories that were demonstrably false. Boutrous said no, while Velchik articulated a more malleable standard. "From our perspective, it's within the discretion of the president," Velchik said. Kelly emphasized that his assessment of the issue was constrained by longstanding precedents that forbid the White House from barring access to the West Wing press areas based on disagreements with content, along with requirements that revoking such access must be based on clear standards and potential consequences spelled out in advance. The Justice Department has said it disagrees with those decisions, but the judge made clear he is bound to follow them. This story originally appeared on POLITICO and is courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms. events.title: Trump: Anyone saying "AI" is "THE ENEMY!" The White House uses it
events.summary: President Trump on Thursday called anyone who uses "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" "THE ENEMY!" — even as the White House continues using the term "AI." Why it matters: Trump's push to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" clashes with established terminology in the technology industry. Trump's branding blurs the distinction between AI and super intelligence , a hypothetical version of AI more advanced than human intelligence. What they're saying: "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday. Zoom out: Trump's executive order from September doubled down on using "SI" over "AI," though it did not offer a penalty for using the term. The order specifically defines "Super Intelligence" using the existing federal legal definition of AI. The order calls on federal agencies to change how they describe AI in official communications. The State Department already ordered diplomats to use the term after Trump's United Nations speech on Sept. 22. Yes, but: The White House still uses "AI" as a term, including on its AI-focused website, AI.gov . The White House's Office of Science and Technology Policy also makes reference to "artificial intelligence." But when an Axios reporter asked the America.gov chatbot about AI, the bot responded: "The executive branch uses Super Intelligence (SI) for this topic, not the older term you used." What we're watching: Whether the White House could update its websites to reflect Trump's preferred terminology. The White House did not respond to Axios' request for comment Thursday.
