events.title: Ben Affleck is an AI nerd, and the internet is impressed
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. They cast the wrong lead in “Good Will Hunting,” apparently, because it’s Ben Affleck who is the secret genius, as it turns out. The actor who earlier this year sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix for a reported $587 million has gone viral this week for demonstrating his understanding of AI technology, neural networks, machine learning, and the like, across multiple video clips of his recent interviews. He can even write a little Python, he says. The movie star delved into his interest in technology most recently on an episode of GQ’s “One More Question” series this week, where he humbly started with “I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young,” before nerding out on the development of AI as it relates to filmmaking, while using AI terminology like machine learning, neural networks, transformers, tensors, GPUs, inference, and more. In a clip that’s making the rounds, Affleck explains to the impressed interviewer, Zach Baron, that he got into the space when analog film moved to digital. As he spoke, he kept defining terms so the interviewer could understand what he was talking about. “I became more interested in that aspect of it, and the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning,” Affleck began. “So I can write, like, pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that. Because with convolutional neural networks — which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do — which is just much more computation simultaneously — you would do things like, look at what’s called a tensor — which is just the numerical translation of a visual image, in numbers like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame, and how many? It’s just that simple, right?” No, Ben Affleck, it is not just that simple, which is why this video is going viral. The actor then went into how neural networks were used to identify patterns and do edge detection or feature extraction, which he described as “identifying patterns enough to know — like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.” He also admitted he used his status as a Hollywood star to get a peek at emerging AI technology, at times. OpenAI was among those he visited, Affleck said in a separate clip, which ultimately led him to understand how he could get more directly involved in the AI space. As the interviewer continued, Affleck explained how AI can help with filmmaking while not replacing it, leading to the development and sale of his own startup in this space. (He claims the $587 million figure is “not right,” noting that he didn’t own the whole company.) “I gambled on this notion that in order to do this in an ethical way and in a way that could take this technology and actually make it work hand in glove with artists in this community where there are very fixed, long-standing relationships around likeness and so forth, we had to create our own dataset,” he said. “So I raised the money. I shot for about eight months with a lot of cameras and a lot of equipment, and created a dataset that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks, sort of where the training code, the inference code, were related to one another and geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value,” Affleck said. In a separate clip, also going viral, Affleck spoke to Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw at the Screentime 2026 conference in LA, where he talked about how he fine-tuned AI models by taking open source models, unfreezing the weights, then teaching them to meet certain cinematic standards. In the process, the filmmaker retains their proprietary work, while benefiting from the learning they create by training their own unique model for the movie they’re making. Ben Affleck (Hollywood star & Artists Equity CEO) talks about how he fine-tunes open video models by unfreezing weights and trained only the last cinematic layer so a film crew can hit real production standards. for context, Ben Affleck founded InterPositive in 2022, a 16-person… pic.twitter.com/xIOvD0xMyt — Rohan Paul (@rohanpaul_ai) October 1, 2026 The actor used the technique himself in his movie “Animals,” where AI aided in the post-production process. At one point, he also weighed in on the concerns around AI and its world-ending potential . His worries, however, were much more rational. “When I worry about AI, I worry about my kids in school. I worry about the 30% rise in the number of A’s given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use. I don’t worry about Skynet, and I don’t think that it’s going to take over [the movie] business in any meaningful way.

Arena , which originated in 2023 as a research project at UC Berkeley that crowdsourced rankings of AI models, has raised a $200 million Series B round at a $3.1 billion valuation, it said on Thursday. This comes after the company said it reached $100 million in annualized run-rate revenue in June. The round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures, with Salesforce Ventures, 01 Advisors, Dell Technologies Capital, Endeavor Catalyst, a16z, Felicis, and others joining in. Arena previously announced a $150 million Series A in January at a $1.7 billion post-money valuation. At the time, its annualized revenue was $30 million , it said. So that means its valuation has nearly doubled in about 10 months. Arena provides a crowdsourced platform that is free for consumers to use. People enter prompts or request vibe-coded projects and then rate which model does it better. Arena claims it has tens of millions of monthly visitors. In September of last year, it introduced its commercial product, AI Evaluations , a service that provides model labs and enterprises with detailed performance analytics based on its community feedback. The timing proved impeccable. This year, AI labs realized that their models were gaming benchmarking tests, finding ways to rack up good scores without truly earning them. At the same time, enterprises wanted help determining which model works best for their own internal needs rather than relying only on standardized benchmarks. “AI is advancing faster than our ability to evaluate it, and static benchmarks break down once models recognize they’re being tested,” the company said in its funding announcement. “The world needs a neutral third party to measure how safe and aligned AI actually is once it’s in the hands of real people. Arena is stepping into that role today,” it added. To that end, Arena has also added a new category to its leaderboard: alignment . This is where it ranks models based on issues like unauthorized action (taking actions it wasn’t asked to take); false attribution (wrongly crediting statements or facts to the wrong source); and what it calls “deceptive completion” (lying about completing tasks that it didn’t do). Currently, a slate of OpenAI’s models are at the top of its preliminary alignment leaderboard, with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable in sixth and ninth place, respectively. events.title: Google brings agentic AI to Gemini, starting with businesses
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface. The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work. Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these. Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future. The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others. It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network. Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person. The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers. Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control. events.title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
events.summary: Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo. The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused. The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile. The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday. In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957. The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark. White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims. It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items. This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim. The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind". Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs. Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops. In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes. A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image. In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes. White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024. In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters The GPU giant released a fix for the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-47483 Microsoft N1Xes Intel in favor of Nvidia's shiny new SoCs in Surface Laptop Ultra 22 hours ago The question you would ask HPE and NVIDIA if nobody was recording 3 days ago Californian accused of shipping $300M worth of Nvidia chips to China without Uncle Sam’s approval 6 days ago Nvidia debuts $4,999 DGX Spark with half the RAM and storage, amid memory crunch 6 days ago RAM supply set to worsen, says Micron, as CEO celebrates ‘much higher’ prices 7 days ago Researchers found thousands of GPU servers exposing Nvidia's DCGM Exporter to the internet, with hundreds potentially vulnerable to a high-severity flaw that could let unauthenticated attackers crash the GPU monitoring service and disrupt AI workloads. DCGM Exporters read telemetry from the GPUs on a host, including its hardware, utilization, memory usage, power consumption, and error events. Each GPU has its own unique ID, or UUID, and all of these metrics are exposed in plaintext over HTTP. This exposure provides would-be attackers with detailed information useful for reconnaissance, including mapping GPU infrastructure, identifying potentially vulnerable systems, and monitoring workload activity. Michael Katchinskiy, a researcher at datacenter security startup Lava, found and reported the bug in the GPU health and performance monitoring service. In September, the GPU giant Nvidia released a fix for the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-4748 3, and gave it an 8.2 CVSS high-severity rating. “Once we realized how much these endpoints revealed, the next question was: How many of them are exposed to the internet?” Katchinskiy said in a Thursday blog. So the researchers started scanning the internet for exposed DCGM Exporters. And the scale of exposure proved “especially significant,” he wrote. Over the course of four scans between March and May, the threat hunters found about 2,100 GPU servers exposing DCGM Exporter metrics to the open internet. These included 12,000 GPU UUIDs. None of these required authentication. The hosts belonged to about 300 organizations, according to Katchinskiy, and nearly half - 5,274 of the exposed GPUs, or 44 percent of the total - were located in the US. These GPUs represented about $100 million in hardware, and included Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs, H200s, and H100s - used to run large-scale AI workloads - plus consumer RTX 5090 and 4090 systems. While investigating the exposed systems, the Lava team found that about 25 percent of the exposed DCGM hosts also revealed data from Go’s /debug/pprof/ built-in profiling tool. The profiler collects and exposes runtime performance data such as CPU and memory usage for running Go applications. This includes CPU usage, memory allocations, goroutine states, and blocking events. “With enough concurrent unauthenticated requests, the exporter could run out of memory and crash, cutting off visibility into GPU health and activity,” Katchinskiy wrote. The CPU and memory pressure could also affect AI training or inference workloads. Nvidia fixed the issue in version 4.8.2, and operators should upgrade to that version or later. In addition to GPU telemetry, Lava looked into Prometheus Node Exporter, which monitors server hardware and operating systems, and also exposes metrics over HTTP. The team found 12,096 public Node Exporter hosts exposing data on server models, operating systems, firmware versions, hostnames, storage paths and networking hardware commonly used in GPU clusters. This information reveals how environments are built and configured, which could also be used by attackers for reconnaissance, matching the system to known vulnerabilities. The publicly exposed monitoring services affected customer infrastructure across neocloud and GPU cloud providers including Nebius, Voltage Park, Lambda, Northern Data, and DigitalOcean. Lava reported all of this to the affected providers, and Katchinskiy says that these providers worked with customers to address the exposures.

events.title: U.S. Lawmakers Launch Sexual Abuse Probe of Youth Sports Giant AAU
events.summary: Left image: A scene from an Amateur Athletic Union-affiliated volleyball game in 2026. Right image: Rep. Brett Guthrie, R-Ky., left, chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and ranking member Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., D-N.J. Collage by ProPublica. Photos by Sarah Blesener for ProPublica and Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images. What Happened: Bipartisan leaders from the powerful House Energy and Commerce Committee launched an inquiry on Wednesday into the Amateur Athletic Union, criticizing the sprawling youth sports organization for its handling of child sexual abuse allegations and demanding answers, citing reporting by ProPublica and The Washington Post . What They Said: “It is unacceptable that AAU is failing to implement standard reforms to protect child athletes, and is misleading the public, parents, and athletes about preventative measures in place within AAU sports,” the letter reads . The committee chair, Kentucky Republican Brett Guthrie, called ProPublica and The Post’s reporting “deeply disturbing” in a statement on Thursday, saying it “raises serious questions about the organization’s actions over the past decade.”  “Our Committee is seeking information on how the AAU’s policies have potentially fallen short, and what needs to be done in order to protect young athletes,” Guthrie said.” The members of the committee, which in 2018 investigated systemic failures surrounding sexual abuse by former USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar and others, said in the letter that they were “seeing parallels” between its past investigation and “what is being uncovered within the AAU today.” The letter is addressed to Jo Mirza, the AAU’s president, and asks detailed questions about the organization’s operations, taking the extra step of demanding a briefing from Mirza to the committee by Oct. 21. Among questions about its safety policies and coach training, the committee asks Mirza to lay out how many sexual abuse allegations the nonprofit receives each year and how many coaches it disciplines, information that has long been shrouded in secrecy. The AAU declined to provide the data to ProPublica and The Post. The AAU does not publish a list of banned coaches like many other youth sports groups do, and ProPublica and The Post found that it has used confidential arbitration clauses to keep lawsuits from child sexual abuse victims from being heard in open court. The letter is signed by Guthrie, ranking Democrat Frank Pallone Jr. from New Jersey and representatives in charge of oversight and investigations. Read More A Youth Sports Giant Promised Reforms to Protect Kids From Sexual Abuse. Most Never Happened. Background: ProPublica and The Post found that the AAU, which has some 760,000 athletes and coaches nationwide, is failing on nearly every level to adequately protect young athletes from sexual abuse — breaking pledges it made in the wake of a 2011 sexual abuse scandal involving its CEO and young basketball players. The investigation found that the AAU has become a haven for coaches suspected of abuse, according to a review of public disciplinary lists and interviews with current and former executives from six national sports governing bodies and other key stakeholders. The AAU, the investigation found, does not offer child abuse prevention training, though it claims to the public that it does. And ProPublica and The Post found that it has suppressed allegations of sexual misconduct, including against another top executive in 2018. Why It Matters: The committee is one of the key congressional groups charged with overseeing the federal youth sports safety system. It has the power to push for changes in child safety law — and to force transparency from organizations like the AAU, which has repeatedly failed to deliver on past promises of reform. In 2018, in the wake of the allegations against Nassar, scrutiny from Congress led to the passage of a law known as the Safe Sport Act. It created the U.S. Center for SafeSport, an oversight group, to investigate allegations of sexual misconduct and gave it the power to suspend or ban coaches for life. But SafeSport has jurisdiction only over national sports governing bodies, like USA Gymnastics and USA Volleyball, that are overseen by the Olympic and Paralympic Committee — meaning much of the law does not apply to the AAU. The law does require “all amateur sports organizations” — not just governing bodies — to “offer and provide consistent training to all adult members … regarding prevention and reporting of child abuse.” The Energy and Commerce Committee’s letter cites that provision of the law and demands that the AAU explain how it complies. Response: In a statement, the AAU said, “As always, we will cooperate fully and respond appropriately to any questions or requests from congressional committees or U.S. government agencies.” Previously, the AAU told ProPublica and The Post that it is “committed to protecting its athletes through comprehensive protection policies overseen by our Compliance Department,” and said it has an “ongoing commitment to providing a safe, secure, supportive, and trusted environment where athletes can thrive.” The post U.S. Lawmakers Launch Sexual Abuse Probe of Youth Sports Giant AAU appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Israel opens first-ever pavilion at Morocco defence show
events.summary: Israel opened its first national pavilion at Morocco’s Marrakech Air Show, joined by Israel’s top military contractors. Israel’s Ministry of Defence says it is participating for the first time in a defence exhibition in Morocco, as it announced its first-ever national pavilion at the Marrakesh Air Show 2026. “This marks Israel’s first official participation in the defence exhibition held in Morocco since the signing of the Abraham Accords”, Israel’s Defence Ministry said in a statement on Thursday. The ministry said eight Israeli defence companies exhibited “advanced, combat-proven technologies at the show” in Marrakesh, which runs until Saturday. The Marrakech Air Show, taking place from October 7 to October 10 this year at the Marrakech Royal Moroccan Air Force Base, is organised every two years and is meant for civil and military aeronautics and space industries to highlight their latest offerings. “Israel’s three major defence industries, Elbit Systems, IAI, and Rafael, also exhibited, presenting solutions across the air, land, sea, space, intelligence, cyber, and digital domains,” it said. The announcement is the latest sign of increasing ties between the Arabic-speaking North African country and Israel, since the two established ties in 2020 as part of the US-backed Abraham Accords. Last month, Israel and Morocco agreed to upgrade their diplomatic ties, including elevating their respective missions to embassies and appointing ambassadors to both countries. The move followed a meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers, hosted by the US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. They also agreed to expand air travel, including by reinstating direct flights operated by carriers from both nations, and confirmed plans for high-level bilateral visits in the coming months. Morocco is also one of the five countries that have pledged to send troops to Gaza, under the US-backed International Stabilization Force (ISF) as part of US President Donald Trump’s so-called Board of Peace.

events.title: OpenAI’s math solutions aren’t meeting the field’s standards yet
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When OpenAI released hundreds of claimed solutions to some of the world’s hardest math problems this week, the frontier lab said that it had consulted an advisory group of elite mathematicians to avoid the controversy that came with the last time one of its models solved a long-standing problem in the field. But OpenAI fell short of those standards, particularly where the mathematicians emphasized the need for human understanding of a mathematical result. That’s especially concerning after a new paper highlighted gaps between the natural language and formally expressed solution to a million-dollar problem ostensibly solved by OpenAI’s models. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), hosted by Princeton University’s Institute for Advanced Studies, is made up of nine prominent researchers at institutions around the world. The organization released guidelines for frontier labs solving math problems at the end of September. In a statement on the latest set of proofs, the AGMAI said that “it is ultimately up to the mathematical community to assess the extent to which our recommendations were followed successfully.” However, the organization’s first request was “to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.” OpenAI’s release explicitly says that it is evaluating its proprietary models using open research problems in mathematics. The advisory group did not respond when asked by TechCrunch for a more thorough evaluation of OpenAI’s latest proof release. The lab clearly followed some of its principles, including releasing results as soon as possible and including information about how the models reached their conclusions. But not for all of them: Just 10 of the 719 manuscripts included releases of the model’s chain of thought. For papers that people don’t understand, the mathematicians suggested the proofs should be formalized — but just 42% of the proofs released by OpenAI had not undergone this process. Ultimately, it’s still not clear that OpenAI is taking “responsibility for ensuring that human understanding will follow” when releasing its proofs, in accordance to the AGMAI principles. AGMAI suggested that OpenAI should help fund the work of human mathematicians who will be required to make the lab’s solutions meaningful in any real way. “Problems are being solved autonomously by AI prompters who have no interest in the broader field itself once their initial target is ‘solved’, and do not understand the AI output well enough to answer questions on the result, give talks, or otherwise interact with the rest of the field,” Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician who has criticized OpenAI’s approach, wrote on social media after the release. That problem is exemplified by a paper released this week by mathematicians at the University of Cambridge and King’s College in London that questions the way frontier labs are approaching these challenges. When AI models solve mathematical problems, they first create a “natural language” explanation, then try to express that result in Lean, a programming language that in theory confirms the accuracy of the proof by compiling it as code. However, there may be problems with the way the models translate their natural language proofs into code; this paper documents at least two discrepancies between the natural language proof and the Lean code behind the solution OpenAI has offered to a problem derived from the Navier-Stokes equations that describe the complex behavior of fluids. These discrepancies don’t necessarily disprove either solution, but they do raise questions on whether we can simply rely on models to formalize their own solutions without human involvement. That’s one reason that AGMAI asked OpenAI to “include machine-readable metadata correlating the natural language and formal artifacts,” something that the frontier lab did not do with these releases. “Because of the phenomenon of mistranslations — as highlighted in this paper — the NL proof by OpenAI and other autoformalised Lean proofs should not prima facie be trusted without the same peer review process and scrutiny that other proofs are subjected to,” the authors of the “lost in translation” paper conclude. Mathematicians stress that when new results are discovered by humans, they take responsibility for them and engage with the broader community through papers, talks, and seminars. That process increases understanding of the solutions, finds strategies that can be used to solve other problems, and allows the new knowledge to be applied in practical fields.

events.title: Top bosses at Goldman Sachs to share bonus pot worth up to $500m
events.summary: Eye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s history Top bosses at Goldman Sachs are in line to share a bonus pot worth up to $500m (£378m) this year, marking one of the biggest payouts in the Wall Street bank’s history. The eye-watering sum will be shared between 20 bankers, with its chief executive, David Solomon, due to take about $100m (£75.6m) of the reward, which is made up of Goldman Sachs stock. That is more than double the value of the record $47m (£35.5m) annual pay packet he was granted last year. The $500m bonus pot is the culmination of a long-term investment plan first crafted by the bank in 2021. The final sum, which is due to be confirmed later this month, is tied to how high Goldman’s share price has climbed over the past five years, as well as how its stock price has performed compared with peers such as JP Morgan and Bank of America over that period. Goldman Sachs said the bonuses were meant to persuade bosses to stay at the bank “in an increasingly competitive market”. The bank’s president, John Waldron, who is widely expected to succeed Solomon as chief executive, is also in line for a payout, alongside other top bosses such as the co-heads of global banking and markets, Ashok Varadhan and Dan Dees. News of the bumper bonus, which was first reported by Bloomberg, comes days before Goldman is due to report third-quarter earnings on 13 October. The bonuses reflect the value of Goldman Sachs stock, which has surged roughly 146% over the past five years, and climbed about 300% since Solomon took the helm as chief executive. A spokesperson for the bank said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market. It’s no secret our firm has performed exceptionally well in the years since.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The payouts are the latest in a string of large payouts for executives in the US, particularly on Wall Street. The US lender Citigroup announced earlier this year that its chief executive, Jane Fraser, had been paid a record $42m (£31.8m) for 2025. Meanwhile, JP Morgan’s chief executive, Jamie Dimon, took home a total pay package worth $43m (£32.5m) last year , up 10% from a year earlier. Dimon’s own long-term incentive award is worth about $270m (£204.1m), according to Bloomberg.

events.title: Colombian embassy to open in Jerusalem, Israeli FM says
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella had promised closer ties with Israel on the campaign trail. Israel has announced that Colombia will open an embassy in Jerusalem, becoming the latest country to establish a diplomatic mission in the disputed city claimed as a capital by Israelis and Palestinians. Most countries have their embassies in Israel in Tel Aviv. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Thursday the Latin American country’s embassy would open next week as he touted expanding relations with the region. list 1 of 3 Has Israel shut the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – or downgraded it? list 2 of 3 Will Brazil’s Lula halt the right-wing wave sweeping Latin America? list 3 of 3 Protesters in Colombia rally against ties with Israel “Next Wednesday, we are going to inaugurate … the Colombian embassy,” Saar told attendees at a conference in Jerusalem. An official at the Colombian Foreign Ministry in Bogota told AFP news agency the country’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar would travel to Jerusalem on Sunday ahead of the opening. Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella , who was sworn in as president in August, promised close relations with Israel during his election campaign. When he came into office, he restored diplomatic ties between Colombia and Israel. Colombia had previously severed ties with the country over Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza. The announcement comes as a small but growing list of countries has opted to route their diplomatic ties with Israel through Jerusalem. Since 2018, the US, Guatemala, Paraguay, Kosovo, Honduras, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Nauru and Somaliland, which has been recognised as an independent entity only by Israel, have opened embassies in the city. Other countries that have diplomatic relations with Israel have located their embassies in Tel Aviv, as Jerusalem is not recognised by the international community as Israel’s capital. “We will work hard because this is the diplomatic battle over the truth. And the truth is, Jerusalem was always the capital of one nation,” Saar said, dismissing Palestinian claims to the capital. The Israeli minister said the Democratic Republic of the Congo would open its embassy in Jerusalem “very soon” and hinted at another opening. “I think that with the possible results in Brazil, they might have the same move,” he said after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro won the first round in the country’s presidential election. Protesters in Colombia took to the streets of Bogota on Wednesday to rally against the new far-right government’s policy towards Israel, including the decision to open the Jerusalem embassy. “When diplomatic relations with Israel were broken off, the message was that we would not be a nation complicit in their atrocities,” Nicolas Isaza, who took part in the protest, told Al Jazeera. “Today our government is no longer drawing a line against the atrocities being committed in Palestine,” he added.

events.title: Trump's foreign worker crackdown comes for Microsoft, Adobe, IT firms
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the Trump administration is suspending Microsoft , Adobe and several other IT firms' ability to hire foreign-born workers for permanent residency in the U.S. Why it matters: The move will affect hundreds of companies owned by the tech giant, escalating the Trump administration's crackdown on immigrant labor. What they're saying: " We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector," Vance said during a Thursday news conference. "We're the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers." "And so our message to Microsoft is, you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants." Zoom in: The permanent labor certification program , which is administered through the Department of Labor, allows a company to hire foreign workers to live permanently in America. It's typically the first step in receiving an employer-sponsored green card. It's also separate from H-1B visas, which allow workers to live and work temporarily in the U.S. H-1B visas primarily go to highly skilled workers in specialized occupations. Technology companies are among the program's biggest users. The Trump administration has made reducing the number of foreign workers in the country a rallying cry, and accused foreign-born workers of taking jobs that could — and, in its view, should — go to Americans. Driving the news: Vance specifically singled out Microsoft, slamming them for laying off 6,000 workers last year. Vance said Thursday that "[a]t the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. Now that is a scandalous system that we've allowed in this country for far too long." Microsoft owns hundreds of companies, including LinkedIn, Skype and gaming studio Activision Blizzard . Adobe and IT outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini are also suspended from the program. Worth noting: Trump will award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House today. Microsoft did not respond to Axios' request for comment. events.title: America shut out Chinese EVs. Britain welcomed them — and now faces a difficult choice
events.summary: Britain faces a finely balanced choice over whether to follow the EU in imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs, as it seeks closer post-Brexit ties while risking retaliation from Beijing. Chinese automakers are rapidly gaining ground in Britain. Analysts warn EV tariffs alone may not curb China’s advance, with hybrid sales also surging and Chinese brands benefiting from advantages in cost, supply chains and product development. The U.K. broke with the U.S. by opening its doors to China's electric vehicle juggernaut . Chinese EVs face only a 10% standard import duty in Britain, one of the largest major overseas markets without additional China-specific tariffs. Japan and Norway also lack them. It's in contrast to the U.S., where a 100% tariff effectively shut Chinese EVs out. The European Union , the U.K.'s biggest trading partner, has manufacturer-specific duties on Chinese EVs of up to 35.3%, in addition to a standard 10% import duty on all foreign cars. Now, the U.K. faces a difficult choice, as EU proposals may force it to impose tariffs to match the bloc's. At the weekend, The Sunday Times reported that U.K. Business Minister Jonathan Reynolds is considering matching the EU's levy on Chinese EVs to avoid the pain of so-called Made in Europe proposals, which could hurt domestic companies selling into the EU. A U.K. government spokesperson reiterated to CNBC that it had not imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs but added, "We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector's and UK's national interests." The Made in Europe legislation, part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act , is designed to protect the bloc's industries from unfair international competition by prioritizing European-made goods. An EU official told the Financial Times in September that London would need to raise tariffs on Chinese EVs and align more closely with EU trade policy to avoid "Made in Europe" barriers. The decision is finely balanced, given Prime Minister Andy Burnham's desire to reset relations with the EU , which the U.K. formally left in 2020, and the likelihood of China responding with retaliatory measures. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said it had expressed "serious concern" to Britain about the reports about potential tariffs. "China is firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products," a spokesperson said Tuesday. "We will continue to follow developments and respond accordingly," they said. Chinese automakers rapidly made inroads in the U.K. Chinese car brands have swiftly captured market share in the U.K. Analysis by Jato Dynamics found that registrations of Chinese automakers, or original equipment manufacturers, across both battery-electric and hybrid powertrains, rose to 519,424 between the start of January and the end of August, lifting their total market share to 28.1%. That's up sharply from 12.9% in the same period in 2025. Hybrids accounted for the larger increase, adding 62,655 registrations versus 32,565 for battery-electric vehicles. "That matters for policy," Paul Hilton, head of retail at Jato Dynamics, told CNBC by email. "Tariffs aimed only at Chinese-built battery EVs could slow one part of the expansion, but would not address hybrid growth, vehicles made outside China or the underlying advantages in cost, product cadence and supply chains," Hilton said. "A durable UK response should pair any evidence-based trade remedy with incentives for local production, competitive energy and battery costs, charging infrastructure, skills and alignment with European market-access rules." The bestselling car in the U.K. last month was not a Tesla or a Ford — but the Jaecoo 7 from China. The mid-size SUV, nicknamed the “Temu Range Rover,” starts at about £29,000 ($38,350) in the U.K., compared with roughly £45,500 for a Land Rover Discovery Sport. The Jaecoo 7's nationwide sales climbed to 10,814 in September, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, outpacing the Tesla Model 3, Ford Puma and Kia Sportage. Rico Luman, senior sector economist for transport and logistics at ING, said the growing policy gap between Britain and the EU is leaving the U.K. with limited options, besides tariffs, if it wants to maintain a level playing field with the bloc. Speaking to CNBC by email, Luman said exclusion from the Made in Europe initiative could have “significant consequences” for existing businesses, making closer alignment with EU trade policy increasingly difficult to avoid. "It's generally quite remarkable that batteries from China are exempted from EU tariffs," Luman said. "At the same time this is logical as production in Europe isn't up to speed and Europe lacks the rare earth minerals and refinery capacity behind it," he added.

events.title: Two Latvian men arrested inside UK military base after breach
events.summary: Police say nothing so far suggests the incident at RAF Molesworth is linked ​to events surrounding RAF Fairford last month. Two Latvian men have been arrested inside a military base in southeast England that houses United States and NATO intelligence hubs after the perimeter fence was breached, police have said. The arrests come amid heightened concerns about security at military bases in the United Kingdom after a separate incident last month. list 1 of 3 Mapping where US bombers are based globally list 2 of 3 UK police arrest British national linked to RAF Fairford airbase incident list 3 of 3 UK police charge Royal Navy member accused of working with foreign power Counterterrorism police said on Thursday that the two men, aged 36 and 32, were arrested at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in Cambridgeshire. They are being held on suspicion of trespass and of entering a prohibited place “for a purpose prejudicial to the UK”, said police. A security patrol had spotted an abandoned vehicle near the base late on Wednesday night. Police found a “small breach” in the perimeter fence before locating and arresting the men in the early hours of Thursday, they said. The men were taken to a police station in Cambridgeshire where they are still in custody. Both are Latvian nationals residing in the UK. The arrests come after a major incident at RAF Fairford in western England on September 27 that led to the arrest of seven men, all in their 20s, who have since been released on bail. One is a dual UK-Iranian national. Due to the nature of the incident, UK counterterrorism police are leading the investigation into the security breach, police said. “We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites,” said Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London. “But at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford,” she added. Flanagan said that the investigation at RAF Molesworth is at an early stage but added that enquiries would home in on “any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site”. RAF Molesworth, formerly a World War II airbase, is now a non-flying facility managed by the United States Air Force. US intelligence has based its operation centres for Europe and Africa at the base near Huntingdon. It is also a NATO intelligence hub, according to a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) website. On Sunday, US military planes were abruptly flown out of the RAF base at Fairford in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vehicles were seen near the base, prompting a major incident to be declared. That base had been used by the US military to conduct strikes in its war against Iran.

events.title: I made 5 game-day appetizers in my slow cooker. The Buffalo wings were a major crowd pleaser.
events.summary: I loved every recipe, but the crispy and juicy Buffalo wings really impressed me. Erin McDowell/Insider Game day is the perfect time to use your slow cooker for easy, hands-off recipes. I made five game-day foods in my Crock-Pot, including creamy queso dip and mac and cheese. I loved every recipe, but the crispy and juicy Buffalo wings really impressed me. Football season is back, and Sundays are once again reserved for touchdowns, quality time with family and friends, and an all-important game-day snack spread. In a bid to find simple game-day foods  that didn't require hours in the kitchen, I decided to test five slow-cooker recipes. I've made classics like Buffalo chicken dip countless times in my Crock-Pot , but this time I branched out with options like spicy wings, meatballs, and mac and cheese. Every dish impressed me, though the wings were the clear MVP. Here's how I made five game-day appetizers in a slow cooker. The first game-day recipe I made was classic Italian meatballs. Erin McDowell/Business Insider These slow-cooker meatballs from Chef Savvy are an easy, versatile game-day option. Serve them in tomato sauce, pile them into rolls for meatball subs, or pair them with pasta. I used a store-bought beef-and-pork meatball mix, but the rest of the ingredients are pantry staples. It's best to mix the ingredients by hand in the bowl to ensure the eggs, breadcrumbs, and meat are well incorporated.  I formed the mixture into medium-sized balls and placed them on a lightly greased sheet pan so they could brown in the oven briefly. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I could see flecks of chopped onion and parsley throughout the meat mixture. The recipe yields about 24 meatballs, and I ended up with exactly that many, so I knew I had portioned them correctly. Next, I broiled the meatballs for about four minutes per side, keeping a close eye on them so they wouldn't burn. Once the meatballs were perfectly browned, I took them out of the oven. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I then started gathering the ingredients for the tomato sauce: crushed tomatoes, tomato paste, bay leaves, red pepper flakes, and Italian seasoning. The meatballs fit in a single layer inside the slow cooker. I then added the tomato sauce ingredients and let it all cook on low for four hours. Erin McDowell/Business Insider It's fine if the meatballs overlap slightly in a smaller slow cooker. After four hours on low, mine still looked a little underdone, so I cooked them for another 30 minutes on high. Check that yours are fully cooked before serving, since timing can vary depending on the slow cooker and the size of the meatballs. Finally, the meatballs were done — they were delicious. If you have any leftovers from your game-day party, they're tasty the next day, too. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I thought the meatballs were perfectly juicy and well-seasoned, while the tomato sauce tasted like homemade marinara that had been cooking on the stove for hours. I enjoyed the meatballs on their own as an appetizer. However, later in the week, I served some of the leftover meatballs and sauce with pasta for dinner, which really impressed me as well. The next slow-cooker appetizer I made was a personal favorite for game days: Buffalo chicken wings. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I started by mixing together Buffalo sauce, minced garlic, chopped yellow onion, and brown sugar.  While I had heard you could make Buffalo wings in a slow cooker, I was admittedly skeptical. I was nervous that the wings wouldn't turn out crispy enough, since that's usually done in a traditional oven or a fryer. However, Spend With Pennies ' recipe called for broiling the wings after cooking them in the slow cooker, which would crisp them in just a few minutes.  After adding the chicken wings to the slow cooker, I poured the sauce mixture over the top. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The chicken wings that I bought didn't have the drumsticks and flats separated, which added a bit of time to my preparation. I cooked the Buffalo wings in the slow cooker for three hours on low. Erin McDowell/Business Insider After they were fully cooked, I removed them from the slow cooker and placed them on a sheet pan with foil. I then brushed some of the Buffalo sauce still in the slow cooker over the wings. I then put them under the broiler for about three minutes on each side until they were crispy and slightly blackened. I decided to serve the wings with blue cheese dressing, but you can also choose ranch or any dipping sauce of your choice. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I was pleasantly surprised by how easy these wings were to make, and loved how the slow cooker made the wings extremely tender. I was really impressed by this Buffalo-wings recipe. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The wings were crispy on the outside, while the meat inside was tender, juicy, and moist. I also thought they were the perfect spice level — they had a kick but didn't set my mouth on fire.  I thought these would fit in well at any game-day or Super Bowl party.  The next slow-cooker recipe I tried was Martha Stewart's queso dip, which only called for a few ingredients. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I've tried a number of Martha Stewart's slow-cooker recipes in the past, and I've enjoyed a majority of them. I was excited to see how Stewart's queso dip recipe would turn out. Like a lot of her slow-cooker recipes, this dip only required a few ingredients, which I really appreciated. events.title: 'I don't know what my partner earns': How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?
events.summary: You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns? Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all. We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries. Willa says she doesn't know what her partner earns even though he knows her salary Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all. "It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says. Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return. He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does. "He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'" Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees. "It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills." Vik says if someone brought up salary and spending on a first date they probably wouldn't be the right person for him For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple. Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone. Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make". Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship." He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy". "If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me". Others feel even more strongly about being asked too soon. Twenty-six-year-old Bridget Shurdut, who works in sales, says she would find it "incredibly odd" if someone asked about her salary within the first few dates. "I don't think I'd continue to see that person. I'd answer the question, but it would be a red flag for me." For her, someone's current salary isn't necessarily particularly useful information anyway as she says she's much more interested in "whether someone is ambitious and driven than what they earn monetarily". Dating and relationship coach Kate Mansfield, says money conversations "should start much earlier than many people think". "In the first few dates you should talk about how each of you approaches spending, saving, generosity, lifestyle and financial independence as these things shape compatibility." Emily's been in a relationship for two years and has not discussed salaries yet Becoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though. Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make". She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask. "Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it. events.title: Hurricane Isaias charges towards the US Gulf Coast with dangerous winds
events.summary: The storm is forecast to strike Florida, Alabama and Mississippi with up to 10 inches of rain this weekend. Hurricane Isaias has intensified into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season as it barrels over record-warm water toward the northern shoreline of the United States Gulf Coast, prompting school closures and local government shutdowns. According to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center, the storm is forecast to make landfall in parts of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi late Friday or early Saturday. The low-lying areas are especially vulnerable to flooding and storm surges. list 1 of 3 US court blocks Trump administration plan to cut disaster agency workforce list 2 of 3 Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry? list 3 of 3 Hurricane Polo lashes Mexico as Nolo strengthens near Hawaii The center warned residents in likely impact zones on Thursday to complete all emergency life-safety and property protections without delay. It has also issued a hurricane watch from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, through Indian Pass in the northwestern part of Florida in anticipation of torrential downpours and the substantial risk of localised flash and urban flooding. A rainfall total of 3-6 inches is forecast with isolated peaks up to 10 inches. “We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said in a Thursday morning update, adding that he expects “up to near-major hurricane strength” by Friday as the storm pounds north of Mexico’s Yucatan Peninsula. On Thursday morning, Isaias was packing maximum sustained winds of nearly 130km/h (80mph) with higher gusts. Heavy rain and flash flooding also threaten the inland areas throughout the weekend, extending as far as the Tennessee Valley and potentially encompassing a broad stretch from the inland southeast up through the southern Appalachian Mountains. Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the US Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 percent of crude pumped annually in the US. As of Wednesday, about 25 percent of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated. With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries. When Isaias was first declared a hurricane on Wednesday, it marked the latest date for an Atlantic season’s first hurricane in 121 years, falling just short of the record set in 1905, according to data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The season normally runs from June 1 through November 30.

events.title: RIP, Amazon Fire tablets: 2011-2026
events.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos introduced the Kindle Fire tablet in 2011. EMMANUEL DUNAND/AFP via Getty Images Amazon is phasing out its Fire-branded tablets after 15 years. The company's new line of tablets has its Alexa+ voice assistant built in and likewise lean into Alexa branding. The new Alexa Tablets cost between $229.99 and $499.99 and run on Android. Goodbye, Amazon Fire tablets. You lasted longer than the Fire Phone. After 15 years, the e-commerce giant is discontinuing its Fire tablets and replacing the budget-friendly devices with a new line of pricier tablets that have its Alexa+ voice assistant built in. An Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider that the company will continue to sell through its current inventory of Fire tablets, but is no longer manufacturing new units with that branding. The new Amazon Alexa Tablets, which run on Google's Android operating system and come with access to the Google Play Store, are now available for purchase and will ship on October 14 in the US, Mexico, and Canada. Amazon's new line of Alexa tablets. Amazon Amazon's aluminum-cased Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, Alexa Tablet 11, and Alexa Tablet 8 run from $229.99 to $499.99. "The Alexa Tablets are a new product line built for what's next — they don't change anything about the experience Fire tablet owners have today," the Amazon spokesperson said. "Fire tablets remain their own product — fully supported, with continued security updates. Customers who love their Fire tablets can keep using them." It's not the first time Amazon has moved on from a Fire-branded device. Its Fire Phone was a high-profile flop that Amazon founder Jeff Bezos later called a "tiny little blip." events.title: Trump: U.S. won't attack Iran before midterms
events.summary: President Trump said Thursday the U.S. will not attack Iran ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Why it matters: Trump had been considering for several days resuming major combat operations before the midterms. However, his past statements about his intentions in Iran haven't always matched what he ultimately did. If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include large-scale strikes on Iranian energy facilities, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say. Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterms, in part because oil prices might rise in response. It could also influence Israel's elections, which are scheduled for Oct. 27. What he's saying: "I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait ... we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Flashback: In June 2025, before Operation Midnight Hammer, the White House said Trump would decide "within two weeks" whether the U.S. would join Israel's war against Iran. When he made that statement, he had already decided to attack Iran's nuclear sites. On Feb. 27, less than 24 hours before Israel and the U.S. launched the war against Iran, Trump claimed he hadn't made a decision on going to war. In reality, Trump had already decided to authorize the attacks. Driving the news: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran , Axios reported on Wednesday. Behind the scenes: On Tuesday, Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke with senior U.S. officials who briefed him on the U.S. military's preparations for the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a U.S. official and another source briefed on the call. Zamir said during the call that resuming the war within that timeframe could lead to the postponement of the Israeli elections, given the assessment that Iran would respond by launching missiles at Israel, the sources said. The IDF declined to comment on conversations between Zamir and his U.S. counterparts. Between the lines: It's unclear whether Trump's statement will reassure Iranian leaders that an attack is not imminent. U.S. and Israeli officials say Iranian leaders are deeply suspicious of Trump's statements. The officials said Iranian leaders were surprised twice and want to avoid a third surprise attack. What to watch: Trump said the U.S. and Iran "are having productive discussions." But there are no signs that the major differences between the two sides have narrowed.

events.title: Little relief expected for gas prices ahead of Election Day, according to prediction markets
events.summary: Gas prices have been elevated ever since the start of the Iran war, and little relief is expected ahead of the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi place more than 80% odds that gas prices will remain above $4 per gallon on Election Day. On the same day, speculators think there's a 2-in-3 chance that diesel prices will also stay above $6 per gallon. Affordability is seen as one of voters' top issues heading into the 2026 midterm elections . And gas prices — one of the items where consumers are getting squeezed the most — are expected to remain elevated through Election Day. Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi give an 87% chance that the AAA national average for gas prices will remain above $4 per gallon on Nov. 3. But while they expect prices to stay above that mark, they do think there's a chance they'll come down from the levels where they currently are, giving just a 42% chance the average is above $4.25 on Election Day. As of Thursday, the national average is currently at $4.36 per gallon. Gas prices peaked at an average of $4.56 per gallon in late May, following an initial spike in March after the start of the Iran war and the latter country's closure of the Strait of Hormuz , a critical passageway for oil exports from the Middle East. They then fell to as low as $3.79 per gallon in early July before rising again throughout the rest of the summer. Diesel prices hit new peaks in September, though, reaching almost $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22. Prices have since fallen to $6.28, though traders on Kalshi place 68% odds that figure remains above $6 per gallon on Nov. 3. Rising diesel prices have a particular impact in states with larger agriculture industries , such as Iowa and Kansas, and states such as Alaska that rely on diesel fuel for electricity. All three are home to competitive races for the U.S. Senate this November. As gas prices have remained elevated, Democrats' chances for flipping the Senate have improved . Traders on Kalshi give the party 63% odds of taking the upper chamber from Republican control. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: I moved from Oregon to Philadelphia for the city life, but missed the outdoors and my car. I left less than a year later.
events.summary: After living in Philadelphia, I realized how much I value easy access to mountain hiking and snow sports. Tristin Hoffman/Business Insider I went to school in an outdoorsy Oregon city, but moved to Philadelphia for a job after graduation. I've since moved back to my college town, largely because of the lifestyle differences. I was surprised at how much I missed my car and the easier access to outdoor activities. When I moved across the country for a job after spending my entire life in outdoorsy West Coast cities, I didn't expect the homesickness that would follow. I spent four years in college in Eugene, Oregon, a medium-sized city situated between the Cascade Mountains and the Oregon Coast, where my life revolved around physical and outdoor activities. My social circle included surfers, skaters , snowboarders, and mountain bikers, and taking an after-class hike with friends was the norm. Having grown up in San Diego, I'd been used to an outdoor-focused lifestyle for as long as I could remember. But after graduating, I accepted a job in Philadelphia and moved in the fall of 2025, drawn to its walkability, big-city energy, and the chance for a change of pace and scenery. I knew there would be differences between life in Eugene and Philadelphia, but I struggled with not having a car, the harsher-than-expected winter weather, and the extra planning it took to get outdoors. I ultimately moved back to Oregon less than a year later because it was a better match for my lifestyle. The cold weather wasn't just uncomfortable — it was painful. The snow was comforting to watch fall while indoors. Walking around in snowy conditions, however, was both uncomfortable and exhausting. Tristin Hoffman/Business Insider After treading through the rain in Oregon for four years, I thought that adjusting to the Philadelphia winter would be a breeze. But I found the city’s combination of wind, snow, rain, and humidity hard to adjust to. On my walk to work, the city's frigid wind tunnels would leave my face red and numb by the time I reached my desk. Without a car, there was no quick dash from a parking lot. The swings in Philadelphia's weather — from snowstorms to thunderstorms — made it difficult to plan my week and even harder to imagine enduring it for years. I missed the convenience and freedom of having a car. When I first arrived, I was most excited about how walkable Philadelphia is. Running errands without a car, however, proved to be quite a hassle. Tristin Hoffman/Business Insider Philadelphia is a city known for its walkability. It was a huge selling point for me as I decided where I wanted to move to after college. I was tired of driving and wanted to experience the charm of getting lost walking through the big city. In Philadelphia, I lived in Old City, within walking distance of work and much of downtown. When walking became necessary, however, that "charm" was a different story. I found my personal bus route was quite unreliable, and I ended up walking more than I expected, which was a pain when I had to haul groceries back home for a mile, twice a week. When temperatures dropped below freezing, walking around became something I dreaded: I had to pull on four to five layers of clothing just to stay relatively warm, and constantly being surrounded by people on the street became exhausting. I missed the solitude of my car. Nature takes more planning when living in a city. Philadelphia's streets were straight out of a storybook. But I found myself craving open expanses more than the city itself. Tristin Hoffman/Business Insider I am an avid runner — I run at least four times a week and have enjoyed scenic trails by beaches and rivers my whole life. During my first weeks living in Philadelphia, I realized I no longer had the easy, everyday access to shorelines, trailheads, and open space that I’d taken for granted. Instead, my running routes during the workweek would have to weave through the city itself, full of traffic and pedestrians, or along a loud highway next to the Delaware River. Philadelphia has parks and trails, but getting to the kind of mountain nature I craved often required setting aside time for a weekend trip and arranging transportation . I once took about an hour to reach Philadelphia's Wissahickon Valley Park by bus from Center City, where I ran past waterfalls and beneath tree canopies brimming with fall foliage, but the headache of planning transport made it a tough sell to do again. It was a big eye-opener about how much I value the easy, convenient access to Oregon's dense forests and mountain trails. My social life was more centered on indoor hobbies. I found that people often did indoor hobbies, such as chess, knitting, and reading. Tristin Hoffman/Business Insider In Oregon, my experience hanging out with friends largely takes place outside: at the beach, on hikes, lying out in parks, or doing something sporty . I had a similarly outdoors-oriented social life growing up in San Diego. Among the Philadelphia friends and coworkers I met, indoor plans — book clubs, chess clubs, trivia, knitting, or drinks — came up more often. While they were great and I enjoyed the time with friends, I'm a busybody at heart — I felt myself getting antsy to move. It was costlier, too. A few hours at a bar a few times a week adds up. The days felt busier and more regimented. The city's tight living quarters made it feel like I had less agency to leave. Tristin Hoffman/Business Insider Compared with the slower pace I was used to in Eugene, life in Philadelphia — surrounded by constant honking, ambulance sirens, and people rushing — felt more hurried. It felt like everyone had their own rigid schedules, and I fell into pretty strict routines myself, both during the workweek and on weekends. The city's close quarters also made me feel cramped, and I realized I prefer smaller places with more room to spread out. Now that I'm back in Oregon, I love the open spaces, slower pace, and the ease my car brings to everyday life — especially the freedom to go to the mountains without turning it into a weekend project. events.title: I spent 10 hours flying Virgin Atlantic's upper class. My seat had its drawbacks, but the flight mostly won me over.
events.summary: Before my Virgin Atlantic flight, I hung out in the Delta One Lounge at LAX. Alesandra Dubin I've flown business class many times. Virgin Atlantic's version of it has never been my favorite. I don't love how its upper-class seats cannot smoothly transition from upright to lie-flat. That said, my flight had great food, top-tier service, and fun vibes that I really enjoyed. As soon as I learned what business-class life was like, I never wanted to go back. Now, my husband and I use credit-card points to get the experience whenever we can, especially on long-haul overnight flights . That's mainly because the lie-flat seat is an absolute game changer, and I was especially looking forward to it when my husband and I booked Virgin Atlantic upper class aboard a 787-9 Dreamliner from Los Angeles to London this summer. It's a leg and an airline I'd flown before, so I knew all the perks of this airline's version of business class. I also knew one thing I probably wouldn't love as much as the other posh details of the flying experience: the seat. Unlike most business-class seats I've experienced — I'm fortunate to have flown long-haul business class on about 10 different airlines — Virgin Atlantic's doesn't smoothly recline all the way from upright to lie-flat. Instead, it's a seat or a bed. When you're ready to sleep, you get up, and a flight attendant flips the seat over and makes it up with bedding. It's pretty seamless, but I still find the setup a bit cumbersome. I'd rather just be able to gradually recline into a comfortable lounging position. Nevertheless, I tried to head into this flight with an open mind. For this overnight flight, I had a window seat Our upper-class seat configuration wasn't my favorite, but it worked. Alesandra Dubin Our overnight flight from LAX to London Heathrow was scheduled to take 10 hours and 25 minutes. I was traveling with my husband while our kids were in summer camp (a rare grown-ups-only escape !), and we'd booked an upper-class seat configuration that was both interesting and slightly awkward for a couple. This part of the plane has a 1-1-1 configuration, and every seat has direct aisle access, which is a great perk. However, I was seated by the window, and my husband was across from me in the middle section of the partially herringbone-style cabin. I liked that I could see him from my seat, but we were foot-to-foot across the aisle, so our heads weren't actually close enough to have a conversation without one of us standing up. We could've been physically closer together, separated only by a short wall, if he'd been in a window seat behind or in front of me, but those seats weren't available when we booked. My seat had another quirk: Because of the seat position relative to the window, I had to turn and look backward to see out of it, which felt a bit strange and awkward. The seat was comfy, but I still wish it seamlessly flowed between upright and lie-flat positions The seat felt spacious, but it wasn't my favorite. Alesandra Dubin The seat itself was comfortable, with plenty of room (up to 22 inches wide, according to Virgin Atlantic). And once it was made up into a lie-flat bed, I found it plenty comfortable to sleep on. My issue wasn't with the seat's comfort so much as how it functioned. In most business-class seats I've flown, I can use the controls to find exactly the position I want: upright for eating or working, partially reclined for watching a movie, and fully flat when I'm ready to sleep. This setup did not offer that same range with ease. I wish I could've reclined from upright to flat more easily in this Virgin Atlantic seat. Alesandra Dubin The seat does recline — it adjusts between 17 and 42 degrees, according to Virgin Atlantic — but beyond that, getting it fully flat required me to get up. In the slightly inconvenient manual process, the padded back flips toward the footrest area. I appreciated that a flight attendant handled the seat conversion and added the bedding while I was in the bathroom, giving the whole process a hotel-like, service-oriented feel. However, I like to lounge somewhere between sitting and sleeping throughout a long flight, so I missed being able to gradually recline all the way down whenever I wanted to rest. I've encountered a similarly unconventional seat with only one other airline, and it's simply not my preference. The food and service felt top-tier I've enjoyed the meals I've had in Virgin Atlantic's upper class. Alesandra Dubin As a vegetarian, I find that airline meals can sometimes feel like an afterthought, but I've found Virgin Atlantic's upper-class options to be flavorful and thoughtfully presented. This time, I had a hearty tomato-based pasta for dinner. On past upper-class flights, I've had dishes like warm tofu rice bowls and vegetable gyozas, and the food has felt approachable and tasty rather than overly elaborate for the sake of seeming luxurious. The service has similarly struck the right balance for me: attentive but relaxed, which fits the airline's personality. Everything on board felt stylish and fun Virgin Atlantic's in-air bar for passengers flying upper class felt like a cool touch. Alesandra Dubin The seat may not be my favorite, but Virgin Atlantic's overall vibe is what sets the airline apart. Upper class felt polished without feeling stuffy at all. The cabin looked sleek, with distinctive purplish mood lighting and a playful personality overall. Even tiny details have character. The meal service included airplane-shaped salt-and-pepper shakers, which have become favorites among Virgin Atlantic flyers. The airline's upper class also has a social component that's unusual in commercial aviation. Rather than treating the cabin exclusively as a collection of individual seats, Virgin Atlantic incorporates spaces where passengers can get up, have a drink, or socialize. Yes, there was an actual bar at the back end of the upper-class section on this flight — and, of course, drinks and snacks were all included, as they would be at my seat. It was fun to see a cabin crew member pouring drinks at the bar on my way onto the plane, but I'm usually sleeping rather than chatting over drinks when I fly. Passengers may not be able to enjoy these for much longer, though — the airline has announced plans to remove its in-flight bars in the next few years to make room for more premium seats. All in all, I'd happily fly in Virgin Atlantic's upper class again For me, the seat style is a bit of a drawback. However, a flight experience is about much more than only the seat. Sure, business class is always a splurge — especially on long-haul flights — but this airline tends to offer good value for miles, in my experience.
