events.title: Trump says you're an 'enemy' of the White House if you don't support his AI rebrand
events.summary: Before President Donald Trump spoke of rebranding artificial intelligence, he frequently used the term. Here he is seen speaking at a tech-focused event in Washington in July 2025. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images President Donald Trump wants everyone to get on board with his AI rebrand. Trump threatened those who don't use the term super intelligence or the corresponding "SI" abbreviation. It remains to be seen how tech companies will respond. It's SI or else. President Donald Trump said on Thursday that anyone who doesn't use his preferred term of super intelligence (SI) will be considered an "enemy" of the White House. "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump's statement suggests the White House may punish companies or individuals who do not abide by its preferred speech, which would be a potential textbook First Amendment violation if enforced. The White House has moved to rebrand artificial intelligence , which Trump said suggests that the technology is "fake." While some companies, most notably Meta, which has a SuperIntelligence Labs, had super intelligence embedded in their branding before Trump's recent move, their descriptions were more about the future of artificial intelligence than an outright rejection of the terminology itself. After meeting with industry leaders in late September at the White House, Trump signed an executive order that required federal departments and agencies "to the maximum extent permitted by law" to use "'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, public communications, websites," among other official communications. The order did not apply to private-sector companies like OpenAI because the White House has no legal authority to enforce such a measure. Since Trump's statements and orders, at least one company has followed the White House's wishes. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that the space and technology company would rename its AI unit, SpaceXAI, to SpaceXSI. If Musk follows through on his promise, it would be the second such rebrand for what was originally known as xAI this year. In February, SpaceX announced that it was acquiring xAI, makers of the Grok chatbot, and rechristened the unit as SpaceXAI in July . As of Thursday afternoon, SpaceXAI's X account still said "SpaceXAI." It remains to be seen what other leading AI and tech companies will do. There was a bit of awkwardness after Trump made his wishes known on the same day of the highly anticipated AI lunch. During a White House panel discussion, Nvidia CEO Jensen Wang corrected himself when he said "AI" instead of "SI." In comments made with Trump standing just feet from him, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said the company "builds artificial intelligence" to help everyone. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently dismissed the possibility of renaming the company during an interview with Politico. "No plans to do that," he told the Politico Decoded podcast. "But we have been talking about super intelligence a lot and we will continue to talk about it." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump says U.S. will not attack Iran before midterm election
events.summary: Trump said the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm election, explicitly tying potential military action to Election Day. The more diplomatic tone comes as support for the war has waned among the American public and pushed gas prices higher during an election season dominated by affordability issues. The announcement Thursday reverses Trump’s stance from late Wednesday, when he said he did not want an Iran deal and reportedly weighed pre-election strikes. President Donald Trump said Thursday that the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm election , explicitly tying the timing of potential further military action to the domestic political calendar. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," Trump said in a post on Truth Social, adding that the U.S. was having "productive discussions" with Tehran. Trump's declaration came after he told reporters late Wednesday that his administration was considering renewed strikes against Tehran before the election, helping send oil prices higher amid fears of further escalation. Brent crude rose more than 4% Thursday to above $104 a barrel. Trump said the U.S. naval blockade of Iran would remain in place and reiterated that Tehran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon. It's a shift from his posture less than a day ago. At a campaign rally Wednesday night, Trump said a deal with Iran was "not really something that I wanted to do." The more diplomatic tone comes as voters are already casting midterm ballots and public support for the war has fallen. Just 31% of Americans supported U.S. military action against Iran in an August Reuters/Ipsos poll , down from 37% in March, while 83% expected the conflict to be prolonged. The war has helped push fuel costs higher, compounding Republicans' vulnerability on affordability as they fight to retain control of Congress. Poll after poll has ranked the cost of living among voters' top concerns heading into the Nov. 3 election. Gas prices have climbed roughly 40% from a year ago, according to AAA data. The national average stood at $4.36 a gallon Thursday, up from $2.98 just before war began in late February. The political fallout is showing up on the campaign trail. Numerous GOP candidates in competitive congressional races have tried to distance themselves from Trump, often on the Iran war. Inside the White House, the election calendar has reportedly loomed over the administration's Iran strategy for weeks. Reuters reported in September that top Trump aides were pushing to keep the war contained through the midterms to limit Republican losses, while leaving open heavier U.S. strikes after votes are tallied. Trump's latest statement does just that. Meanwhile, the U.S. is sending roughly 9,000 sailors and Marines and a third aircraft carrier to the region, a buildup that could put three U.S. carriers in the Middle East by late October, the Associated Press reported last week. The president also claimed Thursday that 22 million barrels of oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz overnight, with none coming from or going to Iran. CNBC has not independently verified that figure. Kpler data show about 11.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and petroleum products exited the strait during the week ended Tuesday, while total oil flows from the region stood at 20.4 million barrels per day. – CNBC's Spencer Kimball contributed to this report

events.title: Inflation on many everyday items was entirely due to tariffs, NY Fed says
events.summary: The cost of many everyday items would have declined without President Donald Trump's legally fraught tariff policy, according to a report from the New York Federal Reserve. Shoppers saw a 2.9 percentage point increase in inflation on a sample of 67 types of goods as of February due to tariffs imposed in 2025 and early 2026. Without the tariffs, the team found that prices for goods would have pulled back in that period. The cost of many everyday items would have declined last year and early this year without President Donald Trump 's tariffs, according to the New York Federal Reserve . The cost of 67 categories of goods was 2.9 percentage points higher as of February thanks to tariffs, according to a paper from a team of researchers at the central bank's New York arm. Without the levies, the team found that prices for the products they studied would have pulled back by almost 1%. The New York Fed's report offers the clearest evidence yet of the impact of Trump's tariffs — a core policy of his most recent campaign and second term in the White House — on consumers' wallets. Economists had widely expected his levies to push up prices, though the precise effects had been hard to estimate due to the changing nature of the policy and the lack of transparency on how companies set their prices. "The Trump administration has consistently maintained that the cost of tariffs will ultimately be borne by foreign exporters who rely on access to the American economy," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement to CNBC. The researchers didn't say which 67 types of goods they evaluated. For each percentage point increase in the average tariff, the team said that consumer goods prices were higher by roughly a quarter of a percent a year later. Annual price growth in the dozens of goods they tracked peaked at the start of 2026, according to the report. But consumers are still expected to pay elevated prices into 2027 as a result of the policy, it said. Roughly two-thirds of the tariff-related price impact has directly come from the levies themselves, according to the New York Fed's report. The remaining increase was driven by knock-on effects, such as U.S.-based companies that use imported parts and materials in their products. "Tariffs have a larger and more drawn-out impact on consumer prices than the direct effect alone would suggest," the study's three authors, Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise and David Weinstein, wrote. Trump argued that companies could absorb the increased cost from tariffs rather than pass them down to shoppers in the form of price hikes. The New York Fed team said that around 26% of last year's tariff increases ended up trickling into higher prices. The Supreme Court in February struck down many of Trump's tariffs, resulting in billions of dollars in refunds to retailers. The White House has vowed to push forward with levies through alternative measures, and products imported from many countries now often face tariffs of about 10%. In many cases, that is significantly less than what they were under the earlier round of tariffs.

events.title: Trump administration blocks tech companies from visa program
events.summary: The News The Trump administration on Thursday suspended more than a half-dozen tech companies, including Microsoft, from the program that allows permanent hiring of foreign workers — escalating its long-simmering clash with the tech industry over immigration. “The H1-B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers,” Vice President JD Vance, who helms the administration’s fraud task force, told reporters. “Unfortunately, the program has become rife with fraud.” The administration has tangled with tech companies since President Donald Trump returned to office over its interest in reining in H1-B visas for highly skilled workers. That tension has resulted in a partial pullback of some attempted policy shifts, such as May’s clarification of an announcement that H1-B holders would have to start applying for permanent residency from outside the US. The administration has also recently moved to charge more than $100,000 for a single H1-B visa. Thursday’s announcement formally bans Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and four other companies from the permanent labor certification process. Representatives for Adobe, Cognizant, and Infosys did not immediately return requests for comment. Microsoft said in statement that “we look forward to providing the Administration with additional information.” The company added that it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category. Notably, Trump plans to award a medal to the CEO of Microsoft later on Thursday. In addition, the administration announced it had served subpoenas for a new investigation into multiple universities over their use of J-1 visas for exchange students. Among the educational institutions targeted by the probe are Pitt, Yale, Harvard, Stanford, Brown, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and MIT, officials said at a press conference. “We will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research,” said the Labor Department’s inspector general, former Republican member of Congress Anthony D’Esposito. Know More Foreign workers made up almost a quarter of the US’ STEM workforce in 2023, according to the American Immigration Council . Businesses, which challenged the proposed H1-B fee in court, say they need visas to overcome worker shortages that stem in part from lagging workforce development . Thursday’s announcement marks a continuation of Vance’s focus on fraud heading into the midterms and 2028. The vice president has portrayed the issue as bipartisan — though Trump, when he announced the task force earlier this year, suggested it would focus “primarily” in blue states. Asked Thursday to explain his allegations of visa fraud, Vance pointed to “a couple of certifications” companies must make to receive the visas, including “that the person that you’re bringing in has a specialized, hyper-capable skill set.” “That’s clearly not the case if you’re just replacing one American worker with a foreign indentured servant and undercutting their wages in the process,” Vance said. “So the fraud is that they’re making representations when applying for this program that are fundamentally illegitimate and therefore ultimately illegal.” Notable Vance declined to directly address a Wall Street Journal report that US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle requested a donor pay off debt in exchange for access to government officials, though he told reporters he doesn’t “love that.”

Howland Capital Management, based in Boston, is CNBC's top-ranked firm for 2026. CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 methodology considers assets under management, years in business, regulatory and compliance records, firm size, and the number of investment advisors, among other factors. CNBC receives no compensation for placing advisory firms on the Financial Advisor 100 list. Many consumers face tough investing decisions amid rising inflation , the artificial intelligence boom and geopolitical uncertainty , among other factors that affect the stock and bond markets. An experienced financial advisor can help. But the best advisors do more than manage your portfolio . They can help craft a roadmap to meet competing goals such as saving for retirement , reducing your taxes , protecting your family , building a legacy and more. CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list ranks the country's best financial advisors and top financial advisory firms. Investors can use this list as a starting point — along with referrals — to find an expert who is well-suited for their family's needs. To make a list of prospective advisors, always verify credentials and check for complaints via the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority's BrokerCheck or the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission 's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure . Then you can interview your short list of candidates. CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list is determined through a blend of data analysis and editorial review. Firms do not apply or pay to be considered, and inclusion and ranking are based solely on the list's methodology. The list takes months to compile, with multiple steps and checks designed to ensure rigor and consistency. To prepare the 2026 list, CNBC worked with AccuPoint Solutions, a wealth management data and research firm specializing in advisor intelligence and industry analytics. The process started with 41,578 registered investment advisor firms, or RIAs, narrowed to 1,015 that met CNBC's requirements. These firms also passed a due diligence check, including any regulatory disclosures. To get more details, CNBC surveyed the finalists about their practices and fact-checked responses via publicly available resources. AccuPoint used CNBC's weighted criteria to rank the firms. Read more about the methodology below. For 2026, CNBC's top advisors collectively manage $329.7 billion. The firms have an average of 35 years in business. What is a fiduciary financial advisor? Finding the right financial advisor isn't easy, and there's a key question you should ask each prospect: Are you a fiduciary? A fiduciary financial advisor must act in the best interest of clients at all times, regardless of how it affects their compensation or profits. Certain financial advisors, such as RIAs, are bound by the fiduciary standard . By comparison, investment brokers must follow a suitability standard , which means recommendations must be appropriate but not always the best option for the client. What steps should you take when choosing a financial advisor? One of the first steps to finding the right financial advisor could be referrals from your colleagues, friends or family. You'll want to consider those candidates' credentials, including designations such as certified financial planner , or CFP; certified public accountant , or CPA; and chartered financial analyst , or CFA. You should also check each prospect for regulatory violations and customer complaints, known as "disclosures," via FINRA's BrokerCheck and the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure website. You can check state regulators for smaller firms. It's important to meet and interview prospective candidates before choosing a financial advisor. The CFP Board, which sets and enforces standards for CFP professionals, recommends 10 questions to narrow down your list: 1. What are your qualifications and credentials? 2. What services do you offer? 3. Will you have a fiduciary duty to me? 4. What is your approach to financial planning? 5. What types of clients do you typically work with? 6. Will you be the only advisor working with me? 7. How will I pay for your services? 8. How much do you typically charge? 9. Do others stand to gain from the financial advice you give me? 10. Have you ever been publicly disciplined for unethical or unlawful actions in your career?

events.title: CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach: 'There is real value in all of those relationships'

Howland Capital Management ranked No. 1 on CNBC's list of the top 100 financial advisors in the U.S. for 2026. Charlie Clapp, the firm's co-chair, said successful advising is about relationships above all else. Clapp understands the value of working together: He won an Olympic medal as part of the U.S. men's eight rowing team in 1984. Charlie Clapp, co-chair of Howland Capital Management — ranked No. 1 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 for 2026 — knows what it takes to get to the top of his field. In his home office is the silver medal he won in the men's eight rowing competition at the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. It has tarnished over time, a testament to years of being handled by clients and friends. He credits that accomplishment to hard work, discipline and the ability to pick yourself up after a setback and keep going. "If you look at it in a business sense, some of those same attributes spill over," Clapp said. More from CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors: CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor for 2026 takes a family-office approach CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 FAQ: Who is eligible and how rankings work Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Bessent says to adjust paycheck withholdings, but mistakes may trigger a tax bill But above all, "having a consistent group that you train with, race with, that's what allows you to achieve success," he said. "There is real value in all of those relationships." The firm, which was No. 7 on the 2025 list , landed at No. 1 this year after CNBC analyzed data from about 1,000 firms using a proprietary methodology that weighs factors including assets under management, industry experience and other key metrics. 'There is always going to be something that trips the world up' Howland, which started in 1967 as a family office based in Boston, maintains its tight-knit, family-office approach even as the number of clients has expanded to include over 400 families, foundations and small institutions after nearly 60 years in business. "A lot of what appealed to me when I first met Tony still rings true today," Clapp said of Weston "Tony" Howland III, the firm's co-chair and CEO and son of its founder. "We take care of families, we go to weddings, we go to funerals, we get to know our clients extraordinarily well." Together, Howland Capital Management has $4 billion under management and more than 500 accounts. With multigenerational financial goals in mind, a key focus of the firm's planning process is structuring assets through trusts that can benefit future generations. Taking a long-term view, often 10, 20 or even 30 years ahead, helps guide estate and wealth transfer decisions, Clapp said. About 65% of client assets are held in trusts, he said. Rather than trying to predict future tax law changes, the firm works within the current code. "You can guess where Congress will go, and it never works," he said. "We are dealing with the cards that are on the table." That strategy also helps the firm support clients during tumultuous times, Clapp said. "There is always going to be something that trips the world up," Clapp said. The first nine months of 2026 have been marked by inflation , war, tariffs and the Federal Reserve 's first rate hike since 2023, among other market-moving events. The key, he said, "is making sure you have a good, disciplined plan in place — that's what really lets you ride out the uncertainty." 'It's important that you are not reacting' Wall Street has been on a bumpy ride in recent weeks, with Treasury yields hitting multiyear highs as traders anticipate more Fed rate hikes due to persistent inflation. Still, Clapp remains largely unbothered by shifting Fed policy: "If the Fed chair is the Wizard of Oz, the only lever he has is the fed funds rate," he said. Clapp said the firm focuses on avoiding highly leveraged companies and floating-rate debt, instead favoring investments with dependable cash flows to support clients over the long term. TJX Companies, Inc. is a perfect example of a high-quality, long-term holding for Howland Capital Management, according to Clapp. Strong and consistent cash generation has enabled the retailer to increase its dividend and "provide for a nice 'annual raise' for our clients," he said. As a result, an investor who held the stock for 25 years now receives annual dividend income that represents a substantial return on their original investment. This position enabled a client to make a charitable gift of more than $100,000 earlier this year through the transfer of 700 shares that originally cost less than $1,800, Clapp said.

The move comes as the White House ramps up pressure on companies to hire more Americans. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” US Vice President JD Vance said at a news conference on Thursday. list 1 of 4 Trump administration suffers double legal setback over immigration rules list 2 of 4 US court blocks Trump plan to deport migrants to third countries list 3 of 4 Anti-South Asian ‘hate speech’ on X surges by 240%, US report finds list 4 of 4 Attorney General announces record number of cases to strip US citizenship Vance claimed that the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant laid off 6,000 American workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B foreign work visas and almost 3,000 permanent residencies known as green cards. “You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. Across the technology sector, there have been more than 131,000 layoffs in 2026 alone, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job cuts across the tech and startup industries. “When someone comes in, they are completely subordinate to that company. If they lose that job, they have to leave the country.” Microsoft pushed back on Vance’s claims in a blog post, saying that “80 percent of the visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.” “The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said in the post. Microsoft is No 5 among US employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No 1. Adobe did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling also said that several major information technology firms will be suspended from the programme as well. Among them are Indian tech giants Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services. The H-1B programme has long been a target of supporters of US President Donald Trump who say that the programme undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse. H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find US workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India. The Department of Labor also said it had uncovered $22bn worth of visa fraud. “Today we are protecting something far more valuable than any dollar amount. We are protecting the American worker,” Sonderling said. The news came hours before Trump was to honour Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. India-born Nadella was one of six business leaders to be awarded on Thursday. Five of the leaders were foreign-born, including Tesla boss Elon Musk and Google co-founder Sergey Brin. During the news conference, officials also announced a crackdown on alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine universities, including MIT, Harvard, Yale, Stanford and Cal State, amid allegations that they brought in international students to undercut US wages. A J-1 visa allows foreign nationals to enter the US temporarily for education or cultural programmes. Universities use these visas to bring in international PhD candidates or scholars. Vance claimed that when schools employ an American as a researcher, that person earns $20,000 more than someone brought in under a J-1 visa. Al Jazeera asked for data supporting this claim, but the White House did not respond. Microsoft’s stock slumped 1.5 percent on the heels of the news, while Adobe was up 2.1 percent in late day trading on Thursday.

US-based wafer-fab GlobalFoundries announced a $2 billion partnership with TSMC on Thursday to shore up American manufacturing of advanced semiconductors, like those used in AI datacenters. Under the multi-year deal , GloFo will produce silicon interposers for TSMC's chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) advanced packaging spec at its Malta, New York fab site. Silicon interposers are essential to the production of many multi-die chip assemblies like GPUs and AI accelerators. These interposers sit under the compute logic and memory and provide a higher speed and lower power path for communications between the chips than would be possible using conventional organic packaging. Basically every chip that employs high-bandwidth memory (HBM) today relies on some form of interposer or interconnect bridge to stitch everything together. GlobalFoundries' partnership with TSMC appears to target the former. Advanced packaging has become a major bottleneck for American chip manufacturing. Notably, when TSMC began producing Nvidia's Blackwell generation of GPUs in its Arizona chip plant last year , we noted that the final product would still need to be round tripped to Taiwan and back for final assembly. TSMC has contracted with Amkor, an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider, for CoWoS compatible packaging services in the US and has broken ground on its own advanced packaging facilities in Arizona. However, neither of these facilities is expected to come online until 2028 and 2029 respectively. GlobalFoundries, for its part, plans to add additional capacity at its Malta plant to meet demand, but volume production won't begin until the first half of 2028 at the earliest. The partnership is expected to last five years with the option to extend as needed. While CoWoS packaging remains a bottleneck for America's domestic chipmaking ambitions, it's not the only option, just the most popular. Intel Foundry already offers both leading edge process and advanced packaging tech comparable to TSMC's CoWoS offerings. What's more, this tech is compatible with silicon produced at TSMC fabs. Intel routinely employs chips made by TSMC but packaged in its facilities. Doing so does require designing parts for Intel's packaging, but if making chips in America did become a priority, customers wouldn't necessarily have to wait for TSMC and Amkor's facilities to come online. ® High-severity Nvidia bug could crash GPU monitoring on exposed servers The GPU giant released a fix for the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-47483 The VMware exit is a protection upgrade PARTNER CONTENT: VergeIO says an exit is also an opportunity Gremlin now uses AI to break distributed systems faster If there's one thing AI can do well, it's failing more quickly than the average SRE Brighter isn't better and more is less.

events.title: FTC advancing on its AI safety probe
events.summary: The News The Federal Trade Commission is close to sending investigative demands to frontier AI companies, a senior agency official told Semafor — a sign that its AI probe is moving forward after its unusual disclosure to the public. The FTC’s planned AI inquiry emerged in a New York Post story as the White House raced to project seriousness about the rise of tech that President Donald Trump has made clear he wants to treat with a light touch. Less than 24 hours before news of the FTC probe, the agency’s chair appeared alongside Trump and AI CEOs to announce a nonbinding accord that pledged industry self-regulation. It’s rare for the FTC to reveal an investigation before it sends civil investigative demands, which have subpoena-like force. And it’s even less typical to do so well before any decision has been made about a potential lawsuit or settlement. The leak of the AI probe raised the question of whether FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson — who was since appointed to Trump’s AI task force — plans an in-depth inquiry or a probe that’s more designed to convey the appearance of serious action ahead of the midterms. Yet the senior FTC official reiterated to Semafor that it plans a significant probe, revealing it to the media due to public health and safety concerns about AI systems. The CIDs being sent to AI companies are dozens of questions long, according to the official, encompassing what the companies have said about the dangers of their products and other questions around consumer harm. While two people with knowledge of the matter told Semafor that career FTC staff learned from the press — not agency leadership — about the AI investigation, the senior official disputed that. Career staff attorneys in the Bureau of Consumer Protection are drafting the CIDs, the senior FTC official said. “Career staff who do not leak to the media are working hard every day on issues of importance to the American people, including” the AI inquiry, the official added. Know More One well-known exception to the FTC’s practice of not publicizing investigations was its revelation of an inquiry into Meta’s privacy practices after the 2018 Cambridge Analytica data release scandal, a move that responded to overwhelming public interest. A similar step occurred in 2017, when the agency confirmed it was investigating Equifax after a massive data breach. One former FTC official told Semafor that the agency tries not to “publicize investigations in advance, because you don’t want people to prejudge the investigation. The simple fact that there is an existing investigation will impact a company’s stock price and operations.” Yet William Kovacic, a former Republican FTC chair, said confirming an investigation in the press is “unusual,” but not without precedent and “not in any sense improper.” “You don’t do this unless you want to make clear to the larger public that you’re looking at a particular issue,” he said. The announcement, which may also target independent AI evaluator METR, aligned with Trump advisers’ approach to AI safety: Apply the laws on the books without adding new regulatory requirements. That differs wildly from what many bipartisan members of Congress, state regulators, the public and even AI companies have said they want: new rules and restrictions for AI as the technology reaches alarming capabilities. Ferguson has said that he does not consider the agency to be an AI regulator . The Trump administration’s 2025 AI Action Plan called for a review of all FTC investigations commenced under former President Joe Biden to “ensure they do not advance theories of liability that unduly burden AI innovation” and even modify existing orders that may “unduly burden AI innovation.” The AI industry appears unsure about where Ferguson is heading: “We’re trying to find out more about that,” OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane said in an interview last week when asked about the investigation. Anthropic, also named in the initial report, declined to comment. METR didn’t respond to a request for comment. Room for Disagreement Former FTC chair Lina Khan told ABC on Sunday that she doubts Ferguson is serious: “You have on the one hand, these CEOs of these AI companies wining and dining at the White House, the idea that the next morning they’re going to get some type of credible subpoena from the same administration I think just strains credulity.” Asked about Khan’s remarks, Kovacic said: “When you’ve tied your destiny so close to the White House, you’re inevitably going to raise questions about the sincerity and the aggressiveness of the inquiry … The only way to dispel those concerns is to carry out a serious inquiry and explain what you’re doing along the way.” Ashley’s view Ferguson is wearing very different hats here, and we are seeing him embody the resulting tension in real time. As Trump embraces a hands-off approach to AI growth, he’s made clear by his task force participation that he aligns with the president. But he’s also the country’s top consumer protection official, and he has shown he can go after tech when he wants to. On the antitrust side, he’s taken Meta to court and will face Amazon in court next year ; he also previously asked AI companies about kids’ chatbot practices; it’s not clear what will come of that. With AI safety is very much on the public’s mind ahead of Election Day, we might be seeing the Trump administration’s best recipe to assuage voters for the rest of the year: an investigation alongside a pledge for self-regulation. That investigation, of course, may not result in much. These probes can take a long time, and AI companies are a long way from any finding of wrongdoing.

events.title: ‘Everybody knows you’re out of touch’: Palantir CEO Alex Karp says his own exec told him to stop hyping Foundry
events.summary: Alex Karp says one of his top executives once told him to stop talking about how big Foundry would get. “Please stop talking to Palantirians about how big Foundry is going to be,” Karp recalled Ted Mabrey saying. “It’s depressing, and everybody knows you’re out of touch.” Karp spoke Thursday with Zeta Global CEO David Steinberg at Zeta Live ’26 , Zeta’s annual AI marketing conference. The Palantir CEO said Mabrey, who now runs the company’s commercial business, told him the constant hype was coming off a tad aggressive for employees who had to hear him boast about Foundry constantly. The idea stuck—albeit for a little bit: “I had stopped talking to people for like six months,” Karp said. Instead, the CEO said he has a particular way of making decisions, and that often comes at odds with what people think is possible. “I have an esthetic idea of what could work and what won’t work,” Karp said. “About once a month, I have some idea that I think is important, and then I know it’s important. Everyone tells me we can never do that.” ‘Tell me something I want to hear’ He said he relies on colleagues he has worked with for years to tell him the truth, and that those relationships are “very harsh.” “In fact, I often tell them, ‘Can you tell me something I want to hear, please?'” he added. Foundry, Palantir’s platform for pulling a company’s data into one place and controlling who can see it, is now at the center of its fastest-growing business. In the second quarter, U.S. commercial revenue grew 149% year over year to $764 million, according to the company’s earnings release . Palantir raised its full-year U.S. commercial revenue guidance to more than $3.4 billion, a growth rate of at least 134%. After those results, Karp told investors “for the first time people believe us.” Zeta is one of the companies building on it. In June, the two firms announced a deal under which Zeta’s Data Cloud will be rebuilt on Palantir’s Foundry. Steinberg told Adweek the seven-year partnership would bring in “over $100 million a year in sales” within “the next year or so.” ‘Where’s the parasite?’ During the talk, Karp explained that getting Palantir to the point where it is now took plenty of convincing, simply because investors didn’t get the business. He said Palantir struggled to raise money in its early years because it refused to build software the way investors wanted. “Normal software is built to force you to adopt something that’s parasitic,” he said. “They take every one of those things, turn it into a commodity, and sell it to everyone else.” According to Karp, VCs wanted to hear that clients would be unhappy but couldn’t leave. “‘Sticky’ is a metaphor for parasitic,” he said. “I get your data. I get it into something you can’t get rid of. The thing turns into something I can sell to everybody else.” So when he pitched making special operators “more lethal” and bringing them home, Karp said, investors asked, “But where’s the parasite?” He said Palantir was also mocked for sending engineers to work inside client companies, a model it calls forward-deployed engineering. It has since become one of the fastest-growing jobs in Silicon Valley . Steinberg said Zeta has copied it. “We pivoted a huge part of our business to follow you guys on this because it’s so freaking efficient,” he said. Karp said Palantir has about 4,500 employees and is “not everyone’s cup of tea.” Some of its best references, he said, come from former staff who left after “another crazy lecture from Karp” and later wanted to come back. In March, Mabrey publicly called on “former hobbits” to return to “the Shire,” making more references to its namesake from the Lord of the Rings . Second-rate AI is costing businesses Also during the AI-focused lecture, Karp argued the tech has changed what poor execution costs a business. In the past, a second-rate software rollout cost a company time and money but rarely sank it, since a firm with a strong moat could get by. He used defense as an example. A German government will buy a German company’s missile “even if it’s B minus because it flies and it’s German,” he said. But a missile that can’t hit targets against Russian weapons is no longer good enough, and getting it there now depends on an AI application layer. “Your B-minus missile is a triple-plus with this, and your A-plus missile is useless,” he said. “So that’s just binary.” He said the same logic applies to every company. Asked what one decision the CEOs in the room should make, Karp told them to identify what makes their business special, get full visibility from the factory floor to the cost of goods, and use AI to strengthen it without letting a model company or a rival learn how it works. “If your person down the street gets it right, even if they’re inferior to you, just like the missile, they will outperform you,” Karp said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Harvey Nichols’ Birmingham store to close in January
events.summary: Closure will cost at least 60 jobs, while Leeds and Bristol outlets to be converted to Flannels brand Harvey Nichols’ Birmingham store is to close in January, with the loss of at least 60 jobs, while its Leeds and Bristol outlets will be converted to the Flannels brand in a shake-up under Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group . The owner of Sports Direct bought the department store chain , whose headquarters are at the Knightsbridge site in London, for £43m on the day it was put into administration in mid-August. About 1,000 of the group’s 1,200 jobs and six UK stores were saved in that deal. Harvey Nichols’ Oxo Tower restaurant was sold to a separate buyer, saving 130 jobs. The chain’s branches in London, Edinburgh, Birmingham , Leeds and Manchester and Bristol are accompanied by outlets in Riyadh, Dubai, Doha, Kuwait and two in Hong Kong. A further store in Dublin was closed by administrators in September. The Harvey Nichols Group owed about £100m to unsecured creditors at the time of its administration, including dozens of brands from Canada Goose to Victoria Beckham. Ashley previously said he would keep Harvey Nichols’ Knightsbridge and Edinburgh stores, but rebrand the four other UK stores – in Birmingham, Leeds, Manchester and Bristol – as House of Fraser or Flannels. It has now emerged that Frasers plans to close the Birmingham store, which opened 25 years ago, with staff informed earlier this week, as first reported by the fashion trade journal Drapers. Frasers will rebrand Leeds and Bristol to Flannels, while the future for the Manchester, Edinburgh and London Harvey Nichols stores is unclear. Michael Murray, the chief executive of Frasers Group, recently said in a statement about the group’s luxury division: “Our ambition is clear: to continue scaling Frasers Group Luxury globally through organic expansion, acquisitions and strategic investments, creating long-term value for our brand partners, customers and the group.” Ashley has bought a series of struggling premium brands in recent years after starting out with a single sports shop. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Frasers bought the House of Fraser department store chain out of administration in 2018 and has since closed about 40 of its 60 stores. It has been building its interests in luxury fashion with the Flannels chain and large stakes in brands such as the British handbag maker Mulberry. The group recently celebrated lifting its stake in the German label Hugo Boss to 48%, just short of taking full control, despite opposition from the company’s board. Frasers did not respond to a request for comment.

events.title: Everything we know about the suspected plague case in Russia so far
events.summary: This undated photo released in 2019 by the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, shows the institute workers in a lab. The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East via AP On October 2, an Irkutsk lab employee died from pneumonia. There's confusion over what illness the woman died from, with conflicting reports out of the region. The World Health Organization says the US is at "very low risk" of being exposed to the plague. After a technician at an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia died, Russian officials are attempting to calm global concerns. Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, died on October 2 after being hospitalized days earlier for pneumonia in Shelekhov, a nearby town . The World Health Organization told the Associated Press on October 6 that the plague presents a "very low" risk to the broader European region. That doesn't mean we know everything — or really, much of anything — as of now. While there's no confirmation of a plague outbreak so far, conflicting reports about how Shipilova got infected, whether she was infected at work, and Russia's current safety protocols have given some medical experts pause. On October 7, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organization had requested more information from Russian health authorities. "It's an odd situation that needs more transparency and requires more information for clarity," Dr. Nahid Bhadelia, the founding director of the Boston University Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases, told Business Insider. Here's everything we know so far. What happened to Darya Shipilova? Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, said that Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology." A friend told CNN that she died on October 2. WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said Wednesday that the health agency doesn't know how Shipilova and urged Russian officials to provide more information. People of Baikal , an independent regional news outlet, reported that Shipilova was "deeply anxious about ever infecting anyone if something happened," according to one of her colleagues at the institute. Other colleagues called her "responsible" and described the anti-plague institute as "a serious facility" in terms of safety measures. Did she die of pneumonic plague? Reports from Russian exiled publications — ones forced to operate outside Russia or use decentralized reporting methods — speculate whether Shipilova died from the pneumonic plague. The Moscow Times , an independent publication located in Amsterdam, reported unconfirmed claims that Shipilova may have broken a test tube containing plague bacteria at the institute before she fell ill. It also reported, citing Russian Telegram channel Mash, that she was hospitalized with pneumonia symptoms and placed on a ventilator before her death. A maintenance worker walks out of the headquarters of Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor in Moscow on October 5, 2026. (Photo by Igor IVANKO / AFP via Getty Images) Igor IVANKO / AFP via Getty Images Why has Shipilova's case raised alarm? Reports from Russian state media and independent publications have often clashed, leading to more questions than answers. "The scenario, to me, doesn't fit together," Bhadelia said. If the reports of a broken test tube were true, an anti-plague institute should have several safety measures in place, such as protective equipment, ventilation, and clear treatment protocols. "She needs to have broken a test tube, have a breach in her personal protective equipment, not reported the incident, not gotten the antibiotic prophylaxis, just gone home under no one's observation, shown up at a local district hospital, and exposed 200 people," Bhadelia added. That explanation, however, is at odds with another report from the People of Baikal. Rospotrebnadzor said authorities identified and monitored 197 people who had contact with Shipilova. By October 8, the agency said it had completed the health checks, and nearly 5,000 laboratory tests found no dangerous pathogens. It had previously reported two COVID-19 cases and two rhinovirus cases among those tested. "It could be that we just don't have the perfect information, that there might be some media sensationalism in the regional media, or there may be something else going on that we don't know," Bhadelia said. Still, the current risk is nowhere near a COVID-19-level threat. What is pneumonic plague — and how does it spread? Yersinia pestis, or plague , is a bacterial infection that progresses very quickly, Bhadelia said. Patients with pneumonic plague can sometimes develop symptoms in under 24 hours. It can be fatal if left untreated. Luckily, when caught early, treatment is also pretty straightforward: A course of antibiotics. In July 2025, an Arizona man contracted pneumonic plague from two ill cats. He was medically evaluated after two days of abdominal pain, chest pain, and dry cough. He died eight hours after admission. However, all 46 people exposed to him recovered after taking antibiotics. Bhadelia said it points to one of the biggest mysteries of the Russia case so far: If Shipilova was reportedly experienced, knew she was exposed, and reported it, why wouldn't she be under quarantine and quickly treated with medication? "Early identification and post-exposure prophylaxis is one of the ways that this could be avoided," she said. Is there any risk to people in the US? The WHO says the risk outside Russia is "very low," and there is no evidence of cases in the US or beyond the Irkutsk area. Still, US officials are seeking more information. At a press conference in Iceland on October 6, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, "It's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world." President Donald Trump also said he had expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of pneumonic plague, but the Kremlin said a call hadn't been scheduled yet. When asked if he thought the incident was somehow connected to Russia developing a bioweapon, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, "We hope not," and "we're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so." President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House on October 05, 2026, in Washington, DC. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images What we're missing from Russia Bhadelia, who is also the founding director of the Biothreats Emergence, Analysis, and Communications Network, said the organization is trying to provide the most up-to-date information on the pneumonic plague in Russia. It's not easy. For one, under international law, Russia is required to report any suspected global public health emergency to the WHO within 24 hours. events.title: Treasury sanctions 17 tankers linked to Iran's 'shadow fleet' in economic pressure campaign
events.summary: The U.S. Treasury Department is sanctioning 17 additional vessels it says are connected to Iran's "shadow fleet" used to transport oil and gas out of the country, as Washington tries to choke Tehran's economy to end the war that began over seven months ago. The new sanctions are part of "Operation Economic Outcast," the name given to the U.S. pressure campaign against Iran. The new designations are aimed at further limiting Iran's ability to transport and profit from petroleum and petrochemicals. The new sanctions are part of " Operation Economic Outcast ," the name given to the U.S. pressure campaign against Iran. The new designations are aimed at further limiting Iran's ability to transport and profit from petroleum and petrochemicals. "Treasury is starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime's oil sales," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "No enabler of Iranian sanctions evasion is safe from the full force of Treasury's authorities." Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' The new vessels being sanctioned are registered under more than a dozen jurisdictions, and Treasury said in a press release they are responsible for the transport of millions of barrels of Iranian crude, petroleum and petrochemical products. The U.S. has long said Iran uses illicit oil revenues to fund its regime and related terror proxies and hopes to cripple Tehran's economy by stemming that revenue. All the vessels targeted by the sanctions are newly designated. And though the specific action announced Thursday is not expected to cause massive changes in Iran's economy on its own, Treasury said it is targeting the "remnants" of Iran's shadow fleet to complement existing sanctions aimed at limiting Iran's ability to attack vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and sustain its regime. The vessels targeted include the Vanuatu-flagged TINA 5 , which Treasury says transported over 1.5 million barrels of Iranian crude in August; the Comoros-flagged LPG tanker SOGL , which Treasury says has moved more than two million barrels of Iranian propane and butane since September 2025; and the Cameroon-flagged crude oil tanker SHENZHEN , which Treasury says has moved more than 3.5 million barrels of Iranian crude oil since November 2025. A Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading oil due to the ongoing U.S. blockade of the country's ports. Kpler data says Tehran has not loaded any crude oil for export since Aug. 25. The U.S. war with Iran has greatly disrupted the global economy, whipsawing oil and gas prices as Iran has sought to hold the Strait of Hormuz shut. The channel is one of the most crucial gateways for moving oil and gas out of the Gulf region. The war has also caused gasoline prices to spike in the U.S. ahead of November's midterm election. The national average for gasoline on Thursday was $4.36 per gallon, according to AAA . — CNBC's Spencer Kimball contributed to this report.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters If there's one thing AI can do well, it's failing more quickly than the average SRE Shai-Hulud worm makes jump to AI infrastructure with Tensorlake compromise 3 hours ago Argonne scientists create chatty X-ray microscope that zooms in where you tell it to 23 hours ago Get rid of Apple's AI bloatware and reclaim 12 GB of storage with this open source tool 3 days ago OpenAI to flood your eyeballs with visual ads 3 days ago Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it 3 days ago What better way to find out what your system can take than by breaking it? Popularized by Netflix more than a decade ago, chaos testing is the practice of deliberately introducing controlled failures into working systems to test their resilience. Now, a startup that built its business around this practice is using AI to automate more of the testing and troubleshooting process. Gremlin’s Foresight AI , a new add-on to its current “chaos engineering” services, autonomously breaks software infrastructure to uncover hidden bugs before they pop up in production. Chaos engineering can be deliciously dangerous for an engineer: Turn off a random server, load balancer or even an entire region of a cloud deployment, then observe how well the rest of the system tries to keep serving customers. If it does, job well done. If it's borked, more reliability work is afoot. Kolton Andrus , one of the Netflix engineers who did chaos engineering at the streaming service, founded Gremlin to bring fault injection to enterprises, along with business-friendly accoutrements such as scoring, executive reporting, and organizational accountability tools. Adding AI into the mix speeds the process considerably, Andrus told The Register , by automating many of the preparatory and post-testing tasks that used to be done by hand. AIOps services are nothing new for the site reliability engineer (SRE), but most of these tools diagnose issues only after the system has already crashed. "A lot of AI solutions are, 'Hey, we took a guess. Here you go. Good luck,'” Andrus said. Instead, Gremlin purposefully tips over the system and then offers expert advice on how to prevent that from happening again. To use Gremlin, the user installs agents on their system that can inject latency, kill pods, or max out memory. A Gremlin cloud service then observes the subsequent telemetry alerts for telltale signs of systemic weakness. Gremlin’s secret sauce is its Failure Atlas, a repository of millions of chaos engineering experiments that the company conducted over the past decade on “tens of thousands of systems,” Andrus said. Gremlin developed a harness that yokes the LLM to the Failure Atlas, allowing it to generate more technically grounded answers about what went wrong, rather than simply drawing on its own collection of random information found on the Internet, the company asserts. Gremlin uses a variety of closed and open LLMs for the job, depending on which one is working best at the time. The Atlas keeps the LLM on point, minimizing hallucinations, Andrus said. Not creating problems, just pointing them out Gremlin’s existing guardrails are built around the enterprise’s own access permissions and other security precautions to keep the “blast radius” (company’s words) to a minimum (if the blast isn’t contained at all, well, that’s an access control issue right there). Once a system failure is induced, Foresight AI determines the root cause, generates code or the configuration change it thinks will fix the issue, and then can either apply the solution, or prepare a report for an SRE to read. It’s basically an agentic loop of test-and-replace – keeping humans in the loop at critical junctures – that runs until the failure is no longer induced. Gremlin’s current user base tends to be larger compute-heavy enterprises, many specializing in financial services, retail and enterprise SaaS, Andrus said.

events.title: Plans to shut Marston's Brewery in Burton revealed
events.summary: Marston's Brewery, its history and legacy in the town were "iconic", Carlsberg Britvic said Published 8 October 2026, 15:03 BST Marston's Brewery could close in Burton-upon-Trent, under plans revealed by its owners. Carlsberg Britvic said it was proposing to shut the facility together with its primary logistics operation based at that site next summer. About 310 people are affected. Burton-upon-Trent's connections with the brewing industry date back centuries, with the firm describing its own history and legacy in the town as "iconic". However, it said the "stark reality" was that UK cask ale volumes had more than halved in less than a decade and "this trend looks set to continue across the UK". The company said "priority brands" including Hobgoblin, McEwan's and Brooklyn were expected to remain in its portfolio, but it is unclear where they will be brewed. Other, smaller brands could find a home under specialist or local brewers, the firm said. Some have described Burton as the "beer capital of England", and at its height more than 30 breweries once operated from there. The Staffordshire town's connection with beer dates back to the 11th Century when monks first started brewing, and Marston's own links to Burton date back more than 200 years. Camra chairman Ash Corbett-Collins said the announcement was "an absolute disgrace" Camra chairman Ash Corbett-Collins, who grew up in Burton, said statements from Carlsberg about understanding the importance of the brewery to the town "come far too little too late for most people". "This announcement is an absolute disgrace, and the latest in a string of actions that show how little they care about our brewing heritage or the nation's drinkers." But he agreed "with Carlsberg on one thing", adding the "time is right to think about alternative, independent, brewers who are willing to become custodians of Carlsberg's cask brands". Carlsberg Britvic said it told colleagues and trade union partners the news earlier on Thursday. CEO Paul Davies said the proposal was "by no means a reflection on any of our people, and every effort will be made to help them through this period of uncertainty". He added Marston's Brewery and the primary logistics operation were expected to continue to operate "during the transition period, while the company works through the detail of the consultation". "As and when key decisions are taken over the coming months, we will share further information with the industry, but always with our colleagues first." Carlsberg Britvic said it was important to ensure the firm's portfolio was focused "where consumers are today" Davies said it was important to ensure the firm's portfolio was focused "where consumers are today, and where customer demand is growing". He added: "That said, smaller ale brands are much loved by select consumers, and we will do everything we can to ensure they thrive under more specialist or local ownership in the future." It is not the first big brewing firm to move operations in the West Midlands. Banks's Brewery in Wolverhampton ended operations in 2025, with production moving to Burton. Then prime minister David Cameron gave US president Barak Obama a crate of Hobgoblin at the G20 summit in Toronto in 2010 The brewery opened in 1875, but in 2024 Carlsberg Marston's Brewing Company (CMBC) announced it would close as part of a company restructuring. That year, Carlsberg acquired Marston's PLC's remaining 40% shareholding in CMBC, giving Carlsberg full ownership of the brewing business, including Marston's Brewery and its portfolio of beer brands. Hospitality firm Marston's PLC is now a completely separate operation. It runs more than 1,300 pubs across the UK from its base in Wolverhampton and is unaffected by Thursday's news. Burton beer is known for its earthy, eggy smell - known in brewing circles as "Burton snatch" - a sure sign of the ale's quality and provenance. This is created by the water trickling through unusually thick bands of gypsum under the town, before resting in underground aquifers. Staffordshire County Council's leader, Reform's Martin Murray, said British beer was famous across the world and over the years much of that had come out of Burton. "For us to lose that heritage personally saddened me greatly," he said. The leader of the opposition at the authority, Conservative Philip White, said the "decision means Marston's Pedigree and Bass Ale will no longer be brewed in Burton". He added: "We must do everything we can to try and reverse this decision and look after all of the workers and their families." events.title: Senegal-Morocco AFCON title decision within days, says CAS
events.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport to rule within days on appeal against decision to strip Senegal of AFCON title. A speedy resolution to Senegal’s appeal after being stripped of the Africa Cup ⁠of Nations (AFCON) title has ⁠been promised by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), who heard arguments on Thursday and said it will have a decision in days. Senegal are contesting the Confederation of African Football’s (CAF) ⁠decision to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal beating the hosts 1-0 after extra time in January’s final in Rabat. list 1 of 3 Man City must ‘stick together’ after Premier League charges, says Haaland list 2 of 3 ‘Utmost respect’: Ronaldo pays tribute to Messi after Argentina farewell list 3 of 3 ‘He is our idol:’ Why Lionel Messi means so much to fans in India Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes after a penalty was awarded against them late ⁠in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play. Morocco failed to convert the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal scored the winner to secure victory. However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal ‌had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to Morocco . Senegal quickly followed with an appeal to sport’s highest court, CAS, which was lodged on March 25 but heard on Thursday . “I know it’s a long wait for the fans a few months after the final between Senegal and Morocco,” said CAS Director General Matthieu Reeb. “The timetable and the procedural calendar were established with the agreement of the parties involved in this case. So ⁠everybody knew about the timeline, and our objective as CAS, as the ⁠last instance authority, is to provide a reasoned award as soon as possible after the hearing today,” he told reporters. The long-running saga over the winner of this year’s Africa Cup of Nations title will be concluded within days, although Reeb did not ⁠give a definite date. “I expect the decision to come not today, not tomorrow, but a few days later. The facts are set, are clear, and ⁠the discussions will be on some procedural issues and legal ⁠aspects,” he added. The CAS panel, presided over by French sports law expert Gerald Simon with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based lawyer and professor of law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas, heard the pleadings of the parties ‌who were represented by their lawyers, with the hearing completed on Thursday. Morocco’s delegation did not speak to the media. Senegal General Secretary Abdoulaye Sow said they were confident. “But the important thing is that sports law ‌is ‌upheld, and that this particular match is put to bed, for the sake of dignity and for Africa,” Sow told reporters outside the hearing, which was held behind closed doors.

events.title: MoD has objected to four windfarms in past year over radar interference fears
events.summary: Complaints risks putting defence ministry on collision course with Department for Energy Security and Net Zero The Ministry of Defence has objected to at least four planned windfarms in the past year over fears the spinning blades could cause “unacceptable interference” with radars used to detect military aircraft. MoD officials raised concerns in late June over plans for an onshore windfarm in County Durham that could result in aircraft “not being detected” within an RAF Low Flying Area, according to a letter to Britain’s planning authority. The objection to the planned Hope Moor project, which could see 23 turbines built to heights of 200m, is understood to be the latest of at least four objections made against a planned windfarm on national security grounds in the last year. The complaint risks putting the MoD on a collision course with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which ended a decade-long block on onshore wind developments in England when Labour came to power in 2024 after it was put in place by the Conservatives almost 10 years earlier. The government aims to double the UK’s onshore wind power capacity by 2030, and has designated Hope Moor a nationally significant project whose fate will be decided upon by the energy secretary. The MoD has also warned against plans to build an onshore windfarm of six turbines at Burton Agnes, near Driffield in the East Yorkshire Wolds, and of the “unmanageable” risk of building a 13-turbine windfarm near the Scottish borders. Meanwhile, plans for a far larger offshore windfarm in the Irish Sea have also raised concern within the ministry on the grounds that the proposed 87-turbine array could interfere with aviation radar systems at the Warton Aerodrome base in Lancashire, on the west coast of the UK. The MoD has a long history of objecting to windfarm developments, but industry sources note that the precautionary concerns do not usually rule out development. The “well-trodden path to the negotiating table” usually leads to minor adjustments to the size or height of the turbines, which means they can move ahead, they said. However, the ministry’s “routine” interventions are often used by those opposed to windfarms to support their campaigns, the sources added. Hope Moor is one of four windfarms under fire from the “Not One Moor” campaign , led by former England cricketer Lord Botham. Others include the Scout Moor windfarm in Lancashire, the Walshaw Moor windfarm in West Yorkshire and Ray Fell windfarm in Northumberland. Angus Thompson, a Conservative councillor in North Yorkshire, said: “The MoD’s stark warning is the nail in the coffin for this scheme … This hopeless project should be abandoned without delay.” Alexandre Davies, the head of aviation at trade group Renewable UK, said the industry “works closely” to find solutions to radar issues, “and has done so for many years” to “deliver projects faster”. A DESNZ spokesperson said: “We work closely with the Ministry of Defence. All onshore wind projects are subject to a rigorous planning process in which defence and security, the views of the local community and impacts on the environment are considered.” The MoD was approached for comment.

events.title: The military shrank the MRE for a future fight. Now it's deploying the new food rations with troops on the ground.
events.summary: A Marine eats a field ration during a training event in Japan last year. LCpl Weston Brown/US Marine Corps Marines are deploying a new combat ration built for the first days of war. C-CARs replace three MREs with one lighter daily ration for mobile operations. Less food weight means more room for gear and fewer early resupply missions. Marines are deploying with a new combat ration — that is, stuff to eat — built for the first days of war After entering service last year, the Close Combat Assault Ration, or C-CAR, is now deploying with frontline Marine units. The new ration condenses what would normally be three Meal, Ready-to-Eat packets into a single daily package, reducing the weight troops carry to free space for ammunition, batteries, and other mission-essential gear. The Defense Logistics Agency, which manages and develops the rations, told Business Insider that the C-CAR is intended for use during the first 72 hours of a conflict, when troops need a lighter, less bulky alternative to traditional MREs. Carrying less food gives Marines more room. It reduces the need for risky resupply missions during the first few days of a conflict, Capt. Matt Burdick, a logistics officer with the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit , told Business Insider. A soldier holds a Close Combat Assault Ration. US Army The 13th MEU recently deployed to the Middle East with the new rations after they entered service last year. Business Insider spent three days on the USS Makin Island with the 13th MEU off the coast of California this summer as they prepared for their deployment. Unlike traditional MREs, which are designed to be heated and eaten during longer pauses, C-CARs are built for troops on the move, Burdick said. Meals come in squeeze pouches that can be eaten without heating or utensils, eliminating the need for water to prepare them (though most service members rarely heat MREs). There are just three menu options— spaghetti, chicken burrito bowl, and beef stew. Troops have frequently stripped MREs ahead of training, throwing away unwanted extras or heavier food packets to pack more compactly and carry less weight. The C-CAR, Burdick said, arrives in a more bare-bones fashion. An Army display showing military rations, including the new Close Combat Assault Ration, third from left. The CCAR is smaller and lighter than its predecessor, the First Strike Ration, second from left. Katie Lange/Defense Department Burdick said his unit first encountered the rations during an exercise last year— because each of the nearly 300 Marines he was responsible for feeding carried enough food from the outset, logisticians conducted fewer resupply missions , reducing both the supply burden and its signature in the field, he explained. The new ration won't replace the MRE, which Burdick said is designed to be distributed at scale and for longer-term operations, though it does replace the older "First Strike Ration," which was also meant to provide troops more food in a smaller package. The rations remain in the early stages of fielding, Burdick said, with Marines using them alongside traditional MREs as the Corps gathers feedback from units to guide future ration development. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Credential-stealing malware detected within minutes of npm release, but impact remains unknown Gremlin now uses AI to break distributed systems faster 2 hours ago Argonne scientists create chatty X-ray microscope that zooms in where you tell it to 23 hours ago Wikimedia Foundation comes forward as latest OpenAI agent assault victim 2 days ago Get rid of Apple's AI bloatware and reclaim 12 GB of storage with this open source tool 3 days ago OpenAI to flood your eyeballs with visual ads 3 days ago The credential-hijacking Shai-Hulud worm has struck again, this time burrowing its way into a popular AI agent platform SDK. Multiple security researchers reported Thursday that they had detected Shai-Hulud infection in a recent release of the npm package for version 0.5.144 of Tensorlake’s SDK. That package has somewhere in the neighborhood of 12,000 downloads per week, while its GitHub repository has more than a thousand stars, suggesting it’s quite popular and that the infection could pose a serious risk to anyone who installed the malicious version. Analysis of the malicious release suggests it shares code and techniques with the Shai-Hulud variant dubbed ChainDrop by researchers, which was used in August to compromise npm dependencies including keyv and flat-cache. Like other variants of Shai-Hulud, the worm is designed to steal credentials and self-propagate. This particular version, according to supply chain security firm SafeDep, is designed to steal everything from crypto wallets to browser passwords, GitHub Actions secrets, cloud credentials, service-account tokens, and whatever else it can get its hands on. It exfiltrates that data and keeps an open line to its C2 infrastructure to await further instructions. To make matters worse, this Shai-Hulud variant monitors certain stolen GitHub tokens and, if one is revoked, can trigger the deletion of the infected user's home directory under specific conditions, making removal tricky. Socket recommends rebuilding compromised systems from a trusted source before restoring access to secrets, while researchers warn that the malicious token monitor should be disabled before revoking affected credentials. Tensorlake, for those unfamiliar, is a cloud-native platform for running isolated AI agents and untrusted AI-authored code. The infected npm SDK is used to create and manage Tensorlake environments. Socket warns that the malicious SDK's installation script can execute on the developer's machine or build server, outside Tensorlake's sandbox protections, potentially compromising the host before any AI-generated code is run. “Teams may isolate an agent’s generated code while installing its SDK on a developer workstation, application server, or build runner with access to deployment credentials and other secrets,” Socket noted. “Code executed during that installation inherits the permissions of the installing process.” That may sound bad, but it’s worth noting the malicious version wasn’t up for long - according to security firm Socket, the infected version was published to npm earlier this morning, UTC, and was flagged by its engine 11 minutes after publication. Npm removed the version, and Tensorlake has pulled the package as well, updating the version to 0.5.145. events.title: Netflix drops trailer for new series about Sam Bankman-Fried, Caroline Ellison, and the FTX scandal
events.summary: Netflix's "The Altruists" series depicts Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison navigating the FTX scandal. Netflix Netflix's "The Altruists" dramatizes the FTX fraud scandal and premieres Nov. 19. Anthony Boyle plays Sam Bankman-Fried, while Julia Garner portrays Caroline Ellison. Bankman-Fried is serving a 25-year prison sentence; Ellison served about 11 months. Netflix has released its first trailer for "The Altruists," its upcoming series dramatizing the massive multibillion-dollar fraud scheme that led to the collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried's cryptocurrency empire , FTX. In the eight-episode series, which hits the streaming giant on November 19, Anthony Boyle stars as Bankman-Fried, opposite Julia Garner, who plays Caroline Ellison , a former crypto executive and Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend. "Over the course of the years that our show depicts, Sam and Caroline, with the very best of intentions, talked each other and themselves into committing a number of terrible crimes," creator and showrunner Graham Moore said. Ellison, who had pleaded guilty to conspiring with Bankman-Fried and served about 11 months in prison, was recently hired at Manifund , a grantmaking platform. Bankman-Fried was sentenced in 2024 to 25 years in prison after a jury found him guilty of all seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. He remains behind bars at a low-security federal prison in California. Federal prison records show Bankman-Fried is projected to be released on Christmas Day in 2043. events.title: Paul Graham says Amazon's AI-agent ban opens the door to a new rival
events.summary: Amazon barred Meta's Muse from its website, citing concerns about access to and storage of customer data. Bloomberg/Getty Images Amazon banned Meta's Muse. Graham thinks that's an opportunity for other tech companies to pounce. The Y Combinator cofounder said it's the first time he's seen Amazon exposed to a competitor. Amazon has said it's worried about data security. Execs say AI agents could complicate returns. Paul Graham says he thinks Amazon is opening itself up to competitors. In a Wednesday night X thread, Graham, the cofounder of tech VC firm Y Combinator, criticized Amazon's recent decision to block consumer AI agents from its platform. It's the "first opportunity I've seen since Amazon was founded for a startup to create an Amazon competitor," he wrote. "People will want agents to buy stuff for them. It will be one of the main use cases. And they won't want to use some Amazon-supplied agent to do it." Amazon banning agents is the first opportunity I've seen since Amazon was founded for a startup to create an Amazon competitor. People will want agents to buy stuff for them. It will be one of the main use cases. And they won't want to use some Amazon-supplied agent to do it. — Paul Graham (@paulg) October 8, 2026 SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk reposted the thread with a one-word endorsement: " Seriously. " Graham's post comes as Amazon clashes with Muse, Meta's consumer-focused AI agent that can complete multi-step tasks, like making purchases. Amazon banned Muse from its marketplace, saying the agent didn't identify itself when shopping and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse itself cannot see users' passwords or payment methods. The company says credentials a user shares are stored securely in Muse's dedicated cloud computer, rather than visible to the agent. Graham's theory is that Amazon wouldn't bother blocking agents if shoppers didn't want to use them — but blocking the agents could come at Amazon's peril, he warned. "Your usage restrictions are my opportunity." The post also comes as AI companies are moving deeper into the consumer agent arena. In late September, OpenAI launched Dots , its Muse-like competitor. Amazon has not publicly said if it has blocked Dots. Not everyone agrees with Graham. Imran Khan, the founder of investment management firm Proem Asset Management, wrote that Amazon likely believes that more agents shopping on their platform risks increasing costly returns and "completely mess up their unit economics." Amazon is hardly sitting on the sidelines of the consumer AI race. It has its own shopping assistant, Rufus, and a "Buy for Me" feature that buys products from some outside brands. Amazon didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Read the original article on Business Insider
