events.title: Today marks a new chapter for Windows, as we bring unmetered intelligence to every desk and every home, and make every PC a place where agents can work securely on your behalf. [Read more]
events.summary: Today marks a new chapter for Windows, as we bring unmetered intelligence to every desk and every home, and make every PC a place where agents can work securely on your behalf. Some highlights of what we announced: • MAI-Code-1.1 Flash: 137B parameter coding model w/ 256K context window, which is now optimized to run on your PC! • GitHub Copilot now hands off work to local models like MAI-Code-1.1 Flash, helping projects cost a lot less without sacrificing quality. • With Hybrid Intelligence, Copilot can now take action directly on the PC and keep sensitive work on your device. • And with Code in Copilot, you can essentially build any software you need on your desktop, without any cloud token spend, and it’s just super at it. You’re no longer limited to what’s in an app store! Your PC becomes an infinite software factory. • Security is foundational to all this, which is why we are also bringing together Windows and Agent 365 so agents can work within secure boundaries on-device, including MXC a local sandbox for agent execution. Windows becomes your secure agent box! • All this comes to life on a new generation of devices, like Surface Laptop Ultra, powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark. Can’t wait to see what you build with all this. Read more about what we announced: https://lnkd.in/gFaRcv_X This is a significant shift in how we think about the future of work. AI agents moving directly onto PCs could change not only how software is built, but also how teams operate, collaborate and solve problems. The combination of local AI, security and Copilot makes this especially interesting. The next question is: how quickly will businesses adapt their workforce and skills to this new model? Lowering cloud token costs cannot come at the expense of auditability and governance defensibility. Microsoft’s own 2026 Digital Defense Report emphasizes that AI attacks now compress intrusion-to-impact timelines from days to minutes, while overreliance on Human-in-the-Loop controls introduces systemic oversight failure. Deploying trillion-parameter models and autonomous token factories directly onto endpoint silicon decentralizes execution into local memory—stripping away central visibility and granting persistent, high-privilege access to the device. 🛑 Cost efficiency is meaningless if the resulting execution architecture is not board defensible. Huge moment Satya Nadella and the team. Turning every desk into a secure, self-contained workshop where you can actually build without handing your work off to someone else's servers. Exciting to watch this unfold. Satya — this is where the governance problem becomes much more concrete. Once agents can act locally, continuously, and across files, applications, credentials, and software on behalf of a user, the question is no longer just whether the sandbox is secure. It is: does the authority for this exact action still stand now? A local agent may still have capability after consent changes, policy changes, account state changes, or the underlying evidence moves. So secure execution needs two distinct layers: can the agent execute safely? is the agent still legitimately authorized to execute this consequence now? The first is containment. The second is Temporal Standing. As PCs become agent execution environments, both are going to matter. I should be able to choose if I need it or not. You leave consumers with no choice I dont need this extra load on my PC and unnecessary AI that I dont use. Seriously considering moving to Linux. Windows getting out of hands A lot to like here. Hybrid intelligence also means we'll need a much better understanding of what happens locally, what leaves the device, and who's responsible for each piece. This is where agentic AI gets really interesting. Moving intelligence closer to the user means agents can actually operate within the environment where the work happens, with lower latency, better privacy, and less dependence on cloud inference. The idea of turning every PC into an agent execution environment feels like a major shift in how we think about software itself. Is this is a complete U-turn where individuals and businesses once again wanting to have more powerful computers/laptops instead of offloading the heavy lifting to cloud! Not to my home computer Satya Nadella I'll probably move off Windows to Linux Mint. I want a solid OS for consumers. Nothing more. The hybrid intelligence piece is the one I'm watching most closely. Keeping sensitive work on-device is the real unlock for teams that want agents but can't move data off the box. Will be interesting to see how Agent 365 holds up in practice. events.title: Apple, The King’s Trust launch initiative to empower young creatives
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Apple and The King’s Trust launch initiative to empower the next generation of creatives Text of this article October 7, 2026 UPDATE Apple and The King’s Trust launch initiative to empower the next generation of creatives Apple and The King’s Trust are building on their longstanding partnership by launching an immersive new education program to help young people build careers in the creative industries. The Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs will offer young people meaningful engagement with Apple experts across industries as they explore a variety of career pathways, equipping them with the technology, resources, skills, confidence, and expertise needed to realize their potential. A first cohort of up to 20 young people ages 18 to 30 will join specialized workshops to learn valuable, industry-aligned skills using Apple technologies. The immersive educational experience began this week with music industry and creative workshops, aligned to the recent opening of Apple Music Hall at Battersea Power Station in London, with more sessions and cohorts to come over the course of the next year. Apple has long supported educational programming for learners of all ages and backgrounds in the UK and around the world. Its offerings aim to help participants gain needed skills, access a wide range of resources, and succeed in the workforce. “At Apple, we believe education is a powerful force for equity and opportunity,” said Alisha Johnson Wilder, Apple’s senior director of Global Community Impact. “For years, we’ve been proud to work alongside The King’s Trust to spark creativity and open doors for young people across the UK. With the launch of the Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs, we’re taking that commitment further, connecting the next generation of creators and innovators directly with our experts, technology, and mentorship to help them build vital skills, discover their passions, and thrive in the workforce.” This year marks the 50th anniversary of The King’s Trust. Since it was founded by His Majesty The King, as the Prince of Wales, in 1976, it has helped 1.3 million young people across the UK reach their potential by developing life skills, preparing for employment, accessing job opportunities, and launching their businesses. At least $15 billion of social value can be attributed directly to the impact of The Trust’s programs over the last 50 years, and many of the participants it has supported over the last five years have moved into work, education, or training. “Together with Apple, we have already opened up valuable opportunities for thousands of young people across the UK through our longstanding partnership,” said Jonathan Townsend, The King’s Trust’s UK chief executive. “We are proud to build on this work with the Creative Labs program, an exciting new chapter in our partnership that will help even more young people develop the confidence and creative digital skills they need to take their next steps toward employment. We cannot wait to see how they use these experiences to realize their potential and discover where their talents can take them.” Since 2019, Apple’s support has enabled The King’s Trust to expand STEAM programming to schools in every region across the country through the Achieve program. Using Apple’s coding education resources, young people work collaboratively and think strategically to develop apps that address the needs and goals of their communities. Additionally, The King’s Trust’s 12-week Team program offers young adults access to Apple technology and learning resources to support their efforts to earn a Personal Development and Employability qualification. Apple is also working with The King’s Trust to develop resources that build AI literacy, creativity, and agency among educators and young people, and to empower educators to thoughtfully integrate the latest technologies within their teaching practices. events.title: OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties
events.summary: When OpenAI introduced dots last month, it pitched them as "always-on agents" running in their own cloud computer, but that may be overstating the readiness of the technology and of the people trying to use it. Presently, multiple users are reporting task failures and connection issues with their dots. Others have flagged cloud connectivity problems, dots that disappear, and dot refusals that appear to be related to abuse prevention. And the OpenAI Developer Community forum shows several similar concerns. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment about the usage of dots. ABI Research argues that "AI claws" – always-on agents – will shape enterprise AI adoption. The biz sees "a market evolving from isolated assistants toward modular agent ecosystems built for longer-running, enterprise-grade automation." Despite the hiccups that have afflicted dots, some skepticism on social media forums, speculation that OpenAI rushed dots out in response to Meta Muse and Grok Bot, and security issues, dots have some enthusiastic users in addition to detractors who just don't see the point. They also have competition from companies and developers who believe they can deliver a similar service more affordably, with fewer restrictions. A company called Tawkit that makes an SDK called CopilotKit has released OpenDots. "OpenDots is completely open source and gives you the same thing [as OpenAI Dots] as a template you host yourself," the biz said in a post last week. "Bring any agent through AG-UI, use any OpenAI-compatible model, and make every part of it your own." The company previously released OpenMuse and OpenBot. These projects essentially separate the user interface, the AG-UI agent layer, and the backend to provide an alternative personal agent. This doesn't eliminate the token expense of whatever agent is deployed, but it does mean that OpenAI may not be doing the billing. Then there's a potentially lower cost option, called (confusingly) Open Dot, powered by AI models running on OpenRouter. And as it's open source, the code could be altered to run using a local model – a feature that we understand is planned. "Open Dot is an open source version [of OpenAI Dots] that runs on your own Mac with your own OpenAI key, or with open models like Kimi, DeepSeek and Qwen through OpenRouter," the project repo explains. It allows users to connect to various apps like Gmail, Calendar, Slack, Notion, and GitHub via Composio. Prathit Joshi, the project's creator, told The Register, "I enjoy building and shipping tools for developers, especially tools that can support use cases that closed model companies aren't necessarily incentivized to support, like allowing open source models." Joshi is based in Bangalore, India, and works as a growth engineer at Composio. He said he's been using Open Dot to handle personal tasks like setting "to do" lists for the day based on Slack messages and summarizing posts on social media. Open Dot is based on the Electron framework, Joshi said, because he wanted it to be a desktop app. Distinguishing between OpenAI dots, OpenDots, and Open Dot may be confusing, but don't expect things to get any better in the near future. Everyone is busy wrapping increasingly commoditized models in a gatekeeping layer, in the hope of developing a sustainable business. For example, Elon Musk said on Tuesday that Grok Bot would become a model router rather than a front-end for a specific model. "Going forward, SpaceX will use the best back end model for any given task, including Claude Opus 5.5, MidJourney, Suno and other leading APIs," he said. "Whatever is most likely to give you the best outcome." ®

events.title: Data shows rental tenants have hit breaking point
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tenants unable to pay higher rental prices, Domain data finds The rental market is slowing despite prices remaining at record highs. ( ABC News ) Despite severe rental shortages, landlords are struggling to increase rents due to tenants hitting their affordability limit. New data shows rent is flatlining in most capital cities and has even fallen in a few in the past three months. Although the market is slowing, with the national vacancy rate rising to 1 per cent, it is still much tighter than it was a year ago. Australia's rental market is beginning to lose steam despite rents remaining at record highs. It is the rapidly emerging disconnect that experts say could suggest tenants are being pushed to the brink as rents flatline and even fall across most of the major capitals. New data from Domain shows capital city house rents were unchanged at $700 a week over the September quarter, while unit rents rose by 1.5 per cent despite very low levels of rental properties available on the market. That slowdown is challenging the long-held relationship between tight rental supply and growth, according to Domain's chief residential economist Nicola Powell. "Tenants' ability to absorb further increases is really the dynamic that is limiting further rental growth," she told The Business. "There's almost a disconnect now between where vacancy rate sits and what is occurring for rental growth." Lack of supply not translating into rent rises Dr Powell said although it was still "a landlords' market" in all major capitals and regional areas, the severe supply shortage was not necessarily transferring into rental increases as tenants hit their ceiling. Rents for houses are at or near record highs, with Sydney, Darwin and Perth the most expensive cities to live in. But most of that growth occurred earlier in the year. Nicola Powell says the data indicates cannot pay more rent. ( ABC News: Thorsten Joses ) The new data from Domain found rents in Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide flatlined over the past three months. And housing rents fell in Sydney and Canberra by $5 and $10 respectively, erasing gains in June. Only Darwin and Hobart bucked the trend across the capital cities in Domain's dataset, recording rises of 5.3 per cent and 1 per cent respectively in houses in the past quarter. Although the market is slowing, with the national vacancy rate rising by 0.1 percentage points to rest at 1 per cent, it is still much tighter than it was a year ago. Renters compromise to avoid higher rent Cameron Kusher of Kusher Consulting, an independent property economist, said renters were finding other ways to survive as the market squeezed them for all they were worth. How Australian mortgages compare to the US, Japan and South Korea Logan mayor warns of backyard 'slums' as council slashes granny flat tax Terminally ill grandmother to lose home as housing group fails Singles tax costs thousands of dollars a year "Because rents have increased so much over the last few years, what people are doing is they're renting in a less ideal location," he said. "So they're opting for a cheaper rental, maybe not ideally where they want to live but basically a trade-off that they're having to make." Other ways include share housing or adult children staying at home longer. Migration cuts floated to curb rent rises The figures came after One Nation released new modelling for its migration plan on Wednesday, saying it could save Australian renters almost $3,000 a year. The party has pledged that, if elected, it would cut 750,000 temporary visas over three years to reduce rental inflation by 6.5 per cent. One Nation has announced migration policy it says will reduce rental supply issues. ( ABC News ) "I don't know that that's enough to significantly improve rental affordability given how much rents have increased over recent years," Mr Kusher said of the policy. "But I feel like, at this point, renters would probably take any win that would lower their rent." He also said changes in this year's budget that made property investment less attractive were still flowing through the system. But at this stage, Mr Kusher said they did not seem to be causing the massive rent increases initially feared.

events.title: Argonne scientists create chatty X-ray microscope that zooms in where you tell it to
events.summary: Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory have plugged an agentic AI platform into an X-ray nanoprobe beamline, creating a system that can get a closer look at areas researchers ask it to focus on. Argonne reported the success of an experimental run of the agentic microscope this week, with the device initially tested on its ability to locate the interface between two regions on an integrated circuit device, and all by just telling the microscope what they wanted it to determine using natural language. “Microelectronics was simply the example used to showcase the technology,” Argonne computational scientist Mathew Cherukara said of the project. “The real achievement is developing a next‑generation, AI‑enhanced microscope that can benefit many scientific fields.” The microscope itself is part of Argonne’s 26-ID hard X-ray nanoprobe beamline, which uses a tightly focused X-ray beam to perform nanoscale imaging and measurements of target samples. Such devices are considered a prime use case for scientific applications of AI because they produce a massive amount of data that can take human researchers considerable time to comb through thanks to their use of a technique known as ptychography. The method collects multiple diffraction patterns as X-rays interact with a sample, with modern X-ray experiments capable of generating millions of images in just a few hours of beam time. Conventional ptychographic reconstruction and analysis can take hours or days, whereas Argonne says its AI system can reconstruct images in real time as the data arrives. Argonne’s X-ray nanoprobe beamline is the sort of scientific facility the Trump administration is looking to boost with AI through its Genesis Mission. Launched by President Trump in November 2025 and led by the Department of Energy, Genesis aims to find ways to use AI in scientific research, including the Synergistic Neutron and Photon Science - Intelligence (SYNAPS-I) project that Argonne is undertaking in partnership with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, which is leading the effort. Brookhaven National Laboratory, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory are also participating in the project. The inclusion of agentic AI in the Argonne X-ray microscope is actually the second phase of the project; the first was simply to see if, as mentioned above, AI could be used to reduce ptychographic image processing time. That was a success, as the lab reported in April, and phase two’s addition of natural language agentic AI appears to have been a win as well. “Combined, these SYNAPS-I advances lay the groundwork for self-driving microscopes, closed-loop experimentation and automated defect-detection tools that promise to accelerate discovery across fields ranging from semiconductor manufacturing to advanced materials and national user facilities,” Cherukara said of the project’s work thus far. In addition to the speed at which the new machine can process data, the conversational AI added in phase two gives researchers the ability to just ask the microscope to examine an area of interest rather than having to figure out how to aim the beam themselves. The AI can not only handle data collection and processing, but also analyze the results itself and flag additional areas of interest, which it can then further investigate on its own. Tao Zhou, a scientist at Argonne, said in a video from the lab that the new, chattier version of the microscope could open up advanced scientific research to researchers who could benefit from X-ray nanoprobe beamline science but don’t know how to operate a complicated instrument like the one at his lab. “This can be a game changer for a lot of users,” Zhou said. “This kind of interactive chat interface allows them to do their scientific research, get excellent data, without having to spend too much time to learn about the beamline components.” “This will help us attract a lot of new users,” Zhou added. Just be sure not to mention toast. ®

events.title: Trump's executive order on dyed diesel will offer little relief, farmers and truckers say
events.summary: Farmers, truckers, and economists say cutting taxes on diesel may not ease record-high fuel prices SIOUX FALLS, S.D. -- Farmers, truckers and economists say a move to cut taxes on diesel will provide little relief from record-high fuel prices that have soared since the U.S. attacked Iran months ago. Industry groups said they appreciate President Donald Trump’s executive order expanding the use of a diesel now reserved for off-road work, but farmers already have access to the fuel and many have already wrapped up harvest. Truckers will struggle to navigate differing state rules. “In the context of diesel prices that are over two dollars more than they were last year, it just doesn’t come close to closing that wound,” said Matt Perdue, president of the North Dakota Farmers Union. With less than a month to go before the November election , diesel prices continue to hit record highs as some farmers transport their crops for processing and others rush to complete their fall harvest. Many have been feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared thanks to refinery constraints and supply disruptions amid the Iran war. Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon across the country on Wednesday, more than 70% higher than one year ago, according to motor club AAA. The executive order defers the $0.24 federal tax per gallon of regular diesel, used for road projects, until the end of the year. Most states also levy their own tax on diesel. “Dyed” diesel is the same as regular diesel, except for its red dye to help law enforcement enforce penalties for on-road use. It's already allowed for off-road purposes like farming equipment, such as tractors and combines, as well as construction and heating uses. Savings can compound if states take similar actions ; many have eased restrictions or waived taxes on dyed diesel, including South Dakota and Iowa. Perdue said North Dakota has waived the tax on regular diesel. But where the state decision is focused on farmers, he believes the federal decision would largely benefit those on other levels of the supply chain. Farmers who will see the most benefit are those who haul their own product, like livestock or fresh produce, on public roads. Those who have already wrapped up harvesting won't see savings. “Most of our diesel use is behind us,” said Perdue, who grows spring wheat, durum and canola on his family farm. Both trucking companies and independent truckers may not see much relief either. The effect is likely to be negligible for big trucking companies because the order is on a federal level and states make their own rules, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in a social media post. “The largest diesel users are the least likely to use dyed diesel,” he wrote. “A national carrier crossing five or six states in a day faces enormous risk with a patchwork of rules, legal in one state, and subject to fines in the next.” Many states exempt road diesel from sales tax but apply sales tax to dyed diesel instead, he said. Easing limits on red-dyed diesel will likely have a minimal effect for small truckers, who pay for fuel up front, said Todd Spencer, president and CEO of trade group the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association. He estimates every $1 increase per gallon in fuel costs independent truckers about $400 more per week. ISIS-inspired mass shooting plot at Mall of America thwarted, FBI says 2 dead, multiple injured in school bus crash with children on board Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys The savings will be small, but it could still increase competition for dyed diesel, said David Ortega, food economics and policy professor at Michigan State University. “I think there's a real chance this could backfire and make the situation worse for farmers," he said. “Basically anybody that’s running a truck on the highway on regular diesel can now be using this off-highway diesel. Even someone that owns a diesel pickup truck potentially has access to this other type of diesel.” Perdue in North Dakota said he expects a “rush for dyed diesel, and we’ll see how the supply responds.” But not all dyed diesel pump stations are set up for larger trucks like semis, said Paul Mitchell, a professor of agricultural and applied economics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “It’s going to come down to infrastructure ability to get your vehicles to a place that you can use and fill them up with,” he said. Henry Hanscom, American Trucking Associations chief advocacy and public affairs officer, pointed out that the executive order directs temporary penalty relief and potential tax deferral for using red-dyed diesel, not outright tax forgiveness. He said the ATA would review the Internal Revenue Service’s implementing guidance of the policy when it is available. Last month, Trump had threatened a diesel export ban, though he later said it is off the table.

events.title: Microsoft N1Xes Intel in favor of Nvidia's shiny new SoCs in Surface Laptop Ultra
events.summary: Look out, Intel! Microsoft released its first Surface notebook powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark system-on-chip (SoC) during an event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The Surface Laptop Ultra is one of several new Copilot+ PCs powered by the N1X chip that Microsoft says is aimed at "builders," which are available for preorder starting today and expected to begin shipping next week. The machine is arguably the vehicle for a slew of new AI features including hybrid compute functionality that dynamically routes workloads to on-device or cloud models depending on factors like connectivity, privacy, cost, and complexity. The aluminum clad system largely keeps with Microsoft's existing design ethos. It features a high-res, 15-inch mini-LED display capable of reaching a peak brightness of 2,000 nits in Microsoft's signature 3:2 aspect ratio, a standard ten-keyless keyboard layout, haptic trackpad, and a slew of ports including one you won't find on a MacBook Pro. Connectivity includes three USB-C ports, including one equipped with magnets for MagSafe-like connectivity, full-size HDMI, an SD card reader, and a solitary USB-A port because after more than a decade still can't shake the aging connector. But arguably the notebook's most interesting feature is the inclusion of Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X SoC. As we reported earlier this year, these aren't exactly new chips. The N1X is based heavily on Nvidia's now year-old GB10 platform, with a few CPU and GPU cores fused off on lower end models to meet pricing. This tells us that the Surface Laptop Ultra should ship with either an 18- or 20-core CPU designed by MediaTek and Arm and an Nvidia Blackwell-based RTX GPU with between 5,120 and 6,144 cores. In terms of memory, Microsoft says the notebook can be equipped with up to 128 GB of memory, enough to serve large language models up to 284 billion parameters in size, if you can live with just 1.6 bits of precision. As we've previously covered, the GPU is a pretty potent one with a peak theoretical throughput of 1 petaFLOPS at 4-bit precision, not that you're likely ever to see that in many real world workloads. Nvidia's marketing team is leaning on support for 2:4 sparsity to hit that target, so it can theoretically achieve that figure. Unfortunately, almost none of the AI inference workloads anyone cares about these days actually take advantage of the functionality. As a result, the chip's peak performance is actually closer to 500 teraFLOPS, which still gives it an edge over competing chips like AMD's Strix and Gorgon Halo processors. Local AI inference, as we mentioned earlier, is a major selling point for this class of hardware, though Microsoft was also keen to highlight the GPU's capabilities for more traditional creative and gaming workloads, claiming 60 FPS in the latest Gears of War release. We suspect that Nvidia's DLSS AI upscaling tech is probably doing the heavy lifting here. In order to keep the system from overheating, Microsoft says that the Surface Laptop Ultra features a beefed up cooling system with 2.5x more capacity than past Surface notebooks. From the renders we've seen, the extra cooling comes courtesy of a big fat vapor chamber. The Surface is expected to begin shipping next week at a starting price of $2,599 for the poverty-spec gray variant with the lower-end 18-core N1X, 24 GB of unified memory, and 512 GB user serviceable SSD. Jumping up to the 20-core chip, 128 GB of memory, and 1 TB of storage will set you back $5,899, and assuming memory prices haven't gone up even more by then. Alongside the Surface Laptop Ultra, Microsoft also announced a mini PC style development kit based on the N1X priced at $5,999. While by no means cheap, it's still cheaper than the similarly specced DGX Spark, which now retails for $6,950, albeit with 4TB of storage rather than 2TB. The DGX Spark also runs a lightly modified version of Ubuntu, which might be worth the premium for some. If your heart is set on a high-memory config and you don't want to wait for the Surface Laptop Ultra to come back in stock, Lenovo, Asus, Dell, MSI, and HP all are launching similarly specced systems over the next week or so. And if Nvidia isn't your style, it's worth mentioning that AMD has its own AI-tuned chips, which now support up to 192 GB of unified memory, and we strongly suspect will support many of the same hybrid AI features rolling out to Windows 11 over the next few months. ®

events.title: Trump's midterm strategists draw scrutiny over Russia-aligned work
events.summary: President Trump threatened Wednesday to fire two of his top political consultants if he finds a conflict, after reports that they advised a Russia-aligned government ahead of local elections there. Why it matters: Chris LaCivita and James Blair are leading Republicans' midterm election strategy, putting their foreign consulting work in tension with their prominent roles in Trump's political operation. What they're saying: Trump called the pair "outside consultants" in a Truth Social post Wednesday. "They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them. They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C." "I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!" The other side: A source familiar with both consultants and the trip tells Axios that it was "a normal weekend full of calls and texts on the various races and our strategy/tactics in each." Context: The nationalist party warned that new voting machines could threaten its hold on power, echoing Trump's repeated attacks on voting machines in the U.S. A national election commission required the territory to use the new equipment. The source said Blair and LaCivita were there for about 48 hours to give "strategic advice on Election Integrity and what to look for to spot and avoid potential election fraud, because it was the first election where Republic of Srbska was forced to use new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment…which obviously made them nervous." Between the lines: Caroline Wren, a registered lobbyist for Srpska, said the republic's abiding interest is in gaining stronger relations with Trump's administration. "It's not about Russia. It's not about Putin. It's about Christians who want their freedom and autonomy," Wren said. "The Trump Administration has made a huge priority of protecting and promoting Christians around the world and there is no better place to do that than the Pro-Trump Christians in the Republic of Sprska who have been demonized by the Europeans and Brussels for their Western values," she said. Blair and LaCivita were "maybe on the ground for 36 hours," she said, observing that she saw Blair constantly on the phone discussing elections back in the U.S. "Chris and James work around the clock to deliver wins for President Trump and Republicans here at home," she said. Zoom in: Blair , who previously served as White House deputy chief of staff, left the administration earlier this year to work for MAGA Inc., a super PAC affiliated with the president. He was also a senior adviser on Trump's 2024 campaign. LaCivita , the former co-manager of Trump's 2024 presidential campaign , is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc. Catch up quick: LaCivita and Blair visited Republika Srpska, a semi-autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of local elections, according to the New York Times. The two were reportedly recruited to advise the government on voting-related issues. They were hired to work for the government, not the nationalist party that controls it, though the party dominates the territory's government. Yes, but: American political consultants have a long history of taking on foreign clients. Zoom out: Trump's family businesses have expanded their foreign dealings since he returned to office. The Trump Organization and its partners have more than 20 Trump-branded projects planned, under construction or opening abroad — more than triple the number of overseas properties operating before his return. His administration accepted a luxury Boeing 747 from Qatar slated to eventually go to Trump's presidential library, while a UAE royal-linked firm bought a 49% stake in the Trump family's cryptocurrency business. events.title: Attackers hijacked top-level domains, minted fake security certs for Google and other orgs
events.summary: Imagine going to a Google website at its correct URL, only to be redirected to a crim's illegitimate copy. Attackers hijacked top-level domains, allowing them to alter DNS records and mint fraudulent HTTPS certificates for several Google domains, and those belonging to other organizations. Google said it became aware of the series of attacks last week in the .gh (Ghana), .sl (Sierra Leone), and .as (American Samoa) country-code top-level namespaces (ccTLDs). “During these hijacks, attackers modified authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering several Google domains, as well as domains belonging to other organizations,” Google security warned on Tuesday. Google did not say which specific domains or organizations were affected. The attacks did not compromise Google’s systems, and Chrome quickly blocked suspected counterfeit certificates across the affected ccTLDs - meaning Chrome browser users are already protected - according to the Chocolate Factory. “Due to the nature of the attacks, we have no reason to believe the Certification Authorities (CAs) that issued the impacted certificates did anything wrong,” the alert said. These types of attacks allow criminals to impersonate legitimate organizations and websites without triggering any browser security alerts. The attacker controls the traffic routing (via DNS) and the private key associated with the unauthorized certificate, which means they can potentially intercept or modify data sent by users to the impersonated site - and abuse the trusted organization's brand to distribute malware or conduct phishing attacks. “While Chrome took steps during these incidents to identify and block suspected unauthorized certificates across the affected ccTLDs, browser-side intervention should not be relied on to protect your users,” Google warned domain owners. “Due to the complexity of DNS hijacks, we cannot guarantee that our analysis identified every affected domain, nor do Chrome interventions reliably protect non-Chrome users.” To ensure that their domains and users are protected, Google recommends ongoing monitoring of Certificate Transparency (CT) logs across all of an organization’s domains, including parked or regional ccTLD properties. This provides near real-time alerts whenever someone obtains a certificate for one of your domains. And if you operate a domain in .gh, .sl, or .as, definitely review recent CT log entries for unexpected certificates. Organizations can also publish restrictive Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS records, which allow domain owners to specify which CAs are permitted to issue certificates for their domains. While this won’t stop certificates from being issued during a DNS hijacking attack, it helps safeguard domains after DNS control is restored. Google recommends CAA policies that restrict issuance to specific authorized accounts and validation methods and prevent attackers from using cached validation state to mint new certificates after a hijacking ends.®

events.title: Syria considering sending troops to Yemen to fight Houthis
events.summary: Saudi Arabia and Syria are discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to join the counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, three U.S. officials told Axios. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is seriously considering it, but hasn't decided. Why it matters: While the discussion is mostly between Saudi Arabia and Syria, the Trump administration has been consulted by both countries and is not opposed in principle to such a move, the U.S. officials said. But sending Syrian troops could inject a religious dimension into the Yemen war and exacerbate the conflict. The troops could include Islamist Sunni foreign fighters who participated in the rebellion against the Assad regime. They would be fighting against the Houthis, who follow Zaydi Shiite Islam. Driving the news: The Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a massive ground operation over the weekend against the Houthis. The offensive was designed to retake territories the Houthis control, including the capital Sanaa and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. A U.S. official said the issue of sending Syrian troops to Yemen came up during the meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and al-Sharaa in Riyadh earlier this week. The Saudis want al-Sharaa to send troops in order to boost the Yemeni forces that are less trained than the Houthis. While al-Sharaa hasn't signed off on the decision yet, the U.S. official said it is highly likely the Syrian president will accept the Saudi request. Behind the scenes: The U.S. doesn't oppose sending Syrian troops to Yemen. It would provide more support for the Saudi-backed operation against the Houthis without the U.S. having to get deeply involved, a U.S. official said. Trump administration officials also believe that deploying Syrian troops to Yemen would strengthen the relationship between two U.S. allies, Saudi Arabia and Syria. Two U.S. officials said U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed. The White House and CENTCOM declined to comment. Spokespeople for the Saudi Embassy and the Syrian Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Zoom in: A source with knowledge of the discussions said the Syrian military could send 10,000 to 20,000 troops to Yemen. The units under consideration are the 90th division near Damascus and the 84th division based in southern Syria near Sweida. The 84th division includes thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who came to Syria during the civil war to fight against the Assad regime under the umbrella of the HTS rebel group.

events.title: Browser-in-browser attacks use fake Meta Muse Ad lure to steal credentials
events.summary: A phishing campaign targeting advertising managers by impersonating Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Manus to steal credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes has added a fake Muse Ads product to its lure lineup – just eight days after Meta launched its personal AI agent. Meta announced Muse on September 8, and by September 17, a very convincing website – museads.ai – for a product called Muse Ads that promised to help advertisers reach buyers and run sponsored placements popped up online. “The operators already had the platform, so adapting it to a new brand can take minutes,” Oleg Zaytsev, lead security researcher at Island, told The Register. “The striking part is how quickly they turned a timely announcement into a credible reason for someone to act. The same platform could then be repackaged around other familiar tasks, from connecting a business tool to claiming a refund or applying for a job.” The security startup spotted the Muse Ads webpage, and upon digging into the scam uncovered that just the page was new. “Its code, from the sign-in forms to the fake browser window, came from a wider operation that had already run fake ad products for Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Manus,” Zaytsev and fellow Island researcher Ofek Ronen wrote in a blog post published Tuesday. All of these products served as lures for browser-in-the-browner (BitB) attacks designed to trick agency staff, media buyers, and manager-account administrators into handing over their advertising account credentials – along with stored payment methods and client accounts – to digital thieves. “For victims, the potential cost is loss of access to an advertising account, unauthorized ad spend, and exposure of linked client accounts,” Zaytsev told The Register. How the scam works BitB is a clever phishing technique originally detailed by a researcher called mr.d0x in 2022. It involves building a fake login window directly inside a legitimate one. The fake window looks like the real thing, featuring an address bar, title, and URL, but it's just an overlay to steal users’ credentials. According to Zaytsev, this one has likely proved very lucrative for its criminal operators, with hundreds of victim submissions to the platform, and activity still ongoing. “From one frontend alone, we observed submissions involving roughly 200 distinct email addresses over about a month,” he told us. “The operators used the same platform across many similar sites, so we estimate the campaign-wide volume is substantially higher.” Each phony ad product has its own page, with ChatGPT promising users a Monday Google Ads brief, Gemini offering manager account and linked-client support, Claude an advertising portal, Perplexity pitching campaign planning and spend audits, and Manus providing a private Meta integration. Each fake product page also has a “connect” button. When the victim clicks “connect,” it opens the browser-in-browser overlay, with a fake address bar showing accounts.google.com, or an Okta tenant to gain the victim’s trust. The real browser, however, stays on the phishing domain and steals credentials when the victim types them in. A human operator running the campaign sees each submission and chooses what the victim sees and is prompted to do. This includes asking for another password, requesting an SMS or Okta authenticator code to bypass MFA, showing a Google approval code or Okta push request, or displaying a QR code. The platform supports Google, Meta, TikTok, and Okta workflows, and the browser overlay adapts to whatever the victim runs: Window, macOS, iOS, ot Android, and even mimics Safari’s URL pill, Chrome’s custom tabs, and a dark mode. And while the researchers told us they haven’t identified the people operating the kit or found a name under which it’s sold, the operators did expose older source code through misconfigured public GitHub repositories that connected this to a campaign to a larger operation. In addition to the AI ad pages, this operation also used fake refund claims and job recruitment sites as lures with separate builds for Adidas, Google Careers, Robert Half, Tesla, and Louis Vuitton. All of these pages run on one Next.js and Socket.IO stack. Many of the pages also used Vercel frontends with Railway or Render services behind them for state and commands. “A new brand or polished page doesn’t necessarily mean a new attack. Operators can change the lure quickly, but the workflow still has to move someone onto a site they control, collect credentials, and steer them through authentication,” Zaytsev said. “Security teams should maintain a continuous baseline of trusted domains, check the real browser address, and connect similar behavior across different sites,” he added. “Attackers can generate a convincing website quickly; building the domain history and reputation of a legitimate service is much harder. AI can help defenders keep pace with AI-generated websites, especially as they become more convincing and appear more quickly.”. ®

events.title: Town questions $15b data centre set to use enough power for 1m homes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts CDC Data Centres told not to take Wagga Wagga for granted over mega plan Eden Summers has started a petition looking to halt a proposed data centre near Wagga Wagga. ( ABC News: Melinda Hayter ) Residents in Wagga Wagga have started a petition to halt development of a $15 billion data centre campus outside the town. CDC Data Centres plans to acquire 100 hectares to build the proposed 1.4-gigawatt facility. The proponent has submitted a scoping report and has two years to develop an environmental impact statement once the state government sets the guidelines. When residents of the NSW city of Wagga Wagga learnt one of the country's largest data centres was proposed for down the road, they had questions. For resident Liz Warrell, the biggest was: how does it benefit her community? "It's a big box; it sits there," she said. "I don't know if it generates employment, I know it's using resources and I know it's creating emissions. "So what effect is that having on us as a community as our climate dries?" Liz Warrell wants information about how much water and power the proposed data centre would use. ( ABC News: Melinda Hayter ) CDC Data Centres is proposing to build a $15 billion campus on a 100-hectare council-owned site next to the city's landfill. If approved, the 1.4-gigawatt facility is expected to consume more electricity each year than a million typical NSW homes. Just 4 kilometres from the proposed site, Eden Summers is also worried her peaceful rural lifestyle is at risk. Eden Summers is not supportive of a proposed data centre near Wagga Wagga. ( ABC News: Melinda Hayter ) "Government likes to take action on big business projects without actually thinking of the locals," Ms Summers said. The land CDC is eyeing for the project is currently zoned for primary production use, but the company proposes to change the zoning. "We have restrictions on what we can do on our land, but then when it comes to big business, everything changes; there's just no consistency," Ms Summers said. A petition to halt the development, started by Ms Summers, has attracted more than 1,000 signatures and states locals "should not have to sacrifice our rural community for a data centre". "If it was on land designated for this sort of project, opposition wouldn't be as strong," she said. Other residents cautiously open to plan However, some Wagga residents, like Katrina Walker, think the site, 15 kilometres from the city's centre, made sense. "If it's out at Gregadoo, that's a fair way out, so I think it'd be OK," she said. Katrina Walker says the proposed site is appropriate. ( ABC News: Melinda Hayter ) So far, only a scoping report that provides an overview of the proposed state significant development has been made publicly available. Advocacy group Committee 4 Wagga has cautiously welcomed the proposal, having campaigned previously for more industry in the city. But co-chair Richard Pottie said support for the centre would depend on the details. "We can't take on the 'not in our backyard' philosophy," he said. The proposed layout of CDC Data Centre's proposed Gregadoo facility. ( Supplied: NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure ) Calls for information on water and power usage The first community consultation sessions will be held in Wagga on Wednesday and Thursday next week. Once the state government releases its State Environmental Assessment Requirements (SEARs) for the project, CDC will have two years to submit an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). The full outline of the data centre's electricity infrastructure needs, as well as a noise and vibration assessment and a water management plan, will be included in that EIS. An artist's impression of CDC's proposed data centre at Gregadoo. ( Supplied: CDC Data Centres ) A CDC spokesperson said that in the proposed centre's first stage of operation, it was estimated that 1.28 million litres of water, or the equivalent water use of seven households, would be needed for an "initial fill". "CDC typically undertakes this from rainwater collected onsite, with a backup from water trucks or, depending on local conditions, town water," the spokesperson said. The company said on an ongoing basis, the first stage of the project was expected to consume as much water as a typical office building. "We estimate our annual water consumption to be approximately 1,512,000 litres per year. "The town water usage is estimated to be equivalent of a little less than nine Australian households." events.title: Victorians say 'lazy planning' leading to poor social housing outcomes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bendigo residents say 'lazy planning' leading to poor social housing outcomes Michael Jurca and Ben Pengelly say neighbouring residents will suffer from poor traffic and environmental outcomes. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Central Victorian traditional owner group Djaara wants to build 34 social houses for 75 residents in the regional city of Bendigo. Neighbouring residents say state planning laws mean "lazy planning" cannot be contested by local councils or residents. If approved, Djaara says construction is scheduled to begin in mid-2027 and be completed by the end of 2028. Residents living near a proposed social housing project by central Victorian traditional owner group Djaara, in the regional Victorian city of Bendigo, say the state government's fast-tracked planning process is allowing "lazy planning" to go ahead without sufficient scrutiny. Djaara, the trading name for the Dja Dja Wurrung Clans Aboriginal Corporation, is proposing 34 one and two-storey houses for about 75 people at the site of the old North Bendigo Primary School on Nolan Street. But neighbouring residents said Victorians should be able to question planning applications and oppose conditions when there are other alternatives. "We recognise that social housing is needed in Victoria. We know we're under-housed," resident Ben Pengelly said. "But there's a number of issues that we don't agree with. Concept drawings show 34 houses would be built on the site of the old North Bendigo Primary School. ( Supplied: Djaara ) In December last year the Victorian government awarded Djaara $21.6 million for the project. Among the residents' concerns was that the land owned by the Department of Education and Training had been repurposed for social housing without consultation, going against a Victorian government-backed 2019 public space plan that slated the site as parkland. "I feel for some of the people in the area who I know have bought their house according to that Victorian government document," Mr Pengelly said. "That's not transparent. That's changing the rules. "And in the words of a lot of these politicians nowadays, they all say they want to be transparent." Mr Pengelly's neighbour Michael Jurca said Barney Street was already full of Bendigo Health workers needing all-day parking and did not have the space for more vehicles without negatively affecting residents. "If you have visitors or services we already have to move the car three or four streets away," Mr Jurca said. Neighbouring residents say current traffic plans don't properly address the increased traffic conditions. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Fast-track planning an election sore point The proposal is expected to go before Planning Minister Sonja Kilkenny as part of the Victorian government's Development Facilitation Program, which fast-tracks priority projects such as housing and renewable energy developments. The program has taken planning powers away from local councils and strips residents of the right to object at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. Djaara's Transport Impact Assessment (TIA) submitted to the Victorian government shows its consultants, Impact Traffic Engineering, used a New South Wales report to illustrate its assumptions of vehicle movements by each house, each day. Mr Pengelly said the TIA was another example of lazy planning. "That is just ticking a box, making sure they meet some sort of requirement. But let's be realistic, why isn't it a Victorian planning traffic management plan?" Mr Pengelly said. Residents say they bought next to the old primary school site when it was designated for parkland, not social housing. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) The City of Greater Bendigo said it supported the application in principle, but environmental constraints and remediation of the site needed "further consideration". In a letter to residents, the city's senior transport engineer Muaid Ahmed said a review by the city's engineering unit "identified that while the TIA estimates the additional traffic generated by the development, it does not provide a detailed assessment of existing traffic conditions or future traffic conditions following development". Sonya Kilkenny will decide whether the social housing project gets the green light. ( AAP: Joel Carrett ) In a statement, Djaara's acting chief executive officer Harley Douglas said its housing provider subsidiary, Mayam Mayam, would review any submissions received and consider how best to respond, in consultation with the Department of Transport and Planning.

events.title: Exclusive: Inside Trump's AI science summit
events.summary: President Trump will attend a summit Thursday meant to empower scientists and position the U.S. as a leader in breakthroughs driven by "super intelligence," according to an announcement shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The Trump administration is looking for industry to step in amid its cuts to government funding for science research and development. Driving the news: The White House is announcing more than $1 billion in industry commitments for the Genesis Mission from AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and others. The White House is also announcing a compute hub of more than 14 institutions across 10 southeast states, and a $1 billion investment in Georgia for student and faculty compute access. The National Science Foundation and the Energy Department will invest more than $100 million in AI-driven science tools. Leading scientists and "innovators" will attend the summit, the White House says. Zoom in: The summit was inspired by a July report from White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios. It highlights industry's increasing role in driving research and development, plus new mechanisms for funding and organizing research. Catch up quick: Trump last November launched the Genesis Mission, which sets ambitious deadlines to accelerate scientific discovery. In July, the White House announced that the effort would be expanded to more than 15 federal agencies. Last week, the White House held another AI summit that focused on the rollout of America.gov, which aims to streamline government services using AI.

events.title: Former RBA member explains what happens inside interest rate meetings
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Former RBA board member says November interest rate hike 'plausible' The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent. ( ABC News: Kylie Silvester ) A former RBA member says the board has typically had split votes on monetary policy about 30 per cent of the time over the past decade. Ian Harper says none of the treasurers in power during his 10-year tenure ever tried to influence him on interest rate decisions. The market is pricing in a one-in-three possibility of a rate hike on the first Tuesday in November. Another interest rate hike this year is "plausible", but not necessarily likely, according to former Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board member Ian Harper. A distinguished economist, Professor Harper was on the RBA board for a decade, from 2016 until after the Monetary Policy Board's (MPB) August meeting, when interest rates were left on hold. The cash rate was subsequently increased at the bank's September meeting to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent. Speaking at a Centre for Independent Studies lunchtime event in Sydney on Wednesday, Professor Harper declined to offer his view on where interest rates might settle over a five or 10-year horizon, but did make this comment on the short-term prospects for the cash rate. "The bank moving again before the end of the year is plausible, from what I can see of the circumstances," he told the audience. "But, again, I don't have the [board meeting] papers in front of me." In a subsequent one-on-one interview with David Taylor for The Business, Professor Harper declined to characterise the chances of a back-to-back rate hike in November as "likely", repeating his assessment that it was "plausible". This matches market pricing, which has the chances of a hike on Melbourne Cup Day at about a third. Harper offers rare insight into RBA board processes Much has changed since Professor Harper joined the RBA board in 2016, with a major governance overhaul sparked by a federal government-commissioned review of the bank resulting in a split between the MPB and a governance board, taking effect in March 2025. Ian Harper joined the RBA board in 2016 and left in August this year. ( ABC ) However, Professor Harper indicated the biggest change to the interest rate decision-making process was that the meetings now ran over two days. He explained that the board convened at 1pm on the Monday and mets until about 5:30pm, hearing briefings from RBA staff and having the opportunity to put questions to them. He said the governor often took an informal straw poll at the end of that first day about what people thought should be done with rates. Sometimes the board members will go out to dinner together before "people go off and think about it overnight and come back the next day," Professor Harper explained. "The meeting starts at 9[am] and you run through to 11:30. "And in that process, of course, there's further discussion, the decision gets made, the statement gets drafted, the draft gets considered, discussed and agreed." That decision and the accompanying statement get published at 2:30pm Sydney time , before the Reserve Bank governor holds a press conference at 3:30pm, a practice also recommended by the RBA review. RBA board had dissent prior to votes being published Ian Harper explained what happens in the RBA's boardroom when it meets to decide interest rates. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Another change instituted by the review was the publication of how many board members voted in favour of each option considered for rates. Since the board began publishing the vote tallies from its July 2025 meeting onwards, there have been eight unanimous decisions and three split votes. Professor Harper told The Business that such dissent was fairly typical before the board began publishing vote tallies. How Australian mortgages compare to the US, Japan and South Korea The RBA isn't trying to stop inflation. So don't expect prices to fall Bank of America met with Australian super funds and delivered a warning 'Snowball effect' hitting as companies react to rates rise, growing costs "The Reserve Bank Act has always provided that each member of the board has a deliberative vote and the governor the casting vote if there happens to be someone missing," he explained. Recession strikes fear into many and pain isn't evenly shared Pandemic aside, Australia hasn't experienced a recession caused by rising interest rates since the early 1990s. When asked whether any RBA governor over the past decade had ever been on the losing side of a contested vote, Professor Harper said: "That's never happened.

events.title: NVIDIA, Microsoft Kick Off a New Beginning for Windows PCs with RTX Spark and AI Agents
events.summary: At a Microsoft event in San Francisco on Wednesday, Jensen Huang and Satya Nadella outlined how NVIDIA and Microsoft are co-engineering hardware and software for AI agents to run on Windows PCs. NVIDIA was founded because of Windows, Huang said. Now AI agents are coming to Windows. “If you look at the entire journey of our company, Windows was at the core of it,” Huang said, tracing back NVIDIA’s support for Windows and Microsoft over several decades. “If not for Windows there would be no GeForce.” NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang connected that history — and his long-term vision — to the agentic era Wednesday during a fireside chat with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted by Sriram Krishnan, a former senior White House policy advisor on AI at the Windows AI and Surface event, held at Dogpatch Studios in San Francisco. “The thing that I really give Jensen all the credit for, quite frankly, is that consistency of vision of what this can be—not today, not tomorrow, but as a secular trend,” Nadella said. “And that’s what brings us to this moment.” “The personal computer is the ultimate tool, it’s my ultimate tool, and for a whole generation of people, it’s our ultimate tool,” Huang said. “What happens in the era of agents, when the agent is on your computer? It is now your personal assistant.” The event opened with Nadella before Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and Devices, walked through the Windows updates designed for the agentic era. Turning Windows into a secure platform for agents, Microsoft announced general availability of Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), the OS-level infrastructure that lets agents run safely and persistently in the background, under operating system control. “We are building these primitives directly into Windows, so agents can be secured, observed and governed,” Davuluri explained. “With MXC, Microsoft Security, and Agent 365, we’re unlocking the full potential of agents on Windows.” Nadella returned to that theme in his talk with Huang. “We needed to make the desktop the most secure place for agents to execute,” Nadella said. “What Satya just said is going to be the foundation of the next generation of IT as we know it,” Huang said. “Just as Windows and DirectX revolutionized how applications were built, MXC is going to revolutionize how agents are built and deployed.” A New Beginning for Windows PCs: Preorder RTX Spark Laptops Today Among the announcements Huang and Nadella outlined Wednesday, RTX Spark puts the full NVIDIA AI stack into Windows laptops and compact desktops, with laptop preorders open today and available October 16. Compact desktops will be available for sale in November. Windows is bringing local AI closer to everyday work, while new hardware gives developers room to run increasingly capable models right on their PC. Introducing Surface Laptop Ultra, Pavan Davuluri tied that vision to NVIDIA RTX Spark. “We built Surface Laptop Ultra around NVIDIA RTX Spark. With up to 128 gigs of unified memory and up to a petaflop of AI compute, you can run models on this laptop that simply don’t fit on a traditional machine,” Davuluri said. Systems are coming from Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, MSI and Gigabyte with designs ranging from slim laptops to compact desktops built for always-on agents. RTX Spark combines an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores, and an up to 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU connected at 600 GB/s. One petaflop of FP4 AI performance and up to 128GB unified memory makes RTX Spark effective for local AI. It can run models such as Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 125B model with 51B n-gram that matches the intelligence of many cloud models, unmetered and without sending data to the cloud. RTX Spark runs the full NVIDIA CUDA platform — the same software stack that runs across NVIDIA hardware — and is built for every way people use a PC: Developers can move models, tools and workflows without rewriting, running the same NVIDIA AI stack from RTX Spark to DGX Station. Creators get 5th-generation Tensor Cores with NVFP4 support, hardware-accelerated AV1, and 4:2:2 video encode and decode, DLSS and RTX ray tracing across the full production pipeline. Gamers can run AAA games at 1440p over 100 frames per second with DLSS 5, Reflex and G-SYNC. The compact desktop configuration puts the same RTX Spark superchip in a small chassis designed for 24/7 operation — a dedicated local AI system that keeps agents running continuously. Preorder RTX Spark today . NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows: Frontier AI Compute on the Enterprise Desktop The event previewed NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows today — the first deskside AI supercomputer to bring GB300 Grace Blackwell-class AI infrastructure directly into the Windows ecosystem. “This unlocks the power to run frontier-class models locally,” Davuluri said. “Capabilities that once required renting a cluster, now in a deskside supercomputer.” Until now, DGX Station ran on Linux — which meant enterprise developers maintained two separate environments: Linux for heavy AI workloads and Windows for the productivity tools, applications and workflows. The vast majority of Fortune 500 companies are standardized on Windows, and that gap has cost developers time and resources — developers either moved to Linux to access AI compute, or stayed in Windows with limited hardware options for heavy-duty model development and multi-agent workloads. NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows runs on the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip, delivering 748GB of coherent memory and up to 20 petaFLOPS of FP4 AI compute — enough to run models up to a trillion-parameter scale locally. Teams of developers and researchers at AI-native companies, leading research labs and enterprises can build and run always-on AI agents that connect directly to the Windows applications and infrastructure they already use, and fine-tune and inference large models without leaving their primary machine. Linux AI toolchains remain accessible through WSL when needed. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows and sign up to be the first to know when it’s available. events.title: These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out
events.summary: Aditya Ramabadran, Simon Mahns, and Tobias Gessler, three AI engineers at a startup called Axiom , recently fancied In-N-Out Burger for lunch. They weren’t about to drive themselves, though. Sitting in a 2024 Toyota Corolla near the Bay Area restaurant’s drive-thru lane, they opened a laptop and asked OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to take the wheel. They linked a chat interface to a server, which was connected to several windscreen-mounted cameras and the car’s power steering system. A safety driver kept one foot above the brake, just in case. The AI model, which is normally tasked with generating text, code, and the odd image, slowly but surely navigated the vehicle up to the take-out window so they could collect their food. “Maybe AGI is here after all,” one of the engineers remarked, referring to artificial general intelligence , the much-ballyhooed idea of machines that can match human intelligence. Self-driving cars are nothing new, of course, but they’re normally operated by algorithms specifically trained and engineered for the task. In this case, the operation came from a model designed to output text, and it happened on the fly, with no prior coaching by the trio. The fast-food stunt, as well as a number of other experiments , suggest that language-based AI models are starting to gain a rudimentary but useful understanding of the physical world. Though nothing overtly alarming happened during the trio’s lunchtime jaunt, they admit that putting a general-purpose model in charge of a fast-moving, two-ton hunk of steel is a high-stakes undertaking. As physical understanding improves, we could see AI models reach into the real world in impressive—and perhaps dangerous—new ways. Today’s smartest models are incredibly good at answering complex questions and even performing some virtual tasks autonomously , but their skills tend to be limited to the world of computers and the internet. Take these models into the real world and they quickly become befuddled. Despite claims that AGI has arrived , AI companies evidently see physical reasoning as a yet-to-be-conquered frontier for AI. Some researchers have left big companies to found startups focused on solving physical reasoning. Andrew Dai, the CEO of one such outfit, called Elorian AI, previously worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He says better visual reasoning will open up a lot of new applications for AI, like systems that understand whether diners are enjoying their meal in a restaurant or robots capable of functioning in a home. Dai says robotics is a crucial test case for physical reasoning skills. “It’s pretty essential for robotics,” he says. “You can’t really imagine home robotics without this.” Elorian and Scale AI, a company that provides training data to big AI labs, recently developed a new benchmark , Humanity’s Sixth Sense, which measures models’ ability to understand physical scenes. “Most visual AI research is about perception,” says Xingang Guo, a research scientist at Scale AI who was involved with developing the benchmark. “We wanted to ask what it would actually take for a model to understand a scene intuitively, the way a person does without thinking about it.” For Ramabadran, Mahns, and Gessler, the goal with their In-N-Out project, done outside of their work at Axiom, was to measure how well models can operate in the messy real world. They got the idea to test models’ driving skills while hanging out one weekend. They noticed that models like Astra were capable of building complex 3D simulations, and wondered if it might translate to an ability to navigate the real world. “We all live in the Bay Area, and we’re exposed to Teslas and Waymos, so maybe that played a role,” Ramabadran tells me. The engineers tried testing SpaceXAI’s Grok before experimenting with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic. At first, the models refused to take control of the vehicles—they spat back things like, “I can help interpret road images, but I can’t issue motion commands to a physical car.” But with a little careful prompting, they could be coaxed into going further. The three were stunned when models began driving. The engineers say big AI companies seem to be focusing on improving the spatial reasoning capabilities of their latest models, but they doubt this means they’re actually training them to drive cars. The models’ vehicular talents likely materialized as part of training focused on 3D reasoning, they say. “This could be like an emergent capability of just scaling up the multimodality of the model,” Mahns tells me, referencing inputs like images, video, and 3D models that are now used to train models. Still, a new vehicular benchmark from the trio, called DrivingBench , suggests that these models still have a long way to go before they could pass a driving test. The benchmark measures a model’s ability to drive around a simple course, set up in a parking lot. Only Astra is able to complete the course—and very slowly at that.

events.summary: Governments around the world are hardening their AI stances as more agentic hacks breach critical systems. South Korea’s president noted “ considerable public concern and anxiety” following revelations that hackers used an AI system to execute recent cyberattacks against banks in the country. And officials from OpenAI and Anthropic faced questions from lawmakers in Australia on Tuesday, after the ChatGPT maker drew criticism for not alerting Canberra fast enough after one of its models gained unauthorized access to a government health data portal during internal training and evaluation. Tech companies are playing whack-a-mole around the world as their models get up to more hijinks and are used for malicious purposes. (It’s unclear what specific AI was used in the South Korea hack, though hackers reportedly used a Chinese-made open-source agent that can run on models from Anthropic, OpenAI, or DeepSeek.) Insurers are also taking note, and preparing for multimillion-dollar lawsuits over rogue AI agents — and weighing whether executives could be held liable , the Financial Times reported. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: US and China take different approaches to AI agents
events.summary: US and Chinese tech companies are taking differing approaches to bring AI agents to the masses, the industry’s latest fixation. OpenAI’s recently released dots and Meta’s Muse are built around the assistant first and then sent out to use other companies’ websites and services. Chinese counterparts, including Tencent’s Xiaowei — which is built into super-app WeChat — can, for example, place orders from businesses that are already on the app. It’s an obvious use for closed systems like WeChat and Alipay, which Chinese consumers already use for much of daily life. Xiaowei’s strategy may not translate into revenue , the Hello China Tech newsletter wrote: Tencent earns no new fees from purchases, and early tests show it making mistakes. It begs the question whether the super-app strategy limits how useful Chinese agents can become since Xiaowei can only assist with what’s available inside WeChat, and other Chinese platforms have blocked agents from outside. Muse and dots may not be a seamless experience either, given Muse has already been blocked by Amazon and both require users to turn over access to private systems, but their popularity already suggests markets are watching closely. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Microsoft looks to reboot the AI PC with Nvidia
events.summary: Microsoft on Wednesday unveiled a new class of Nvidia-powered Windows laptops, its latest effort to tie the operating system more closely to the AI boom. Why it matters: Microsoft is trying to carve out a high-end laptop category for people who want to run demanding AI workloads locally, rather than rely entirely on the cloud. Driving the news: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House AI official Sriram Krishnan were on hand in San Francisco as the company officially launched Microsoft Surface Ultra, a high-end laptop powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark chip that starts at $2,599. "We have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang said. Microsoft previewed the laptop back in June but left out key details around price and exact availability. It said at the time that Nvidia-powered devices would also be coming from the likes of Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, among others. Those devices, and the Surface Ultra, will be available starting Oct. 16. On the software side, Microsoft unveiled a version of Copilot that can work using local models alongside those in the cloud, and the company also announced that Meta is bringing its Muse personal agent to Windows. The big picture: Microsoft's first push into AI-powered Windows machines, known as Copilot+ PCs, got off to a rocky start after the delay of Recall, its signature feature. Between the lines: Microsoft's pitch for on-device AI is that developers' appetite exceeds their companies' AI budgets, with the ideal being an approach that uses both frontier models in the cloud and local models when they can be effective. "Hybrid intelligence exists because people's appetite for intelligence is effectively unlimited," Microsoft executive VP Pavan Davuluri said. And before it even got to the hardware, Microsoft spent a fair bit of time outlining how it is making Windows more secure, ensuring that agents' actions are separated from those taken by humans and remain within preset limits.
