events.title: Why your boss matters more than remote or hybrid work when it comes to burnout and job satisfaction
events.summary: Long-standing factors contributing to job satisfaction, such as feeling appreciated, still matter more than the type of workplace format. Luis Villasmil on Unsplash , CC BY The post-pandemic push to bring workers back to the office has left many nostalgic for more flexible arrangements , such as hybrid or remote work. But a wealth of data since the pandemic now suggests that workplace factors like feeling appreciated and having a good relationship with your manager are much more tied to job satisfaction than the actual time spent in the office. To understand this insight, it’s important to recognize that a return to the office can mean very different things to different workers. Someone who values uninterrupted time at home may resent the commute. A younger trainee struggling to learn the job may welcome easier access to colleagues. An employee who dislikes their manager may lament having to see them in person. These differences help explain why the return-to-office debate often produces conflicting answers. As a researcher of the ways technology is changing the workplace, I co-authored a study with business and accounting scholar Jason Schloetzer that analyzed responses from nearly 165,000 U.S. employees between 2020 and 2023 from the database Payscale. These surveys let us look beyond location to ask whether employees felt appreciated; considered pay fair and transparent; received useful communication; had chances to develop; and enjoyed a good relationship with their manager. Once we accounted for these and other job-specific variables, we found that the edge in satisfaction for fully or mostly remote workers disappears. The only group of employees who felt more satisfied on the job were those who sometimes worked remotely – and that difference was modest. In other words, long-standing factors shaping job satisfaction outweighed workplace format when it came to making employees happy. The workplace behind the work arrangement Semi- or fully remote workers may appear more satisfied . But other factors, such as having better pay or more supportive workplace practices, need to be taken into account, we argue. Employees’ relationships with their managers is one of those variables. We asked employees to rate the statement “I have a great relationship with my direct manager” on a 5-point scale, with 4 or 5 indicating favorable. The measure reflects the employee’s own assessment rather than a checklist of managerial skills; questions about communication, appreciation and development opportunities were asked separately. A favorable manager relationship was tied to higher job satisfaction across work arrangements, we found. But that association was stronger among employees working on-site than among those who always or sometimes worked remotely. One possible explanation is that working together gives employees more opportunities to benefit from a supportive manager who mentors and offers development opportunities, while distance can offer some relief when the relationship is less favorable. We also used data from the Gallup Workplace Panel to study the same workers over time. These results reinforced our findings: It’s important to consider the workplace as a whole when evaluating remote or hybrid work. Burnout and happiness are different questions Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can like their job while feeling exhausted, or they may appreciate working at home while feeling socially disconnected. That’s why we treat job satisfaction, burnout and happiness as separate values, and why we distinguish stress on a particular day from persistent work exhaustion. Looking at stress, for example, we found that it’s common across work arrangements. According to Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace report , 41% of fully remote employees reported substantial stress the previous day, compared with 46% of hybrid employees, as well as 46% of on-site employees whose jobs could be done remotely. Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can value their work while finding its demands exhausting. Job satisfaction, daily stress and burnout capture different aspects of that experience. Physicians are one example. Among physicians whose organizations participated in an American Medical Association survey in 2024, about three-quarters reporting being satisfied with their job, while almost half reported feeling a great deal of stress because of their job, such as from burdensome paperwork or staff shortages. The published summary doesn’t identify exactly how many doctors reported both, but it shows that satisfaction and widespread stress can coexist within a profession. Meanwhile, separate Gallup research on nearly 7,500 full-time U.S. employees helps explain why working conditions deserve attention. The factors most closely tied to burnout included unfair treatment, crushing workloads, unclear expectations, poor communication and support from managers, and unreasonable deadlines. Work location may ease some pressures while introducing others. Working from home can remove a draining commute, for example, while making it harder to get timely help from colleagues. But neither arrangement automatically resolves an excessive workload or uncertainty about manager expectations. Those problems require attention wherever employees work. Working apart can carry social costs The expression “work-life balance” implies that it’s healthy to engage in social activity with friends and family outside work. But as other research of mine shows, more flexibility for office work doesn’t necessarily translate into more time with other people. Among younger workers in occupations that can readily be done remotely, I found that the share of leisure time spent alone rose from about 25% to 40% from 2017 to 2024. For workers who also spend their workday alone, that means fewer opportunities for socializing both on and off the job. Time alone doesn’t have to lead to loneliness. But the finding raises a concern: Just because you gain more control over your schedule doesn’t mean that friends, family or colleagues will be available to share that time – or that you’ll make the effort to see them. Related research suggests that these concerns about social connection deserve more attention. The expansion of remote work has been tied to increases in isolation and mental distress, according to new research published by economists Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais. In a nonrandomized experiment covering almost 600,000 people, they compared changes in mental health before and after the pandemic in jobs that could and could not readily be done remotely, excluding 2020 and 2021. Remote workers living alone fared the worst. As more people have flexible work options, it hasn’t translated into more time with friends and family but more time alone. events.title: The Download: weight-loss drugs slowing aging and carbon dioxide batteries
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process. Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins.  The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. But how much can we read into these results? Read the full story on what the new findings reveal about GLP-1 drugs and aging . —Antonio Regalado 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Energy Dome and its carbon dioxide batteries Energy Dome is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . Solar and wind are among the cheapest and quickest ways to add electricity to the grid. But they’re subject to variations in weather patterns, so supplies can be intermittent. Energy Dome has an unusual solution: massive batteries that use compressed carbon dioxide to store energy for when the grid needs it. Compressing gas to store energy isn’t new. Utilities have used compressed air in underground caverns to hang on to reserves for decades. But Energy Dome’s approach doesn’t require any specific geology to work, so it could be more easily scaled to help grids around the world. Here’s how the company is using carbon dioxide to store renewable energy . —Casey Crownhart Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from mobile flood barriers and electric buses to next-generation nuclear reactors. MIT Technology Review Narrated: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason —Thore Graepel, a core member of DeepMind’s AlphaGo team Ten years ago, I watched a program I helped build stun the world by beating Go champion Lee Sedol. AlphaGo won after making a move so strange that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch. It was AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks.  This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning, one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 OpenAI has released 377 new math findings, further rattling the field They span number theory, algebra, geometry, and physics. events.title: The 5 future vehicles you need to watch for, according to Edmunds
events.summary: Automakers will debut some interesting new models in the next six months Fall is typically when automakers release the majority of their models for the new year. Most will be continuations of prior designs, but there’s also a good number that are all-new or getting major redesigns. If you’re thinking about buying a new vehicle in the next six months, it can be useful to know which ones have major changes or offer notable breakthroughs. To give you an inside scoop on what’s coming down the pike in the next few months, the automotive experts at Edmunds have picked five vehicles that promise to be well worth the wait. Nissan’s best-selling model is getting its first full redesign since 2021, and it’s a significant one. The fourth-generation Rogue small SUV debuts with a new hybrid powertrain called E-Power that works more like an electric vehicle than a traditional hybrid. A small gas engine acts as a generator, recharging a battery that powers the electric motors driving the Rogue. The result is reduced noise and quicker acceleration compared to the regular Rogue, Nissan says. Nissan also estimates that the Rogue Hybrid will get 38 mpg in combined city/highway driving. That’s a bit less than what the Honda CR-V and Toyota RAV4 hybrids can do, but it’s still very good for a small SUV. Starting price: $37,065, including destination fees The Highlander undergoes a massive change for 2028, becoming an all-electric three-row SUV with a quoted range of up to 320 miles. Buyers who still want a gas- or hybrid-powered three-row Toyota SUV will need to look at the larger Grand Highlander. But you needn’t step up to the bigger version to get a reasonably comfortable third row, even for adults. Edmunds’ first drive in the new all-electric Highlander showed the new version’s way-back seat to be much more comfortable than the outgoing model’s. Besides the Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Kia EV9, there aren’t many three-row EVs aimed at bigger families, so we’re excited to see Toyota offering an all-new alternative. At the same time Audi is sunsetting the longstanding A8 flagship sedan, it’s adding a new full-size three-row SUV. The 2027 Q9 is the largest vehicle Audi has ever built, and it’s aimed squarely at rival German stalwarts like the BMW X7 and Mercedes-Benz GLS. Power comes from a 429-horsepower turbocharged V6. Inside, there’s seating for seven or a more premium six-passenger layout with second-row captain’s chairs. The Q9’s third-row seating area is considerably roomier than the one in the Q7, which also gets a redesign this year. Audi has also fitted the Q9 with all of its latest technology and driver assist features. Starting price: $89,095, including destination No 2027 model has generated more buzz among budget-conscious shoppers than the Slate Truck, the debut model from an American startup automotive company. The Truck is a bare-bones two-seat electric pickup that’s smaller than a Ford Maverick. By design, it comes without factory paint or even an infotainment touchscreen. Instead, buyers are encouraged to personalize it to their liking, up to and including the option to turn the cargo bed into a seating area and effectively turn the Truck into a five-seat SUV. The Slate Truck is an intriguing option for affordable vehicle, but go in with your eyes wide open: It lacks many features you might take for granted in other vehicles, and its estimated range of just 205 miles is a concern. Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Army to execute Fort Hood mass shooter by firing squad Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Starting price: $26,400, including destination Chevrolet’s full-size truck is getting its first redesign since 2019, and that should make it a more capable rival to the Ford F-150, Ram 1500 and Toyota Tacoma. The 2027 Silverado 1500 brings a bolder exterior design, a new interior and a standard 16.3-inch touchscreen. Two new V8 engine options join the carryover turbocharged four-cylinder and diesel six-cylinder. The 5.7-liter V8 produces 402 horsepower, while the larger 6.2-liter V8 cranks out 481 horsepower. Both are more powerful than the Silverado’s previous V8s. Expect Super Cruise — GM’s hands-free driving technology — to be available on top trims. And like all full-size trucks, there will be many variants — seven to be exact, topping out at more than $80,000 for the off-road-oriented ZR2 or the luxurious High Country. The new model year is jam-packed with big updates for some of the most popular vehicles on the market. These models we listed above will have some significant advantages over a vehicle in the here and now. Buyers shopping for new wheels will have a lot of exciting options to choose from in the next few months. This story was provided to The Associated Press by the automotive website Edmunds . Josh Jacquot is a contributor at Edmunds.

events.title: DR Congo uncovers $20B in payments to ineligible mining suppliers
events.summary: The News Fourteen major mining companies in DR Congo paid at least $20 billion to ineligible subcontractors between 2020 and 2025, the country’s subcontracting regulator told Semafor, citing recently completed checks. These findings at mining businesses, among them subsidiaries of Swiss commodities giant Glencore, Ivanhoe Mines and Chinese-Congolese joint-venture Sicomines, have prompted the regulator to plan tougher inspections this month to tackle breaches of subcontracting rules. These include the longstanding use of Congolese figureheads to disguise foreign control. Glencore declined to comment. Ivanhoe Mines and Sicomines did not respond to Semafor’s requests for comment by publication time. The regulator’s move comes as the country courts new mining investment, including from the US, and seeks to ensure that Congolese partners genuinely own and help run the businesses supplying its mines, in line with its laws. “We are open to partnership. But we don’t want people to come just for an extractive economy and leave us with holes,” Juan Ted Beleshayi, head of the Authority for the Regulation of Subcontracting in the Private Sector, told Semafor. In recent weeks, he has ordered miners to terminate about 1,800 subcontracts with suppliers lacking valid registration certificates. These include contracts with 1,540 suppliers at two subsidiaries of Glencore, alongside those involving Ivanhoe Mines, Eurasian Resources Group and Sicomines. “We really only carried out a simple check,” said Beleshayi, who took charge of the agency just over three months ago. He said he had completed checks begun under his predecessor. This month’s inspections would be “very detailed and rigorous,” said Beleshayi. Inspectors will check who owns the suppliers on paper, who calls the shots and who controls the bank accounts. Companies who fail to comply with the regulator’s decisions could face closure, he said. Know More Subcontracting represents billions of dollars to the Congolese economy — in 2025, 167 major companies declared $3.7 billion in contracts. The regulatory agency registers mining suppliers, which typically handle transport, machinery maintenance and construction among other work, and enforces rules based on a 2017 law that requires Congolese investors to own at least 51% of those businesses, with foreign ownership capped at 49%. Chinese companies dominate DR Congo’s copper and cobalt mines and have often faced criticism from the regulator for shutting Congolese businesses out of subcontracting work. Beleshayi’s predecessor, Miguel Kashal, accused Sicomines, in 2023 of keeping all its subcontracts in Chinese hands. Three years ago, Sicomines pledged to give Congolese suppliers its secondary work. A company representative said that a misunderstanding over subcontracting rules had been resolved. Beleshayi told Semafor his own inspections had found the same pattern. Sicomines did not respond to this claim. “We’re not saying foreigners have to leave. We just want a 49-51 split,” Beleshayi said. Limited financing and technical skills prevent Congolese suppliers from handling major mining contracts, researcher Fridolin Kimonge told Semafor. Ownership checks and contract cancellations alone cannot address those weaknesses. “It is not enough to cancel; there has to be a plan behind it,” Beleshayi said. Temporary exemptions would allow foreign suppliers to help Congolese businesses become partners or competitors, he said. “We will look for Congolese who understand American culture or can adapt to it, to build companies together,” he said of incoming US companies. Ruben’s view Like many African countries, DR Congo struggles to enforce laws that exist on paper. Part of the problem with its subcontracting law is finding replacements for the suppliers who break it. Congolese businesses often lack the financing and technical skills to take over major mining contracts, limiting how far the regulator can act without disrupting operations. Washington’s push to loosen China’s grip on Congolese minerals could give the regulator more options. Beleshayi expects American suppliers to accompany new US mining investments and form businesses with Congolese partners. If those companies can deliver the work and meet the ownership rules, existing suppliers would face competitors capable of replacing them. “Yes, absolutely,” he said when I asked whether that prospect could pressure companies already operating in DR Congo to comply. Conflict in mining regions, disputed licenses, slow permitting, and unpredictable enforcement have long deterred Western investors, while Chinese operators have been better able to absorb those risks. DR Congo’s recent reforms and Beleshayi’s crackdown could help signal to the US and European companies it is courting that the country is becoming a more reliable place to do business. Room for Disagreement Transparency has long been a central demand in efforts to improve DR Congo’s mining governance and local ownership alone offers no guarantee that contracts benefit ordinary Congolese, say critics. In a 2020 study of six mining companies, researcher Kimonge found that DR Congo’s subcontracting law required majority Congolese ownership but provided no mechanism to trace where the money invested in those businesses came from. He warned that gaps in the rules also allowed political and administrative officials to own suppliers and steer contracts toward their own businesses. “The situation has not improved much,” he told Semafor. Mining governance analyst Jean Pierre Okenda called repeated denunciations of figureheads as “populist rhetoric” that does not go far enough and urged the regulator to publish suppliers’ real owners and their ties to officials. Otherwise, he warned, replacement contracts could go to another set of politically connected businesses. Notable DR Congo has launched a geological survey aimed at improving knowledge of its vast mineral reserves ​to reduce exploration risk and attract investment into underexplored regions.

events.title: Dutch tax office ditches Microsoft 365 cloud for on-premises alternative
events.summary: The Netherlands Tax and Customs Administration has abandoned its planned Microsoft 365 cloud migration in favor of services hosted on infrastructure it controls, alongside European open source alternatives. Email and calendars will move on-premises in 2027, followed by storage and collaboration services later that year and in 2028. The letter to parliament from Eelco Eerenberg, State Secretary for Finance, follows an earlier decision to pause the Microsoft 365 rollout. The tax authority selected Microsoft 365 in 2025, but the decision attracted criticism. In June, the Dutch Advisory Council on ICT Assessment recommended rolling back the cloud services rollout, which had reached about 5,000 of the 47,500 employees across the tax, customs, and benefits services, rather than completing it as planned by the end of 2026. According to the board, the design of Microsoft 365 in the public cloud "falls short on information security, information processing and future-proofing." On security, the board noted concerns about sending confidential documents, which currently travel over government networks, via American servers. The board also criticized reliance on standard Microsoft encryption for sensitive data rather than Double Key Encryption, which would give the administration greater control. End-to-end encryption was not enabled by default for one-to-one Teams calls and was unavailable for group calls under the chosen configuration. To be fair to Microsoft, many of these concerns (for example, around encryption) stem from the design selected. However, others are harder to dismiss. On future-proofing, other concerns included vendor lock-in and the risk of reduced flexibility and sovereignty from choosing a single-supplier solution with one American (cloud) provider. There was also a concern about a lack of an exit strategy for when the Tax and Customs Administration wanted to move on to more sovereign alternatives. In this week's letter, Eerenberg wrote: "In 2027, the provision for mail and calendar will be realized on-premises. Later in 2027 and 2028, European open source solutions for personal storage and collaboration functionalities will follow. This allows us to work toward a sustainable and more autonomous solution for these functionalities." Increased datacenter capacity has made the on-premises option possible, Eerenberg said. The revised approach will reuse existing licenses where possible to limit additional investment. The reversal creates complications for records management, however. Some planned capabilities in the Microsoft 365 package are unavailable on-premises, and the administration is still assessing how to replace them. Microsoft is no stranger to public bodies in the Netherlands, and a recent report showed that a majority used the company's cloud services. However, concerns about US authorities' ability to compel disclosure of data held by US providers under the CLOUD Act have loomed large in recent years. The risk has prompted European governments to consider reducing their dependence on US providers and moving to more sovereign solutions. It is early days, and agencies report teething trouble switching. A colorful report from Politico quoted an unnamed European Commission staffer describing the Teams alternative supplied by Element as "absolute shit" on an internal message board. The report does not establish how widespread those complaints are. The Matrix protocol underpinning Element's software also powers the French public sector messaging service, Tchap. Element boss Matthew Hodgson was upbeat about the European Commission deployment, telling The Register: "We've only had positive and constructive feedback from our actual customers; the leaders and IT functions that are driving sovereignty. "There's inevitably a few unhappy change-resistant users in large deployments, but we work in lockstep with our customers to gather feedback and incorporate it, especially during the trial phase." As for sovereignty more widely in Europe, Hodgson said: "European governments are moving to alternatives that give them greater sovereignty. They can't leave themselves exposed to being deplatformed, and they recognise that traditional centralised technology isn't resilient enough for an increasingly unpredictable geopolitical climate." Frank Karlitschek, founder and CEO of Nextcloud, a vendor of storage and collaboration software, said: "It is great to see Dutch tax authorities have decided to work toward a sovereign digital workplace. This will benefit the resilience of their operations. "European Public sector organizations mostly use software from a few large, proprietary providers, which has led to strong dependencies. "Organizations have recognized the risks of digital dependencies and are looking for better options to have full control over their data, infrastructure, and underlying technology. The organizations now aim to build a more resilient IT stack." Karlitschek noted a trend forming across Europe. According to Nextcloud, it added more than two million sovereign workspace seats in 2025. Microsoft declined to comment. ®

events.title: Nigeria's $8B oil security costs spark controversy
events.summary: The News The Nigerian state oil company’s disclosure that it spent $8 billion to protect energy infrastructure has sparked calls for an inquiry into how the funds were used and cast fresh light on the country’s inability to protect key economic assets. Nigeria is Africa’s top crude oil producer and exporter, with sales accounting for around 90% of foreign exchange earnings. But oil revenue has been particularly constrained by theft and pipeline vandalism that has cost the country about $300 billion in recent years, compounding in a worsening security crisis that has hampered the overall economy. At the same time, there have long been concerns about the alleged misuse and diversion of Nigeria’s oil money, with the state company NNPC often at the center of the storm . Analysts and government critics are now raising fresh questions about the company’s $8 billion security costs in 2025, which marks a 26% increase over the previous year. “Nigerians cannot tell from these totals what was spent on pipeline surveillance,” Atiku Abubakar, a leading challenger to President Bola Tinubu in upcoming elections in January, said in a statement . “What was paid? Who was paid? For what work? Where are the results?” Tinubu ended a fuel subsidy scheme three years ago that cost $10 billion in 2022. NNPC did not respond to a request for comment. Know More NNPC reported a 33% rise in post-tax profit to $5.4 billion for full year 2025 on the back of Nigeria’s highest crude oil production output in five years. But its revenues fell year-on-year by 24% due to lower crude oil prices in the dozen or so months that preceded the onset of the Iran war this year. It owns a 5,000 km crude oil and petroleum products pipeline network across Nigeria and recorded more than a dozen breaks along its pipelines last year and five in the first six months of 2026. Alexander’s view Election season in Nigeria comes with heightened sensitivity around money flows, especially when it involves the government’s largest moneymakers. And so the discourse around NNPC’s announcement that it will charge the government $8 billion for securing oil and gas facilities has assumed political undertones with polls set to open in about 100 days. It may not account for much, however. NNPC has scaled through several inquisitions over the years, mostly unscathed, and is a much larger, consequential company for the Nigerian government than ever before. Earlier this year, a Nigerian senate committee headed by an opposition party lawmaker ordered NNPC to account for nearly $160 billion in unreconciled figures in the company’s audited financial statements between 2017 and 2023. That matter remains unresolved. Calls for a probe into the latest controversial figures — which are far much smaller by comparison — already seem to be falling on deaf ears. Room for Disagreement Attempts to damage Nigerian oil pipelines fell by 87% between 2022 and last year, a private company contracted to guard the Trans Niger Pipeline in the southern Niger Delta region said in November. It credited the improvement with increased participation of communities in providing intelligence for security. Notable TotalEnergies reached a final investment decision on a $800 million offshore natural ‌gas project last month which NNPC said affirmed the Nigeria gas sector’s “ growing viability .”

events.title: Gallego rolls out ambitious plan to insulate workers against AI
events.summary: The News Ruben Gallego isn’t sure if he’s running for president yet, but he still has big plans for his Democratic Party once it’s back in power. The Arizona senator is launching a huge, wide-reaching policy agenda on Wednesday that’s aimed at confronting a labor market — and workforce — getting reshaped in real time by the AI boom. He wants to raise the minimum wage and boost overtime pay while imposing taxes on data centers and automated jobs, in addition to creating a federal public works program to ensure US workers can cope with AI. It’s a big move by the first-term senator as his party wages a pitched fight for control of Congress in next month’s midterm elections. He said he recognizes that the public needs to start hearing about what Democrats intend to do with control in Washington, if they wrest some of it from GOP hands this fall. “People that are working right now don’t feel like their hard work is actually bringing them anything in return … and going into election season, people want to know where Democrats stand,” Gallego told Semafor in an interview this week. “With AI becoming more and more prevalent in people’s lives and fears, I think it’s also important that we have a real forward-leaning policy that deals with AI and the workforce,” he added. Gallego’s sweeping proposals certainly look like the policy engine undergirding a 2028 presidential campaign. He said he’s “not naive” about his work furthering that speculation, though he demurred on his future aspirations. “No matter what,” Gallego said, “I’m going to be involved in” policy debates after the 2028 race. “I’m not in the space right now to make a decision,” he added. “A lot of conversations have to happen between me and my wife, especially when it comes to raising kids and potentially running for office.” Know More Gallego’s plan, which he pitches with a personal touch by invoking his upbringing and Arizona’s s recent run of rapid growth and economic change, touches almost every aspect of the American economy. But he’s chiefly concerned with evident public views that wages are not keeping pace with rising prices — that the American “dream is slipping away from millions of Arizonans,” as he writes in his proposal. On top of raising the minimum wage to $20 per hour and pegging it to inflation, his agenda would promote sectoral bargaining agreements to establish labor standards for entire industries, require companies to provide paid leave, and raise overtime pay for eligible workers from time-and-a-half to double pay. He’s got equally ambitious plans for the AI industry, calling for a 10 percent excise tax on data center revenues and an end to tax incentives for those projects, a “robot tax” to discourage job losses due to automation, and consideration of a tax on AI tokens. He wants to use that money to help fund a “New Deal-style” public works program to ensure the US won’t experience “massive unemployment” from the adaptation of AI. “Data centers and AI companies cannot just be operating untouched and also unbothered in terms of what they do to our labor markets, to our communities. They need to be part of the solution and not just be a problem,” Gallego said in the telephone interview. He also wants to prioritize reclassifying certain so-called gig workers as employees rather than independent contractors and require companies to give workers more notice ahead of mass layoffs. Gallego said he’s ready to maximize Democratic authority to get it done. He proposed putting as much of his proposal as he can in a party-line budget reconciliation bill that Democrats can pass with a simple majority if they control the House, Senate, and White House come 2029. He added that Democrats should not listen to the Senate parliamentarian if, for example, a minimum wage hike gets ruled ineligible for reconciliation (as it was in 2021). “We shouldn’t be afraid to push the limits on reconciliation, on overruling the parliamentarian,” he said, arguing that Republicans have “already kind of blown up the parliamentarian primacy” anyway. Burgess’s view The rising class of Democrats has big ideas, and you can already start to see the party nearing a big debate about its agenda ahead of 2028. Gallego’s plan is one of the most expansive yet, but he isn’t the first to jump in. Sens. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Cory Booker of New Jersey have tax cut ideas. Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey wants his party to give kids universal health insurance coverage. This bold flurry is a stark contrast with Democratic leaders, who would like to start really shaping their agenda … after the midterm elections. Notable Former President Barack Obama is urging all Democrats to home in on AI as they shape their agendas, per The New York Times.

events.title: FortiBleed still a bleeding nuisance as FBI confirms ongoing attacks
events.summary: The FBI and US Secret Service (USSS) say criminals using credentials linked to the FortiBleed campaign are locking organizations out of their Fortinet firewalls. The agencies published a joint advisory on Tuesday, citing SOCRadar's verification of more than 86,644 compromised devices across 194 countries. "Based on initial responses, some victims may get locked out of their Fortinet devices if the threat actor either deletes or changes the password for original accounts on the system," their advisory [PDF] states. "During the initial intrusion, threat actors create new accounts not previously on the device. In certain cases, threat actors delete existing accounts to block organizations from accessing affected devices and to maintain persistence on the system while attempting lateral movement within the environment." The campaign targets internet-facing FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways. Criminals use credentials from earlier breaches and infostealer logs for credential stuffing and password spraying, then extract password hashes from compromised devices and crack them offline using GPU-accelerated clusters. The agencies urged organizations to restrict internet-facing management access, terminate active administrative and VPN sessions, reset passwords, and enable phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication. The advisory also links FortiBleed to ransomware campaigns, saying initial access brokers supplied compromised-network access to ransomware affiliates. The Register previously reported on the connection, identified by SOCRadar. The current evidence points to affiliates working for the INC/Lynx and Payload ransomware groups making use of the credentials, and SOCRadar said in July that it had seen at least 12 confirmed ransomware attacks stemming from FortiBleed. The agencies encouraged victims to report incidents, while noting that organizations were not obliged to provide information in response to this advisory. The FBI and the Secret Service said victim reports could help identify indicators of compromise and warned against paying ransoms. ®

events.title: Conflict in the Red Sea is forcing cloud giants to find a new route for the internet
events.summary: Google, Meta, and Microsoft are said to be securing expensive land routes as fighting around Yemen threatens the submarine cables connecting Europe and Asia. U.S. cloud giants are facing steep prices to secure backup internet routes around the Red Sea as fighting rages over the Red Sea strait that carries most data cables between Europe and Asia. More than 90% of data capacity between Europe and Asia runs through cables under the Red Sea. The cables enter the sea at Bab al-Mandab, a strait less than 32 kilometers (20 miles) wide between Yemen and the African nations of Djibouti and Eritrea . The Houthis, a U.S.-designated terrorist organization, seized Yemen’s side of the strait in September, including the island of Mayyun. On October 5, Saudi-backed government forces said they had retaken key positions around the strait and the port of Mocha — claims the Houthis denied . In September, Google bought a pair of fiber strands running along Turkish state pipelines, paying two to three times the roughly 6 million euros ($7 million) that newer lines crossing Turkey are expected to cost, said a person familiar with the deal, requesting anonymity because the details are not public. Long-distance fiber is usually sold with a single upfront payment covering 15 years or more of use. Buyers also pay a separate annual fee for maintenance. Microsoft said on September 23 that it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and land links across the Middle East by 2030. Iraq also signed a contract with Qatari telecom company Ooredoo on September 10 to carry data toward Europe through an underground route from the southern port of Al-Faw. Almost all major cloud companies are looking for backup routes around the Red Sea, the person told Rest of World . Google and Meta have started sending some live traffic through a land route across Iraq that they had previously held in reserve, the person said. Google and Meta did not respond to Rest of World ’s requests for comment by the time of publication. With Yemen’s side of the strait now contested, a single cable cut there could take months to fix, because repair crews need permission and safety guarantees to work in the water, industry experts told Rest of World . Switching to another sea cable does not help because almost all of them pass through the same narrow gap, they said. “You can have capacity on multiple cables, but if they’re all routed through the same tight expanse of water, suddenly your route resilience isn’t looking so resilient,” said Paul Brodsky, senior research manager at TeleGeography, a U.S. research firm that tracks telecommunications infrastructure worldwide. “The repair ship issue is very real.” Three Red Sea cables were damaged in 2024, most likely by the anchor of a drifting cargo ship that a missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis had disabled. Those repairs took months because crews had to wait a long time for permits, Brodsky said. “Depending on the availability of a repair ship, a cable repair might take one to two weeks,” Doug Madory, head of internet analysis at Santa Clara-based Infoblox, which runs core network services and tracks how internet traffic moves, told Rest of World . “But the last time there were cable cuts in this body of water, repairs took months because the repair ships needed assurances they would not be fired upon.” The last time there were cable cuts in this body of water, repairs took months.” Doug Madory, head of internet analysis firm Infoblox Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon use about three-quarters of the world’s international internet bandwidth , according to TeleGeography. When Iranian drones struck Amazon’s data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in March, bank and payment apps in the region stopped working, and U.S. software company Snowflake reported service disruptions . Since the start of September, cloud companies have been telling operators the minimum number of fiber strands they will start using, and by when, Martin Frank, a strategic adviser at IQ Networks, an Iraqi company that sells capacity on a fiber line it built from southern Iraq to the Turkish border, told Rest of World . Cloud companies will likely test their land backups so they are ready if a sea cable breaks, Madory said. Until then, most of their data will keep flowing under the sea. “Submarine cable routes are much cheaper, which is why they are so preferred,” he said. “I would expect land route alternatives to remain dormant until pressed into service due to a cable cut.” Cloud companies have been hoping Yemen would settle down under a normal administration, Frank said. What would end that hope is what he called an Afghanistan scenario, in which the international community accepts the reality on the ground as the new normal. “From what I see and hear, I would say that this scenario is getting more and more priced in by the day,” Frank said.

events.title: Dubai home sale transactions fall in third quarter amid regional uncertainty
events.summary: The volume and value of residential property transactions in Dubai fell sharply in the third quarter of this year as buyers became “more cautious” amid regional uncertainty over the Iran war, according to a new report. Dubai recorded home sales worth a total of Dh72.6 billion ($19.7 billion) in the three months to the end of September, down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year. The number of transactions dropped 38 per cent to 34,000, which reflected “the impact of reduced activity as the lag in property sales registrations begins to clear”, the report by property consultants Cavendish Maxwell said. “The Q3 2026 data captures a mix of recent and earlier buying activity, reflecting the time between a purchase being agreed and formally registered as a sale,” Ronan Arthur, director and head of residential valuation at Cavendish Maxwell , said. “Purchasing activity became more measured, with buyers being more cautious in the weeks and months following the start of the conflict.” The off-plan sector continued to dominate residential sales during the quarter, accounting for 65 per cent of total sales values and 72 per cent of property purchases. Dubai's property market has boomed in recent years, benefiting from government initiatives such as residency permits for retired and remote workers, expansion of the 10-year golden visa programme and overall growth in the UAE’s economy on diversification efforts. However, the market started to cool during regional tensions triggered by the Iran war that began in late February. The war also affected hospitality, tourism and aviation as the US and Israel attacked Iran, and Tehran retaliated by striking energy sites and civilian infrastructure across the Gulf region and Iraq. “While the fundamentals driving Dubai real estate demand remain, near-term activity will continue to be shaped by a number of factors, including the frequency and number of launches, regional uncertainty and a broader normalisation in buyer activity,” Mr Arthur added. Residential sales transactions fell for the first nine months of the year, Cavendish Maxwell data showed, with total volumes down 23 per cent on annual basis to 112,580 and values declining 27 per cent to Dh292 billion. A report by S&P Global Ratings also found a significant drop in Dubai's residential property transactions as a result of the war. Citing Dubai Land department data, the ratings agency said total real estate sale transactions averaged 12,644 per month between March and September 2026, a drop of 26 per cent from 17,198 in January and February 2026. It also said prices declined by 5 per cent to 15 per cent between the end of 2025 and September 2026, quoting industry reports. Price correction S&P Global Ratings expects a “gradual” price correction in Dubai’s property market. “Over the medium term, we anticipate that the UAE and Dubai governments will remain focused on developing the emirate's attractiveness through reforms and large-scale infrastructure projects. That is why, for the residential real estate market, we expect a gradual price correction rather than a rapid price decline,” it said. The ratings agency expects secondary-market transactions to become more prevalent as price declines prompt investors to offload their properties. The greatest impact could be on investor sentiment and demand within the luxury and ultra-luxury segments, it added. Emaar Properties founder Mohamed Alabbar also indicated an “adjustment of 5 per cent to 10 per cent” in Dubai’s broader real estate sector because of the war. “But then again, you know, if the situation settles, God knows what could happen in this market. It could become pretty fast [paced],” he said last month at AIM Congress in Dubai.

events.title: Iraq devalues currency as war and Hormuz closure squeeze cash
events.summary: Iraq has officially devalued its currency again, setting a new official exchange rate of 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar, according to a document seen by The National . The Council of Ministers approved the move late on Tuesday, based on a recommendation from the Central Bank of Iraq, the banking regulator said in a directive sent to all licensed banks, electronic payment companies and exchange houses on Monday. According to the directive, the new structure is that the central bank will purchase from the Ministry of Finance at the price of 1,500 dinars. The sale price to banks will be at 1,510 dinars, and then to the public at 1,520 dinars. All institutions were ordered to update their systems, notify branches, stop using the previous rate, and adopt the new price from the start of business on Tuesday, the document says. It is Iraq’s second major devaluation in six years. In December 2020, during the Covid-19 oil crash, the central bank cut the dinar rate from 1,182 to 1,450 per dollar to cover a crippling deficit. That rate was later adjusted to 1,320 as the official rate under the previous government, though the market rate often hovered higher. This time, the decision is driven by a deepening cash crunch since the outbreak of the Iran-Israel war in June 2025 and the intermittent closure and threat to the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq earns more than 90 per cent of its budget in dollars from oil exports, almost all of which must pass through Hormuz – the narrow waterway carrying a third of the world’s seaborne oil. Since the Iran war broke out on February 28, shipping insurance costs have soared , tanker traffic has been disrupted, and Iraq’s oil loadings from its southern terminals at Basra have faced delays and discounts. The result: Iraq gets fewer dollars, and when it converts those dollars into dinars to pay nearly eight million public employees, contractors, farmers and pensioners, it needs more dinars than it has. In recent months, Baghdad has delayed salary payments in several provinces, deferred payments to wheat farmers and construction firms, and relied on short-term borrowing from state banks. The country's finance ministry warned parliament that without adjustment, it could not fund the 2026 budget, which includes 100,000 new public jobs demanded by political blocs as part of government formation talks. Devaluation is the fastest fix. By lowering the dinar’s value from 1,320 to 1,500, the government gets about 13 per cent more dinars for every dollar of oil it sells – enough to print salaries without printing dollars it does not have. But the cost is passed to Iraqis. A weaker dinar makes imported food, medicine, cars and construction materials – almost everything Iraq imports – more expensive. After the 2020 devaluation, inflation jumped and triggered protests in southern provinces.

events.title: America's changing disaster risk hits energy
events.summary: Hurricanes have long dominated efforts to make the power system more resilient to extreme weather . But America's energy buildout is running into growing risks from severe thunderstorms. Why it matters: New energy infrastructure and data centers are being built in harm's way as severe weather risks shift , leaving more for developers and insurers to lose when storms hit. Driving the news: Severe thunderstorms account for 40% of modeled global insured catastrophe risk, compared with 27% for hurricanes , according to analysis from risk analytics firm Verisk. The U.S. accounts for $117 billion, or 68%, of Verisk's modeled global insured catastrophe losses . Threat level: A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, potentially creating more favorable conditions for powerful thunderstorms. But the effects of climate change on severe storms are complicated. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration research scientist Harold Brooks told Axios that other atmospheric conditions needed for severe storms may become less favorable as the planet warms. Reality check: Verisk's Jay Guin said growing exposure, more than climate change, is the dominant driver of rising insured losses, as more and increasingly valuable property is built in harm's way. Guin says climate change contributes, but expanding development and higher reconstruction costs are much larger drivers. Zoom in: America's changing energy system is creating new kinds of exposure. Verisk is assessing risks to renewable projects in tornado- and hail-prone areas, where Guin said large hail can cause major damage to solar farms. "While they are renewable, you have a new asset class that is quite vulnerable," he said. Data center developers must balance natural-hazard exposure against access to land, power and water. Some sites have billions of dollars in property and hardware, raising the stakes for siting and engineering. State of play: Tornado activity has increased about 10% in the mid-South while declining by roughly the same amount from the Texas Panhandle through western Kansas, Brooks said. Population densities in rural areas of the Southeast are roughly 100 times those in the High Plains. "It's 10 people per square kilometer in rural areas of northern Mississippi and Alabama, and so a tornado in that area can't miss buildings and can't miss people," Brooks says. Zoom out: For infrastructure, Brooks said the biggest thunderstorm-related concern is flooding. Heavy rain and flooding are "a huge threat to virtually all of our infrastructure," he said. The bottom line: "There is no ... safe climate zone," Guin said. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

events.title: Exclusive: Paxton privately blames campaign woes on Iran war, gas prices
events.summary: Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately lamented the impact of the Iran war and gas prices on his campaign in a meeting last month, telling a group of donors and lobbyists, "I don't make the decisions," according to audio obtained by Axios. Why it matters: It's a candid admission from a close Trump ally about the challenging environment Republicans face this cycle. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, was speaking to donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser in Washington, D.C. The audio was provided to Axios by a person, granted anonymity because it was a private event, who was in the meeting and is opposed to Paxton. President Trump is set to rally with Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday. Driving the news: Asked by one attendee what issues are "dragging" on his campaign, Paxton responded, "It's not tariffs. ... It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," according to an audio file obtained by Axios. "When it's over $6 per gallon for diesel ... people are feeling the pinch," he continued, adding that the rising cost of fuel "drives up food prices and everything else." The Republican candidate said affordability is "by far our biggest problem" and "why we're having a hard time with numbers." Paxton pointed to his tax cut plan — which includes new housing and health care write-offs and an expansion of the child tax credit — as his proposed remedy on affordability. "I'm just trying to figure out ways I can help people. That's the only way: I can propose legislation," he said. When an attendee posited that Paxton "can't stop the war," the candidate responded "right" and said he has "no control over gas prices." "So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable. I don't make the decisions, and I don't ... know what's behind some of the decisions," he added. What they're saying: "This is a non-story. The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store," a Paxton campaign person told Axios. "President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families' pockets." Between the lines: Paxton said in the same meeting that Trump's midterm convention in Dallas "dropped our numbers," and that control of the campaign is "all coming ... from D.C.," according to separate audio obtained by The New York Times and Politico . State of play: Paxton is facing off with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico after unseating Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in a May primary runoff . Polls of the race have largely shown Talarico narrowly leading. He would be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since the 1980s. Paxton has for years been one of Trump's most loyal allies. Trump returned the favor in the primary by endorsing Paxton despite Senate Republicans' pleas for him to back Cornyn. events.title: 3 years later, Netanyahu faces reckoning over Oct. 7 in Israeli election
events.summary: Israel is marking the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 terror attacks three weeks before an election where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's personal culpability for the country's worst-ever security failure will be a central issue. Why it matters: Netanyahu has never looked more politically vulnerable than in the weeks after Oct. 7, but he has defied expectations by keeping his government afloat — presiding over simultaneous wars and an atmosphere of perpetual emergency. Though the polls are tight, they leave a clear path for the ultimate political survivor to hang on yet again. But Oct. 7 still looms over the country and his candidacy. The opposition lambasts him for refusing to take responsibility or allow an independent inquiry into the Hamas attacks that killed around 1,200 people. Every other senior national security official who was in office at the time of the attacks has resigned, except Netanyahu. Netanyahu's chief opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, lost his son and two nephews during the war in Gaza. Sources close to Eisenkot say he sees his main mission as replacing the man he holds responsible for allowing the Oct. 7 attacks. Netanyahu blames the deep state. His political and media allies — as well as his wife, Sara — have even spread conspiracy theories implying Israel was betrayed by its own security chiefs. Netanyahu himself has claimed those security chiefs deliberately kept him in the dark and suggested he could have prevented the massacre if only they'd woken him up when early warning signs came in. Driving the news: Recent reporting suggests Netanyahu had at least some warning. Haaretz reported that United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu days before the attacks that Hamas was planning a major operation. Three sources with knowledge confirmed to Axios that UAE intelligence gave a general warning to its Israeli counterparts and that MBZ spoke to Netanyahu to make sure he received it. A former U.S. official said then-CIA Director Bill Burns was told several months later by MBZ that he had warned Netanyahu. Other outlets including the New York Times also confirmed the story. The Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal reported that Netanyahu received a similar warning ahead of Oct. 7 from Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel. Netanyahu denied ever receiving warnings from the UAE or Egypt and sued several media outlets and journalists that reported he had. Between the lines: While those stories have been widely discussed in Israel, the three violent years that have passed since Oct. 7 — the leveling of Gaza, the release of the hostages, the attacks on Hezbollah and two wars with Iran — have given Netanyahu ample opportunity to restore his reputation among many Israelis as a strong and decisive leader. By the numbers: Most polls show Netanyahu's Likud party with 20-22 seats in the Knesset, down from 32, and his right-wing coalition with 50-54 — short of the 61 needed for a majority. But the opposition is also unlikely to secure a majority without the support of Arab-Israeli parties, which are projected to win a combined 12-14 seats. Polls reported by Netanyahu mouthpiece Channel 14 show the opposite, projecting the prime minister and his coalition winning a decisive 63-seat majority. Seizing on the right-wing turn in Israeli society, Netanyahu has pressured his main opposition to rule out forming a coalition with the Arab-Israeli parties. That taboo could keep Eisenkot from taking power, though he could try to cobble together a minority government. One possible scenario, if the polls prove accurate, is a hung parliament with Netanyahu staying on as a caretaker prime minister until another election is held. The vote could determine not just Netanyahu's political survival, but his legal future as well. Losing power would also mean losing any levers to delay or influence his ongoing corruption trial. But if he wins, Netanyahu could argue he was acquitted by the people of Israel — and take stronger action to thwart the proceedings. The intrigue: President Trump could give Netanyahu a boost by endorsing him, but so far he's declined. Asked several times recently by Time magazine whether he supported Netanyahu, Trump dodged the question. He added, however, that he didn't believe the press reports that MBZ had warned Netanyahu. Trump has privately blamed Netanyahu for the Oct. 7 failures, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president. He's also mused about Netanyahu damaging Israel's international reputation. However, Trump has stuck close to Netanyahu during the war in Iran and may still endorse him. What to watch: Israel's election takes place a week before the U.S. midterms. If Democrats take back one or both houses of Congress, that will set up a battle over arms sales to Israel and even over the fate of $3.8 billion in annual military assistance. The tenor of that debate may hinge in part on whether Netanyahu remains in power.

events.title: "Not safe for kids": Advocacy group urges OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT
events.summary: Common Sense Media is urging OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT, saying its new teen experience poses an "unacceptable risk" after extensive testing found shortcomings in safeguards meant to protect younger users. Why it matters: OpenAI has made protecting younger users a central part of its effort to make ChatGPT safer, but the findings suggest some of those protections may give parents more confidence than they warrant. "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Driving the news: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute said it tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds. The group found ChatGPT generally did not provide instructions facilitating suicide or self-harm, eating disorders or sexual or romantic role-play, but said it was less reliable at recognizing when a teen needed outside help. Common Sense Media said ChatGPT missed more than 1 in 4 instances in which its testers determined a crisis referral was warranted. The group also said that on more than a dozen newly created, parent-linked accounts, testers could spend up to an hour discussing suicide, self-harm or disordered eating without triggering a parental alert. Common Sense also found that Study Mode could be circumvented: Teens could choose "Show me the answer" and, during parent-set Study Hours, could easily bypass the rules. OpenAI confirmed to Axios that the ability to exit Study Mode during Study Hours is intentional, not a loophole. The company said it designed Study Hours as a more flexible experience after consulting education experts and teens, rather than as a hard parental lock. What they're saying: "ChatGPT is not safe for kids to use," Common Sense Media Youth AI Safety Institute head Tom Siegel told Axios. Siegel said that what OpenAI announced in August still has the potential to be industry-leading, but gaps remain between what was promised and the current reality. "It feels much more of a marketing announcement that really was not backed up with the engineering work." The other side: OpenAI says it has issues with Common Sense Media's methodology and findings. OpenAI says much of Common Sense's testing of parental alerts occurred before the parent and teen accounts had finished linking, a process the company says can take several hours. As for its age prediction system, OpenAI says it deliberately relies on multiple signals rather than simply accepting a user's stated age and can take up to two weeks to make a prediction. During that time, the company says users are given added content protections, though not as strong as the ones used in ChatGPT for Teens. On crisis referrals, OpenAI says its larger-scale data shows an increase in hotline resources being displayed to under-18 users during the period studied. Between the lines: Some of the disagreement reflects different ideas of what the safeguards are supposed to accomplish. Common Sense treats the ability to exit Study Hours as evidence that the parental control is ineffective; OpenAI says that flexibility is deliberate. Similarly, Common Sense's age test treats a user repeatedly identifying themselves as 13 without being moved into ChatGPT for Teens as a failure, while OpenAI says it intentionally requires multiple signals before making an age determination, while offering some strengthened protections during the time it is making its assessment. The bottom line: Siegel says parents need to have strong conversations about AI and its risks with their teenage children and find other ways to make sure they are getting support, whether it be for homework or the challenges of life. "We just can't outsource taking care of our kids to a tech product that is very early on and still quite buggy," he said.

events.title: Goodbye Warner, hello Skydance: how will the major merger really impact Hollywood?
events.summary: After a windier road than expected, Paramount and Warner are now one, under the banner of Skydance, and the film industry is set for a shake-up Hollywood’s big five have officially become the big four. Following a twist-filled saga that saw the century-old studio Warner Bros nearly acquired by the streaming giant Netflix, only to be outbid by Paramount owners Skydance, the company led by billionaire scion David Ellison. After facing legal opposition that ultimately crumbled, Warner Bros and Paramount are officially under the same corporate roof . They are divisions of Skydance, which joins Sony, Disney and Universal as the remaining major-studio players in Hollywood. The merger goes beyond film production. Eventually, the streaming services HBO Max and Paramount+ will merge into a single entity, though a timeline has not been disclosed. The television channels HBO, Showtime, CBS, MTV, Comedy Central, Cartoon Network, Nickelodeon, TNT, TBS and CNN are among many now owned by a single corporation. The presence of CNN on that list has brought particular scrutiny, given the post-Skydance meddling with the once-respected CBS News, resulting in a rocky stewardship from Bari Weiss, who has overseen a dip in both ratings and prestige for the flagship program 60 Minutes. Weiss isn’t expected to add CNN to her purview; current chair Mark Thompson will remain in place for now , and Skydance has insisted that CNN will remain editorially independent. But given Ellison’s chumminess with Donald Trump, who has long ranted incoherently about CNN’s supposed biases, the presence of an oversight board with Ellison appointees has been cold comfort. events.title: The worry hanging over private credit: Can anyone trust the numbers?
events.summary: The News The largest privately held janitor service in the US is either a thriving business or a bankruptcy waiting to happen. It depends on which numbers you’re looking at. Shares of Kellermeyer Bergensons Services, whose janitors clean 2 billion square feet of commercial property every day, have been written down to nothing. And valuations on several loans held by its biggest financial backer, a private-credit affiliate of KKR, range from nearly 100 cents on the dollar — a full recovery that is nearly unheard of when equity is wiped out — to around 10 cents. The chief investment officer of the fund, FS KKR Capital Corp., said on an earnings call a year ago that Kellermeyer had stabilized and was receiving interest from buyers. None has materialized. Kellermeyer is one of a number of companies referenced in lawsuits filed in recent months that accuse funds managed by some of Wall Street’s biggest names of inflating their marks, often to increase their own payouts. The cases against FS KKR, Ares, and Blue Owl strike at the biggest question hanging over private credit: Can anyone trust its marks? The firms dispute the allegations and say the fees they charge are fair and industry-standard. Kellermeyer didn’t respond to requests for comment. Step Back Unlike stocks and bonds, whose prices are quoted on screens across Wall Street, managers of private lenders have broad leeway to value their loans, with varying degrees of input from third-party services. These firms charge fees based on the value of their holdings, adding a financial incentive to keep the marks higher to avoid public scrutiny. Last week, the Securities and Exchange Commission sent a rare warning shot to accountants, urging additional “rigor” in how private-credit firms are valuing the loans they hold and how risks are disclosed to investors. While it was couched in a technical note to in-house accountants, it signaled a watchful eye from regulators that have so far left the market alone. The second-order effects are also crystallizing. Semafor reported this week that the Federal Reserve has been probing how banks that lend to private-credit firms vet the loans that serve as their collateral, an admission that has spooked investors on Wall Street and around the world. FS KKR said it plans to “defend the matter vigorously through the appropriate legal process.” A Blue Owl spokesman said the lawsuits’ claims were “without merit and we intend to zealously defend ourselves.” Know More The series of lawsuits, filed on behalf of investors in the funds, come not from a Wall Street ankle-biter but one of its consummate insiders. Jim Woolery was a dealmaker at the white-shoe law firm Cravath before leaving to run M&A at JPMorgan. He later became a hedge fund investor and now runs a boutique law firm, Woolery & Co., which is accusing Wall Street firms of clinging to high valuations to boost their own fees. The lawsuits also attack the practice of charging fees on paper IOUs that are racked up by borrowers unable to make cash interest payments. The additional debt, known as “payment-in-kind,” gives temporary breathing room to companies but can encourage can-kicking by lenders reluctant to acknowledge a dud in the portfolio. In other words, the lawsuits claim, fund managers are charging fees based on interest they may never collect. More than one-third of the net investment income Blue Owl’s technology-focused lending fund reported last year was PIK interest, according to securities filings. The fund charged $468 million in fees, including an estimated $62 million of incentive fees related to PIK income that the lawsuits say investors should be able to claw back. Notable There’s “good PIK” and “bad PIK.” Not all pay-in-kind is created equal.

The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) proposes that 128 thresholds across banking, insurance and credit unions increase automatically with nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) going forward. These thresholds cover which regulatory rules apply to firms, how they do so, and what firms are required to report to the PRA. The proposals would modernise the framework by increasing the proportionality and decreasing the costs of compliance for many firms by replacing the manual ad hoc updates that currently take place. Providing more certainty for firms would assist in their business planning and thereby reduce firms’ barriers to growth. The largest in-scope threshold is the £320 billion total assets threshold for detailed capital reporting, with the smallest being a £7,500 threshold covering amounts owed to a credit union by an individual. Other significant thresholds involved include the size of an insurer subject to Solvency UK and the Small Domestic Deposit Takers regime total assets threshold. The first update would take place on 1 July 2031, with further updates occurring every five years thereafter. The package is expected to benefit all firms, but particularly small and medium sized firms hovering under regulatory thresholds – thereby supporting competition, economic growth and provision of services to the economy. Katharine Braddick, Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation at the Bank of England and CEO of the PRA, said: “This modernisation will significantly help financial services firms plan for the future, offering crucial stability and predictability, while also preventing out of date thresholds becoming restrictive barriers to growth.” The PRA chose nominal UK GDP – published by the Office for National Statistics – as the indexation metric as it captures both changes in prices and real economic growth, which other measures like the Consumer Price Index or real GDP growth would not do. The regulator proposes every five years for indexation to balance recurring adjustment costs for firms with thresholds being responsive to economic changes – and invites views on the package as a whole. Today’s announcement builds on other recent reforms from the PRA designed to provide a stable environment for growth, including: Implementing Basel 3.1 in a capital-neutral and internationally-aligned manner to support the largest firms, while introducing Strong and Simple for more straightforward requirements for smaller firms; Proposing new liquidity rules to ensure banks can monetise liquid assets quickly in a fast-paced stress event; Consulting on reforms to the ring-fence to allow firms to share operational resources more flexibly. The consultation opens on 7 October 2026, and closes on 7 February 2027. Read the full consultation . The PRA recognises that not all regulatory thresholds are suitable for automatic indexation, and has therefore excluded some from this proposal. Some of these – primarily those where the PRA would particularly appreciate further industry input on their suitability, as well as those thresholds that are jointly owned with the Financial Conduct Authority – have been included in a parallel discussion paper to consider whether they should be part of automatic indexation, which can be read under Section 4 of CP13/26 . events.title: Homeless Shelters Around Phoenix Are Full. His Phone Is the Unofficial Hotline for Struggling Families.
events.summary: Austin Davis, center, a 26-year-old poet and advocate for homeless people, has become a point of last resort for families who are experiencing homelessness in the Phoenix area. For about a year, Austin Davis’ phone has been flooded with hundreds of pleas for help from across the Phoenix metropolitan area. A school employee wanted to help a homeless family but couldn’t find space at a shelter. Could Davis pay for a hotel room? A mother of five living in a storage unit contacted a homeless services organization for help. They told her to call Davis. A mother panhandling with her six children said passersby gave her Davis’ phone number, telling her he might be able to provide shelter. “I feel like the worst mother in the world,” she texted him. Nearly every person who’s reached out to Davis, a 26-year-old poet and advocate for homeless people, says they’d first called 211, seeking help through the official channel, only to learn it could be months before they’d get shelter or a housing placement. His phone has become the unofficial hotline for emergency shelter. Caseworkers, teachers, social workers, police and hospital workers have called and texted to see if Davis can help people without a place to go. Even workers from the official channel — 211 and the Family Housing Hub — have sent people to him. Davis’ path to becoming the de facto advocate of last resort illustrates how the system set up to care for families who are homeless in Maricopa County is failing them. ProPublica found that calling and visiting the official channel to address family homelessness rarely leads to offers of help, leaving families feeling hopeless. Davis’ nonprofit, AZ Hugs, holds daily food distributions at “The Hill” for homeless people in Phoenix. In January, I started coming to Tempe’s Moeur Park, known as “The Hill,” to meet the families Davis was assisting. I was struck by the scene of desperate parents, some of whom had recently been evicted, lost a job or fled domestic violence, surrounding Davis to tell him about their situation. As he listened, he played with their children, always with an energy drink in hand. The scene was both heartening and disconcerting. Davis was helping families stay off the street, which was good. But why, I wondered, in a county of nearly 5 million people, was a man in a park their best chance at getting help? And why were government agencies and multimillion-dollar nonprofits, some tasked with helping the very same homeless families, sending people to him? Davis, who runs a small nonprofit called AZ Hugs, is known for working outside the system. With the help of volunteers, he hosts a nightly meal for homeless people at a suburban Phoenix park. This has drawn the ire of Tempe officials and led to 35 citations against him for trespassing and holding picnics without permits. (In 2024, he reached a deal to plead guilty to one permit violation, and the city dismissed the other citations, according to court documents. He’s spent three nights in jail.) In 2025, Davis and two other advocates for homeless people filed a lawsuit against Tempe, alleging it had violated their free speech protections by citing them for feeding people in parks. The city revised its permit ordinance, and Davis withdrew the lawsuit. In recent months, he has tried to draw attention to what he calls the “family homelessness crisis,” raising money on social media to pay for hotel rooms for families, many with young children, who would otherwise sleep on the street or in their cars. Davis said he cannot assist everyone who asks for help. A much bigger effort is needed, he added, involving nonprofits and local and state officials, but he sees little evidence that it’s happening. The number of people in homeless families in Maricopa County reached 2,103 this year, its highest level since 2015, according to the latest figures that are compiled locally and reported to the federal government. And those numbers are considered an undercount because the tally is taken on a single night by volunteers who can miss people who are trying to stay out of sight. In late September, nearly 200 families were on the waitlist for shelter in the county. It doesn’t include those who couldn’t get on; were kicked off because they weren’t considered homeless; or those who called 211, found it unhelpful and never called back. (Solari, a nonprofit that runs the statewide 211 line, said that the Family Housing Hub, which is run by UMOM, a nonprofit, sets the eligibility criteria for placement on the shelter waitlist.) I spoke to more than 30 families searching for shelter. Parents told me they worried how their situation was affecting their children. Research shows homelessness harms children, disrupting brain development and growth and leading to permanent changes in the brain and body. Davis’ phone is flooded daily with pleas for help from people who are homeless across Maricopa County. Blurred for privacy by ProPublica Candice Ortiz had tried since spring to find stable shelter and housing. As the months dragged on, she noticed the toll on her 8-year-old son. He was hospitalized for heat exhaustion after spending the day outside, and she worried about the school he missed. Davis helped Ortiz as she hit dead ends in her search for a place to stay, according to text messages reviewed by ProPublica. She said she had called 211 over and over, answering the same questions about her living situation, only to receive information she could have found through a simple internet search. She said a worker with the Family Housing Hub told her that since she and her children were sleeping in her car, she wasn’t actually homeless. Another told her the waitlist was full. In June, she spent the day at a Phoenix cooling center to escape the heat. A representative told her to go to UMOM, which runs an emergency shelter for families. She said she used her last $20 on a rideshare to the shelter. They took her information again and told her she wasn’t “in the system.” Nothing was available. UMOM said to protect the privacy of clients, it does not comment on individual families. At the end of August, she connected with the Phoenix Rescue Mission, a nonprofit that offers programs for homeless people. The group sent Ortiz to a local apartment complex where she viewed an apartment. Later, a worker with the Phoenix Rescue Mission told her that it ran out of funding to pay for it, text messages reviewed by ProPublica show. Phoenix Rescue Mission did not respond to requests for comment. UMOM, which during the last fiscal year received more than $7 million in government grants, set aside 23 units of shelter and about a dozen tents for families this summer, as temperatures reached 117 degrees. The program, which is part of the city of Phoenix’s heat relief effort, has helped nearly 300 households so far but is winding down this month. In early April, Davis had tried to force a broader effort to address the crisis by launching an online petition .
