events.title: Trump haters are more confident in election integrity, poll finds
events.summary: Democrats are much more likely than Republicans to have confidence in the honesty of US elections, despite President Donald Trump and his party controlling Washington. Sixty-three percent of Democrats say they have confidence in election integrity, according to Gallup polling , compared with 37% of Republicans and just 35% of independents. For the first time this year, the Americans who disapprove of current US leadership are much more likely to have confidence in US elections than those who approve of it. The polling punctuates widespread Democratic warnings about Trump laying the groundwork for interfering in the midterm elections by asserting more control over mail-in voting and dispatching Justice Department monitors to polling places. It also makes the US an outlier: In the more than 100 countries Gallup polled, people who approve of the country’s leaders almost always have higher confidence in election integrity than those who disapprove. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Trump Account changes could take heat next year
events.summary: The Trump administration’s recent changes to Trump Accounts could come under fire from the next Congress if Democrats win a majority. The Treasury Department moved last week to automatically enroll tens of millions of children and greenlight donations of individual stocks as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent touts the accounts ahead of midterms. President Donald Trump “believes that the American dream belongs to every child and every family — and today, through Trump Accounts, we are equipping the next generation to claim it,” Bessent said in Pennsylvania this week. But Democrats believe that the individual stocks lack statutory authority and that the automatic enrollment could prevent savers with religious or other concerns with the stocks from opting out, House aides told Semafor. Libertarians expressed similar reservations: “There’s more than enough information available to people” that they “can decide on their own,” the Cato Institute’s Norbert Michel told Semafor. “It’s just not the case that the fact that they have something makes them better off.” The Treasury Department did not return a request for comment. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: No Gaza peace three years after Oct. 7
events.summary: Three years since the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks on Israel, the path toward peace in the resulting Gaza war remains murky. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace unveiled a $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan at a recent meeting, but the endeavor’s eventual goals — getting Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw, and then rebuilding Gaza — remain far out of reach. The Gaza war is one of multiple conflicts vexing the Trump administration, which has also struggled to wind down the Iran war and Russia’s assault on Ukraine. The Oct. 7 attacks “were a horrific atrocity, and we remember all the victims who were killed at the hands of Hamas,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. “Three years later, there is a ceasefire, all hostages are home, and President Trump remains committed to ensuring Hamas can never pose this kind of threat again while helping the people of Gaza start a new chapter free from the tyranny of Hamas.” — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Democrat rolls out AI liability proposal
events.summary: A leading House Democrat is rolling out draft legislation to clarify liability for AI developers when their agents cause harm in direct response to the rogue AI hack of Hugging Face earlier this year. According to an announcement shared first with Semafor, Massachusetts Rep. Lori Trahan’s “CLAIM Act” would make it easier for third parties to sue AI developers while clarifying questions around intent related to AI agents’ conduct. “When someone breaks the law and hurts you, you can take them to court. That shouldn’t change just because the wrongdoer is an AI agent,” Trahan said. Trahan, who previously joined Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., in a bipartisan push to draft AI regulations, is framing the liability push as a way to incentivize AI developers to embrace safety. The legislation would also set a federal floor, rather than preempt state laws.

events.title: Progressive groups lay out AI demands for candidates
events.summary: The Scoop A coalition of nearly 40 labor, progressive, faith, and AI safety groups is laying out demands for AI legislation in Congress, warning lawmakers that any bill that crosses their red lines will face “active, mobilized opposition,” according to a letter shared first with Semafor. The letter is spearheaded by Guardrails Action, the nonprofit affiliated with Guardrails Alliance, the super PAC launched in June as a counterweight to pro-AI election groups. The group is calling for “independent, transparent government oversight with real enforcement power” and “a mandate that addresses human impacts from safety to economic disruption.” They also want to ensure that “AI models are not making final decisions such as denying people health care or benefits, firing or disciplining workers, or deploying weapons,” and that AI is a “universal benefit” to society. In 2028, Guardrails will be organizing a coalition around a “populist demand for AI-related policy” but for now, the principles will serve as a floor for what the group and its broader coalition want to see in AI legislation, said Maya Handa, a senior adviser at Guardrails and former adviser and campaigner for democratic socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “We want members of Congress and 2028 candidates to know that it’s not enough to come to the table with half measures, and they need to be ambitious,” Handa said. Know More Handa likened the push for AI regulation to progressive calls for Democrats to support Medicare for All and the Green New Deal. “We want them to be forced to weigh in on what the New Deal for AI looks like in this transformative moment. And what they should say is: that they are not beholden to billionaires,” she said. Other key groups that signed onto Guardrails’ letter include the American Federation of Teachers, the P Street Project, progressive and civil society groups, and the new group Who Decides run by Alex Bores, the former New York congressional candidate who faced a deluge of attack ads from pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. The group is not specifically endorsing or looking to knock down any specific bills in Congress yet, Handa said. The associated PAC Guardrails Alliance announced today an ad spend of $1.2 million opposing candidates backed by the Leading the Future in California, Montana, and Arizona.

events.title: Guyana: The tiny country with big ambitions fast emerging as a global oil producer
events.summary: A tiny South American country is emerging as a reliable oil supplier globally as flows from the Middle East face disruptions and European nations seek alternatives to Russia. Guyana's rapid increase in crude production, from zero in 2019 to about 900,000 barrels per day in the first half of the year, is catapulting the country to one of the world's fastest-growing economies, lifting thousands of people out of poverty with newfound wealth. The non-Opec country's oil output is expected to reach 1 million barrels per day (bpd) imminently, with the country targeting 1.7 million bpd by 2030. “With disruptions in the Middle East, Guyana’s oil is becoming strategically more important to global markets,” Stephanie Rivera, research analyst at S&P Global Energy told The National. “Guyana’s light-to-medium, low-sulfur crude is not exposed to Middle Eastern shipping chokepoints, providing refiners with an attractive option for diversifying away from Middle Eastern supply. As the conflict in the Middle East continues, Guyanese crude can help enhance energy security in an increasingly tight market.” The Middle East conflict, which broke out on February 28 after the US and Israel attacked Iran, has roiled global markets, with prices jumping to an intraday high of about $120 per barrel in April. Tehran carried out retaliatory strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure leading to curtailment of production, with 10 million bpd of Gulf output remaining shut as of August amid heightened security risks, according to the International Energy Agency report last month. The Strait of Hormuz, through which more than 20 per cent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies used to pass before the war, has been a restricted route since the war began, raising supply concerns. Europe focus Countries in Europe, North and South America have been the main importers of Guyana’s oil, but the Middle East crisis has also prompted some Asian countries to look towards Guyana for oil. Europe imported up to 57 per cent of Guyanese crude between March and August this year, Kpler data shows, with the Netherlands, Sweden, Germany, the UK, Italy, Poland and Spain being the main buyers. The Americas took about a third, while Asian nations, including China, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia, imported about 6 per cent of Guyanese crude during the period. Turkey bought roughly 5 per cent. Another factor that is contributing to a rise in demand for Guyana's crude is the Ukraine war. European nations are looking for alternative sources of supply as they seek to reduce dependence on Russian crude and squeeze off Moscow’s oil revenue as it continues to wage war against Ukraine. Guyanese crude is also highly valued for its low sulfur content, high yields of middle distillates such as diesel and jet fuel, and competitive break-even costs of $30–$40 per barrel that "make it particularly attractive to refiners, especially in Europe", Ms Rivera said. Investment of $60 billion An oil boom is a recent phenomenon in Guyana, with production starting only seven years ago following the discovery of oil in 2015. An ExxonMobil-led consortium – including Chevron, and China’s CNOOC have been dominating production, with total investment estimated at between $55 billion and $60 billion at the Stabroek Block. The group hit a milestone last month by producing its billionth barrel of oil at Stabroek less than seven years after production began in 2019. “With an estimated resource base of just under 11 billion oil-equivalent barrels and plans for up to eight offshore developments by 2030, the Stabroek block is helping meet demand across the Americas, Europe and Asia, contributing to global energy security and market stability,” ExxonMobil said in a statement last month. More projects are expected to come online, with Uaru expected to start up by the end of 2026, Whiptail expected to start up in 2027, and Hammerhead expected to begin production in 2029, it added. Last year, France’s TotalEnergies, QatarEnergy and Malaysia’s Petronas also signed an agreement with the Guyanese government to explore a shallow block off the coast of Guyana for oil production. Economic boost Oil revenue, spurred by a rise in production and higher prices, has transformed Guyana from a small, agriculture and services based economy into one of the world’s fastest-growing economies. From an annual growth rate of 5.4 per cent in 2019, when it first started producing oil, the country’s economy expanded by 43.5 per cent in the following year, 20.1 per cent in 2021, 63.3 per cent in 2022, 33.8 per cent in 2023, 43.8 per cent in 2024 and 19.3 per cent in 2025, International Monetary Fund data shows. The country's GDP is projected to grow by 16.2 per cent this year, the highest rate globally, as oil revenue continues to increase due to higher production and rising crude prices. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, is currently trading at about $100 per barrel. "The economic outlook [for Guyana] remains highly favourable," the IMF said in July. "Oil production is expected to continue expanding, and the non-oil economy is projected to grow by about 7 per cent on average over the next five years as the government continues its ambitious plans to address infrastructure and developmental needs."

events.title: Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism
events.summary: Last month at Rails World 2026, Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson gave a relentlessly optimistic keynote in which he suggested AI has all but eliminated the need for developers to manually write code. But perhaps DHH, as he is known online, shouldn’t delete his code editor quite yet. On Sunday, DHH posted about a test in which he had frontier agents implement and optimize his company’s Campfire group chat app in three languages: Elixir, Go, and Rust. He then compared the runtime performance of those versions with the original Ruby on Rails implementation. DHH’s post includes data that seemingly demonstrates the efficiency of the Rust programming language, and AI agent coding itself. But many observers came to another conclusion: Don't trust DHH’s benchmarks. As of press time, the post and accompanying chart garnered over 900,000 views. It showed the Rust rewrite of the chat app outperformed others by a wide margin on five tasks, including searching or posting a message. DHH did not say which AI services he used for these rewrites, but noted that each rewrite took only a few hours, as the original code itself, largely written in Ruby, is relatively compact. Many observers, notably advocates of other languages, quickly surmised from the source material that DHH had optimized the Rust results but didn't do the same for the other languages he tested. Whither high-level languages? Rewriting applications in Rust, often with the help of AI agents, seems to be a popular undertaking these days, with Microsoft's Copilot runtime, the pnpm JavaScript installer, and the Bun JavaScript toolchain all getting the Rust treatment. In DHH’s test, the Rust implementation handily bested the others across all five workloads, sometimes by a wide margin. To serve a “room page,” for instance, Rust knocked out 36,260 requests per second. In contrast, Ruby on Rails was only able to fulfill a paltry 241 requests, while Elixir delivered 722 requests, and even runner-up Golang only knocked out 3,860 requests a second. Rust executed the other tasks with similar alacrity, easily besting the other languages DHH used. The takeaway was obvious to DHH: Rewriting an application in Rust, or better yet having AI agents do the job, may very well result in major performance improvements for an app. DHH suggested that many factors go into choosing a programming language for a particular job, and execution speed is not the sole criterion. Rust can be agonizingly slow to compile, and for many, writing or even reading Rust code is an arduous job. DHH himself began developing Rails in 2003 while building Basecamp in the then relatively obscure Ruby programming language to ease the developer experience. He doesn’t seem to mind that Ruby ranked the slowest in his own tests. “I didn't care about [performance] when the pay-off was huge in terms of productivity and developer joy.” But AI agents don’t give a hoot about joy. “You really have to bury your head in the sand not to see that when agents write the code and validate the output, we need to adjust to a new reality,” he wrote. Chips on the table DHH’s ad-hoc test was quickly met with skepticism, criticism and outright mockery, especially on X. (It’s as if DHH’s conservative views on immigration and his work to bring yet another Linux desktop into the world didn’t give him enough headaches). “What worries me about the future of programming is you see this and don’t immediately know there must be something wrong with the results or what you actually measured,” wrote prominent Google engineer Jaana Dogan in an X response to DHH’s tests. Dogan did not elaborate on the test’s shortcomings, but many others, especially advocates of other languages, were more than happy to provide details. One Elixir advocate called DHH’s implementation “moronic,” while a couple of others actually rewrote the Elixir code to make its performance comparable to Rust’s. After that rewrite, the Elixir version of the app bested Rust’s performance on some tasks, despite further third-party Rust optimizations. DHH expressed surprise that others would assume a high-level language like Elixir or Ruby could even compete with a language like Rust, which runs closer to the metal. But he also noted on X that “It's not exactly extra points for Elixir if frontier agents can't find the magic ‘go fast’ switches.” Elsewhere, observers noted that the Rust rewrite got a lot more post-coding attention than the other implementations of Go and Elixir, both of which seemed to be quickly wrapped up after the initial agent requests. “You're not benchmarking languages, you're benchmarking how much attention each port got,” one observer wrote on X. Golang advocates were likewise unamused. “The benchmark was unfair. More time was put into the Rust code while the rest were one-shotted,” one wrote on X. Someone else even made their own chart showing how much more the Rust code was tuned compared to the quick passes on the other languages. None of these rebuttals actually negates DHH’s advocacy of using agents to code. But clearly, skipping a manual review of the resulting work will still leave a lot of potential gains on the table. ®

events.title: Your Next Great Read Might Be Certified ‘Organic’
events.summary: As scandals involving the use of artificial intelligence by professional authors pile up , a British startup has established a way for publishers to certify their books as “organic”—written by real people, no machines in sight. On Wednesday, Books by People confirmed it had received approval from the UK’s Intellectual Property Office to begin distributing a mark that indicates a published book has been authored by a human. The stamp, which looks like a thumbprint, will be displayed on the cover. “If people are going to be writing AI books or seeking it out for their own enjoyment, that’s their prerogative,” Esme Dennys, cofounder of Books by People, tells WIRED. “But if you want to read something that’s written by a person, you should be able to find that. We’re just trying to create that choice.” Previous book-labeling schemes, like Human Authored , have operated under an honesty system, where an author promises they haven’t used AI in the development process. To try to add more weight to its certification, Books by People asks for an authorship declaration, runs each manuscript through proprietary software, and manually examines early drafts and research materials supplied by the writer and editor for “indicators of humanity.” The organization is "looking at all the things that give us the best sense of whether a person wrote the work—whether the work was made during a natural process of drafting and redrafting,” says Dennys. Books by People will charge publishers a flat membership fee, plus an additional sum for every book they put forward for certification. Five publishers have signed up so far. The startup expects the new mark to feature on its first book by the end of the year. This year, the publishing industry has been caught up in a flurry of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by authors. A literary agent canceled a book deal reportedly worth $2 million; a publisher withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story had been generated with AI. Writers and publishers are not necessarily worried about being replaced by AI , industry insiders tell WIRED. They believe that few people will ultimately want to read machine-generated books. “You are essentially standing at the end of a conveyor belt, watching stuff fall off the edge. Once you know that, it prevents you from getting really emotionally invested in whatever falls into your hands from the belt,” says sci-fi author Ted Chiang, whose 1998 novella Story of Your Life was adapted into the Academy Award–winning film Arrival. “The knowledge of how something was created cannot be separated from your experience.” However, repeated scandals could shake public confidence in the unspoken rule of publishing: That every book that reaches the shelf has been authored by a real person who has not indulged in plagiarism. “Publishing has always relied on trust between the publisher, writer, and reading public. Cases where that trust is betrayed have been rare,” says Sam Jordison, codirector at independent publisher Galley Beggar Press, which intends to adopt the Books by People mark. “There’s almost a feeling of revulsion about the idea of reading an AI text that purports to be human. It feels like a con job.” Against that backdrop, the idea of a certification for human-authored books has received backing from various writers and editors. In a statement praising Books by People, Markus Dohle, former CEO of Penguin Random House, described human storytelling as “the lifeblood of our industry.” But while publishers might relish the chance to signal their commitment to “organic literature,” the routinization of AI detection is a double-edged sword for authors, who risk a false positive result spoiling their reputation . “We need to be quite careful that this doesn’t end up becoming a witch hunt,” says Tom West, CEO of the Publishers’ Licensing Services, which helps publishers to collectively license works to third parties. “Obviously, the devil is going to be in the detail.” New York–based startup Pangram , which has emerged as the leader in the field of AI detection, claims to be able to sniff out generated text with a 99.7 percent accuracy. But authors have questioned the reliability of its approach, which itself involves AI. In September, Jerry Falade, the debut author whose agent reportedly pulled the $2 million book deal, alleged that detection software had misconstrued his Nigerian dialect as evidence he had used AI. Pangram’s software scored the book as 97 percent AI-generated. “It takes months, even years to write a book,” Falade wrote in a recent essay . “It takes AI-detection software two minutes to ruin your life’s work.” (Pangram did not respond to a request for comment.) Others have warned against normalizing extreme scrutiny of authors.

events.title: COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in
events.summary: System76 is banning AI-generated content from contributions to the COSMIC desktop. Some GNOME sub-projects also restrict AI-generated contributions, but one developer is urging them to make an exception for vulnerability reports. The COSMIC desktop project has changed its contributors' guidelines. The latest version now has a clear no-AI rule, insisting that contributors declare: "I have not included any LLM (also known as AI) generated content in this PR, including code, comments, and descriptions." In other words, you can teach yourself using AI, you can find bugs with AI, but if you want to submit your code for inclusion in COSMIC, you can't use AI to write the code, its docs or notes, or even the submission requests. This position is in keeping with some other desktop projects. For instance, the GNOME Calendar guide to contributing says: "This project does not allow contributions generated by large languages [sic] models (LLMs) and chatbots." GNOME Extensions also restricts AI-generated submissions, although it permits AI learning aids and code completion. Its review guidelines spell it out: "Extensions must not be AI-generated." COSMIC is one of the newest complete Linux desktop environments, but even so, it's been under development for years. The Register first reported on the effort nearly five years ago, meaning that it's older than ChatGPT, which debuted in late 2022 (it only feels so very much longer). COSMIC does use some GNOME components, and its default config looks not unlike GNOME, with a top panel and a dock-like launcher at the bottom. There are good reasons for that: the original System76 desktop called "COSMIC" was based on GNOME, quite heavily customized with GNOME extensions. Saying that, though, this new COSMIC is a very different beast. Its first stable release shipped with Pop!_OS 24.04 in late 2025. Although it looks similar, it's an entirely new, ground-up effort, written in Rust using the Iced toolkit. COSMIC itself is Wayland-only. GNOME is much older, larger, and more complicated. The project was announced in 1997, the year after the KDE project announcement. KDE 1.0 came out in 1998, and GNOME 1.0 in 1999. In part, GNOME was a response to KDE. KDE is built on the Qt toolkit, which was not fully open source. As such, in KDE's early days, Red Hat refused to include it in Red Hat Linux. Qt is aimed at C++ developers, so KDE was built in C++. Linux, like Unix, is built in plain old C and many Unix traditionalists scorned the much more complex C++. So GNOME was built in plain old C, using GTK, the toolkit built for the GIMP. In 1998, Red Hat Linux 5.1 included a preview of GNOME, and by Red Hat Linux 6.0 in 1999, GNOME 1.0 was the default desktop. GNOME is still the default desktop in RHEL to this day, and many GNOME developers' day jobs are at Red Hat. As we noted back in March, Red Hat management is noticeably enthusiastic about AI – although six months later, it was capping developers' AI spend. GNOME is largely written in C, which lacks automatic memory safety guarantees, although other languages feature too: GNOME Shell combines JavaScript and C, and some components are written in the GNOME-centric Vala programming language. Michael Catanzaro, GNOME developer, just published a blog post titled "The Era of Software Quality, or the Era of Ostriches?" which argues that the GNOME project must accept AI-generated bug reports. This is not a new subject for him. His post links to an earlier one from June, "Please Do Not Ban AI-Assisted Issue Reports." The following month, he announced a reduction in the disclosure deadline for issues reported to GNOME Security, from 90 days to 30, effective August 1. We recently reported on the 1,313 CVE identifiers listed in Debian's latest Linux kernel security advisory. AI is resulting in the discovery of vast numbers of bugs in the equally vast codebases of modern FOSS. GNOME is one of the biggest desktops in the Linux and BSD world, with much of its code written in memory-unsafe languages. As Catanzaro says: "No matter how much we try, GNOME developers will fail [to] write secure code when using unsafe languages like C, C++, or Vala: it's just too hard for even experienced developers to do properly." We are not arguing that Catanzaro is wrong. Given the stance toward AI of GNOME's biggest sponsor, it is entirely in keeping, and he makes a strong case. All we are noting is that this could in time prove to be the thin edge of a wedge with the weight of Red Hat behind it. First the project allows AI-generated bug reports. From there, it would not be a huge step to allowing AI-assisted triage. From there, to AI-assisted fixes. Once you're letting AI-assisted code in, then AI-assisted extensions may not seem so extreme, then core components, and in time, to the desktop itself. It would be wildly controversial, just as it already is in the KDE project. That doesn't mean it won't happen – in either project. Debian decided to allow it, and of course, the kernel itself does too. ®

events.title: Family offices branch out into private equity, infrastructure and alternative investments
events.summary: EQT, one of world’s largest private markets firms, sees more emphasis on diversification and flexibility Some financial analysts and wealth managers in recent years have suggested that the second- and third-generation leaders of family offices in Asia are moving away from the basic principles that helped to create and accumulate their existing assets, but that is not strictly accurate. Rather, just as the founding generation did, these investors look to assess available opportunities and adapt to circumstances as they build or adjust their portfolios to find the preferred balance between risk and reward. What has changed, though, particularly in the last couple of decades, is the range of options open to them. Previously, the focus would typically have been on making money in property, listed equities and direct business holdings, and then passing on those assets. Now, in tune with the times, there is much greater emphasis on international diversification, flexible structures and time horizons, and active ownership, while still maintaining a prudent, long-term approach. “In our interactions with family offices, we see that the second and third generations think slightly differently about managing wealth,” says Sueann Yeo, managing director and head of Asia-Pacific global wealth solutions for EQT, one of the world’s largest private markets firms. “When in your 20s to 40s, the mindset and expectations about capital preservation, growth and returns will not be the same as someone in their 60s or 70s. In particular, many of the younger generation are now thinking about private equity, infrastructure, alternative investments and different asset-allocation strategies.” Yeo says that a number of the more institutionalised family offices have been doing this for a long time. The change, though, is that many others are now setting up programmes to scale their allocations to these newer areas materially over a five- to 10-year period. Secondaries have evolved from a niche strategy into a core portfolio management tool for family offices, rather than simply an alternative route to private equity exposure. Global secondaries transaction volumes reached a record US$226 billion in 2025, up 41 per cent year-on-year, with momentum continuing into this year as first-half volumes exceeded US$120 billion, up 20 per cent year-on-year. Rather than framing secondaries as a faster-return alternative to primary commitments, Yeo describes the two as complementary: secondaries provide an additional way to access private markets, with differentiated portfolio characteristics, broader diversification and distinct cash-flow profiles. “There are a few elements to this: an increasing level of sophistication in the understanding of private assets; more attention to DPI [distributed to paid-in capital, a metric for measuring the cash returned to investors compared with the money they put into a fund]; and a more hands-on approach to strategic asset allocation and setting limits for each category.” Yeo points to the Wallenberg model as a reference point EQT draws on for its own investment approach – a model built around patient, multi-generational capital, active support for portfolio companies and reinvestment of returns to sustain long-term growth. She believes this style of long-term, engaged ownership offers a useful frame of reference for Asia’s family offices as they weigh how to balance risk and opportunity across generations. This kind of evergreen approach enables eligible individual investors and family offices to invest into the same strategies that previously only institutions could access. It allows investment in private equity without the operational complexity of managing capital calls, distributions and reinvestment decisions typical of close-end structures, while offering more flexible, though not unlimited, access to liquidity. “Family offices are warming up to the idea of having evergreen structures, which mirrors the content of classic closed-end private equity structures for institutional investors, but with more flexibility,” Yeo says. “EQT’s private wealth strategies comprise a mix of primary funds, co-investment deals and a cash portion with a soft lock period to manage the liquidity.” Eligible investors benefit from the immediate deployment with exposure to a diversified portfolio from day one, without the need for continual involvement or decision-making. Yeo emphasises that this is just one of many options available through the EQT Private Wealth platform, which embodies the principle of active ownership to create value for the private companies taken into its portfolio. This entails a focus on governance and careful use of the right levers to improve operating performance and revenue – but without the slash-and-cut type of management overhauls often seen elsewhere.

events.title: From reactive to proactive: How endpoint monitoring is fixing broken meeting rooms
events.summary: The role of meeting rooms is changing. Traditionally, they were formal spaces built around a large central table and inflexible physical setup, reserved primarily for board meetings, client presentations, or official status updates. The rise of hybrid work and advances in collaboration technology have made that approach increasingly obsolete. Employees now come into the office to connect, collaborate, and brainstorm with colleagues rather than to undertake the solo, focused work they can do better at home. The upshot is that many meeting rooms have transformed into fluid, digitized, data-enabled hubs. With modular partitions, movable furniture, and casual seating, they are designed to adapt to whatever task is at hand. As digital nodes, they also bridge the gap between remote and office workers, so remote and in-person participants get a consistent experience regardless of location. That shift is only possible because of the convergence between IT and audio-visual (AV) equipment, explains Yannic Laleeuwe, marketing director for Barco's ClickShare visualization, collaboration, and networking platform. Cameras, microphones, and wireless conferencing, collaboration and presentation tools, such as ClickShare can now connect to enterprise networks. That allows management through centralized cloud-based systems, so IT teams can monitor, update, secure and tune these systems in ways they could not before. "Historically, meeting rooms have sat in a gray zone between facilities management, AV and IT," Laleeuwe points out. "They were physical spaces first with technology added into them over time, so they were rarely managed by IT departments with the same level of telemetry as laptops, servers or network infrastructure." The impact of reactive tech support IT professionals could often tell whether a device was connected to the network, but struggled to see how the room was being used or whether it delivered a reliable user experience. That lack of visibility explains why meeting room tech support has often been reactive, with staff only intervening once something breaks. "A room was assumed to be working until someone complained that a call wouldn't start, the audio was poor, a display failed, or remote participants couldn't follow the conversation," Laleeuwe says. "Without reliable data on usage, performance and failure patterns, IT had limited ability to predict issues, prioritize investments or optimize rooms before users were affected." The situation had knock-on effects at various levels. For employees, faulty technology creates immediate friction: meetings start late, participation becomes difficult, and unsecured personal devices get pressed into service as a fallback. An additional challenge in a hybrid world is that meeting room technology acts as a bridge between remote and in-office colleagues, so when it fails, the meeting fails with it. For IT teams, poorly maintained technology produces operational inefficiency. Rather than working to make collaboration environments more effective, they end up firefighting individual incidents. For the business itself, a lack of activity data makes facilities planning considerably harder. "Some spaces may be over-engineered with technology that's barely used, while others are under-equipped for the way people actually collaborate," Laleeuwe points out. "This leads to wasted investment, inconsistent user experiences, and missed opportunities to design rooms around real behavior rather than just assumptions." The value of telemetry Endpoint monitoring technology, such as ClickShare's XMS Cloud Management Platform, changes that picture. Organizations can measure occupancy patterns and how their meeting rooms are used in practice, track equipment uptime, connection quality, and software and firmware status, and follow adoption levels alongside the volume and type of support incidents raised. The data helps IT professionals judge not only whether a room is operating effectively in a technical sense, but whether it is delivering the experience employees expect. As Laleeuwe explains: "Telemetry changes meeting room management from a reactive discipline into a proactive one. Instead of waiting for users to report problems, IT can identify patterns, spot underperforming rooms, detect device issues, plan maintenance and make investment decisions based on evidence." In other words, meeting rooms can be treated as managed endpoints, with IT monitoring, patching, securing, supporting, and assessing them against clear performance indicators. That matters because meeting rooms are now hubs where business-critical work happens, not just spaces where calls take place. "They influence productivity, employee experience, meeting equity, collaboration culture, and return on workplace investments," Laleeuwe adds. "When IT has better visibility and control, employees get more reliable rooms, IT teams reduce support overhead, and the business can make smarter decisions about workplace design, technology standardization, and future upgrades." IT shapes organization-wide collaboration While the benefits of such technology are clear, the approach requires IT teams to develop a broader range of skills than traditional device support. Endpoint management, networking, security, and lifecycle management all remain essential, but that expertise must now be combined with AV knowledge, an understanding of acoustics, data analysis, workplace experience design, and change management. This mix of skills "changes IT's role", Laleeuwe indicates, because teams are no longer just fixing what has broken. "They're helping shape how collaboration happens across the organization," she explains. "That means interpreting room data, understanding user behavior, working more closely with workplace, HR, facilities and sustainability teams, and influencing standards for how meeting spaces are designed and used." These skills are best developed through cross-functional collaboration and closer partnerships with AV specialists and vendors, Laleeuwe advises. Rather than regarding room analytics as isolated device data, she recommends treating them as part of a broader palette of workplace intelligence. That makes it easier to improve business performance by understanding how physical spaces, digital tools, people, and their daily tasks interact. AI takes meeting rooms to a new level The introduction of AI-driven meeting environments is expected to reshape meeting room experiences further still. Laleeuwe explains: "AI is moving beyond novelty features, such as basic transcription, and becoming part of the operational layer of collaboration. In the room, this can include intelligent camera framing, noise reduction, audio calibration, live transcription, translation, automated notes, action item tracking, room diagnostics and performance optimization." events.title: Fears of NT business closures after delayed dry season and proposed visa cuts
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NT tourism sector calls for resilience fund to support struggling operators after difficult dry season Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry There are fears many NT tourism operators won't survive the wet season after a difficult peak season this year and looming cuts to backpacker visas. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi ) Tourism operators in the Northern Territory's Top End have asked the federal government to establish a dedicated fund to help struggling businesses survive the quiet wet season months ahead. Sector representatives have warned proposed cuts to working holiday visas under the government’s new immigration plan could push businesses into financial collapse. Tourism operators and political leaders are urging the federal government to abandon its policy or create an exception for the NT. Tourism operators in the Northern Territory are advocating for a dedicated resilience fund to be set up to help businesses battling costly fuel, reduced flights and natural disaster recovery survive the upcoming wet season. Representatives from across the Top End tourism sector met in Darwin today for a roundtable with federal shadow minister for tourism, David Littleproud, to discuss their concerns for the industry. During the two-hour session, operators warned many small businesses and family-run tourism operators would struggle to survive the coming months following a difficult dry season period. NT tourism vendors face hundreds of thousands in flood damages After multiple major weather events, tourism vendors are looking at clean-up costs in the hundreds of thousands, with some businesses lost entirely. The rising cost of fuel, reduced flights and the impact of extreme weather earlier in the year which resulted in a delayed start to the tourism season were among the challenges raised at today's meeting. "We are seriously concerned that rising costs and a compressed tourism season will leave small and medium operators without the cash reserves to survive the coming Wet," Tourism Top End chair Chris Chaffe said. "These are local employers, family businesses and experiences that visitors come here for. Tourism Top End, which represents operators in the northern half of the NT, is urging the federal government to establish a dedicated fund to assist businesses without enough cash to survive the wet season. Chris Chaffe says local businesses and tourism operators in the Top End are struggling this year due to a delayed dry season. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) "That should combine tourism vouchers that generate additional travel and bookings, targeted wage support, coordinated payroll tax relief and tax payment arrangements, and interest-free loans for viable operators facing a temporary cashflow shortfall," Mr Chaffe said. "Small grants should also be available where taking on more debt is simply not a workable solution." Mr Chaffe said while immediate financial support was needed, policy changes were also necessary to tackle ongoing hurdles including the rising cost of flights and better management of Kakadu National Park, which is operated by the Commonwealth in partnership with traditional owners. "We need action before businesses close their doors," Mr Chaffe said. Closures of popular Kakadu attractions such as Twin Falls have been a concern for the NT tourism sector for years. ( Supplied: North Australian Helicopters ) Warning immigration cuts could bring NT 'to its knees' The roundtable came amid growing panic in the tourism sector over the federal government's recently announced immigration policy, which would see caps on working holiday visas . The changes announced last week mean that backpackers will have to enter a ballot if they want to remain in Australia for more than 12 months. The number of second-year visas will be capped at 45,000, while just 5,000 third-year visas will be issued, and in total Australia will welcome about 38,000 fewer second and third-year backpackers than it did in 2026. Tourism Top End executive Samantha Bennett said the changes would have "severe impacts" on the NT's tourism, agriculture and hospitality sectors. Samantha Bennett says the proposed changes to backpacker visas will have "severe impacts" on the NT's industries. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) "7,200 backpackers came through the NT in the last financial year," she said. "We need those workers who will come to the Territory in the three months we're busy." Mr Littleproud echoed the sector's concerns and reiterated his plea for Labor to scrap the working visa changes, saying they would "devastate" the industry.

events.title: IMF chief urges countries to do more to curb debt and regulate AI
events.summary: The head of the International Monetary Fund says countries both rich and poor must take faster action to cut debt and counter growing inequality as their economies weather a triple whammy from the AI boom and shocks from wars in the Middle East and Ukr... Countries both rich and poor must take faster action to cut debt and counter growing inequality as their economies weather a triple whammy from the artificial intelligence boom, heavy borrowing and shocks from wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, the head of the IMF said Wednesday. “Some very tough political choices stare us in the face,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said in a speech in Singapore ahead of autumn IMF-World Bank meetings to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world's economic policymakers next week will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action — you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors of 191 IMF-World Bank member countries will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth. So far, the hardest recent hits to global well-being have come from conflicts in the Middle East, Ukraine and elsewhere, Georgieva noted. But excessive debt is a growing burden for wealthy countries such as the U.S., Japan and Germany, as well as low-income countries that must choose between spending on public welfare or repaying onerous loans at a time of high interest rates, she noted. Georgieva pointed to risks associated with the rapid buildup of data center capacity to deliver artificial intelligence, which has helped push stock prices in many places to record highs, supporting strong economic growth despite high energy costs due to the Iran war. Investments in AI are likely to exceed the relative scale of spending on building railroads, electricity grids and telecommunications networks. “Love it, hate it or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy,” she said. A Kelvin wave is impacting the West Coast, but it's less scary than it sounds Russian missile strike in Ukraine's capital kills at least 2 Ebola patient dies in Kenya after traveling from DRC to Nairobi The AI building boom is underpinning robust corporate earnings as well as higher inflation. But there is a lag between the heavy investments involved and the arrival of AI's benefits, Georgieva said. “Should earnings fall short,” she said, “hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock.” Seven of the top 10 countries for AI-related trade are in the Asia-Pacific region, where the share of global economic activity has risen to 43% from 25% in 1991, the last time the meetings were held in Bangkok. While China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and other countries with strong tech sectors are benefiting from the AI boom, it is bypassing most others, Georgieva said, adding to economic inequality. AI also is raising energy demand, pushing prices for fuel, fertilizer, food and other key commodities still higher. She urged countries to rein in public spending and to raise the cost of borrowing as needed to control inflation, while protecting the most vulnerable members of their societies. Policies are needed to ensure AI is well regulated and to train workers, make labor markets more flexible, facilitate entrepreneurship and improve energy security, Georgieva said. events.title: UAE's 'very powerful' cyber defences can repel attacks, says Mistral AI boss
events.summary: The UAE 's “very powerful” cyber defences enable it to defend against threats, especially during geopolitical instability, the chief executive of French company Mistral AI said. The UAE's pursuit of technological sovereignty will help it establish reliable and secure cyber capabilities, Arthur Mensch told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi . “The UAE is under pressure, in particular, on the defence side,” he said. “Cyber capabilities are a must-have when it comes to having capable defence systems. “Sovereignty matters in that. It's important to be able to wield defence systems without having to ask for permission.” Mr Mensch's comments come after UAE authorities reported an increasing number of cyber attacks. Last month, the UAE's cyber security chief, Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, said the country is continuing to contend with daily online threats, with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps behind many of the attacks. Mr Al Kuwaiti said the country faced about 640,000 attacks on September 15 and that Iran remains “one of the main players” in the high-tech offensive, which is being exacerbated by the rise of AI. “Having very powerful cyber models deployed here in Abu Dhabi in a way where the deployment is fully under Abu Dhabi control is going to be quite important,” Mr Mensch said. Investing in UAE data centres Mr Mensch said Mistral AI would consider investing in UAE data centres, a move that would further solidify its co-operation with Abu Dhabi and boost the country's AI ambitions. “We may [invest in UAE data centres]. It's an interesting place for our AI buildout that is currently under way in this part of the world,” he said. On Abu Dhabi's efforts at data sovereignty, Mr Mensch said authorities and the wider industry had “very early on decided” that this aspect will be crucial for the deployment of AI. Data sovereignty is becoming vital for nations as it gives them legal control over the data within their jurisdictions. The most notable project to achieve this is the planned Stargate UAE data centre campus, a 5GW development valued at $30 billion . Mistral AI met more local organisations and companies at the summit, trying to “get a sense of what Abu Dhabi needs to build with AI ... [and] go in depth into the technological aspect of the asks”, said Mr Mensch, adding that the company has worked “extensively” with the oil and gas industry. Mistral AI has already forged partnerships with Abu Dhabi organisations , including AI major G42, to develop advanced platforms and infrastructure, and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence for research and development in AI foundation models, talent development and real-world AI solutions. In June, the company teamed up with UAE AI investment firm MGX and lender Bpifrance for the planned expansion of Campus AI in France, which aims to build a capacity of 3GW across Europe's third-biggest economy. “There is more that can be done ... on being able to have a compute capacity under full Abu Dhabi control; that's something where as a company we can help,” he added. AI accountability Fresh debacles have been hitting the AI industry, most notably AI models, supposedly in secure environments and built by names including OpenAI, Meta Platforms, Anthropic and Google, going rogue and infiltrating external sites. Mr Mensch was clear on where the responsibility should fall. At the same time, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman made a plea at the recent UN General Assembly for governments to do more to rein in AI. “Accountability for AI deployments, when they are hosted by AI companies, falls on the AI companies. This should be very, very clear. There's no way in which the accountability of what we're doing should be offset to governments,” Mr Mensch said. Governments, though, “are accountable for the adoption of the technology, and they should be accountable for how it's being used in the government itself”, he said. Mr Mensch also called for a tempered tone on the call for deceleration – or even acceleration – of the development of AI, as recent events have shown the potential disruption the technology can bring. “I'm very cautious about those warnings [to slow development down] because they serve their own interests very clearly,” he said. “The world we don't want to live in, which would be an extremely dangerous world, is the world where you have a duopoly of companies operated from the US serving the rest of the world,” he said, referring to the strength of the US AI industry, led by OpenAI and Anthropic, which is widely viewed as a counter to China's growing influence in the sector. On Tuesday, at AI Everything, Mistral AI launched its latest Mistral Large 4 AI model, which, it says, is among the fastest in the world and rivals the best open-source models from China. “We see no sign of slowing down when we look at how our model is being improved by the day,” Mr Mensch said.

events.title: 'Could almost speak Mandarin to everyone': Chinese visitors flock to Australia
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australia among top picks for Chinese tourists during Golden Week holiday Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry Fei Chang and her husband relax on a beach in the Whitsundays in Queensland. ( Supplied: Fei Chang ) Australia was one of the most popular travel destinations during China's week-long national holiday from October 1 to 7, according to a popular travel booking platform. The company reported passengers booking "longer and further trips beyond the region" this year. A Melbourne travel agent says many Chinese tourists now prefer "quality trips" in small groups or going on a road trip by themselves over big group tours. When Fei Chang and her husband landed in the Whitsundays for their holiday, they were shocked to find it filled with Chinese tourists. "At some tourist spots, it felt like I could almost speak Mandarin to everyone," she said. Ms Chang and her husband were among the Chinese tourists who visited Australia over the past week, during China's week-long national day holiday that ends today. This year, the timing of the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival public holiday together with Golden Week from October 1 to 7 gave people 13 days off. Fei Chang and her husband enjoyed visiting beaches in Sydney. ( Supplied: Fei Chang ) Australia was one of the most sought-after destinations for Chinese travellers, according to one of China's popular travel booking platforms Trip.com. The company said people were also taking "longer and further trips beyond the region" this year. International Air Transport Association (IATA) data showed that flight bookings from China to Australia for October 2026 were up 19 per cent compared to October 2025. There were also more than 2.2 million inbound and outbound passengers during the Mid-Autumn Festival, according to China's official immigration data, a 16.8 per cent increase compared to the same holiday last year. Zhang Cheng, a Melbourne travel agent and owner of Great Wall Travel Services, told the ABC that she had received a surge in bookings over the past week. Her agency takes bookings primarily from Chinese-speaking tourists. The number of Chinese tourists in Australia is yet to return to pre-COVID highs. ( Supplied: Fei Chang ) However, Ms Zhang was not sure how many of those tourists were from overseas and how many were from the Chinese-speaking community in Australia. "We are fully booked with two-day tours to the Great Ocean Road," she said. This week, Ms Zhang is taking a group of Chinese-speaking tourists to Canberra for one of the biggest horticultural shows in the Southern Hemisphere. Ms Chang says she was shocked to see so many Chinese tourists in Australia. ( Reuters: David Gray, file ) China was Australia's second-largest inbound tourist market in 2025, according to Tourism Research Australia. In 2025 , Australia saw 1.04 million visitors from China, a 17 per cent increase year-on-year. However, this was still below the 1.4 million visitors from China pre-COVID, in 2019. Ms Zhang said before the pandemic, people tended to travel in big groups. But they now prefer "quality trips" in small groups or going on road trip by themselves, she said. Chinese guided-tour groups sometimes operate under the Approved Destination Status (ADS) scheme, which is a bilateral agreement that facilitates group tours from China to Australia, organised by approved agencies. The program was paused during COVID and resumed in 2023. More than 300,000 tourists reportedly joined an ADS group tour in 2019 financial year, according to Austrade data. In the 2026 financial year, the number of visitors on ADS group trips dropped to 70,205.

events.title: Iran war energy price shock large but contained so far, IMF chief says
events.summary: The head of the International Monetary Fund has said the energy price shock driven by the US- Iran war has so far been “large but contained”, but warned that energy demand could lead to further pressure. “Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. This year's gathering, held in Bangkok, comes as supply disruptions from the war in the Middle East pile on to inflationary pressures, potentially leading to higher interest rates for advanced economies. The Federal Reserve and European Central Bank have already begun to raise their key rates, with the Bank of England expected to join them next month. Higher energy prices and rising debt levels have also driven global borrowing costs to their highest levels in decades. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, traded at 5.307 per cent as recently on Monday, its highest level since 2002. That pressure has also spread to markets in other advanced economies including in Japan, France, Germany and the UK. Oil producers in the Middle East are racing to establish alternative routes to bring their exports to the markets. The UAE is fast-tracking construction of its West-East Pipeline , which is expected to double export capacity through Fujairah by the time its expansion is completed in 2027. Saudi Arabia has rerouted its crude through the East-West Pipeline . The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to ship tracking firm Kpler. The latest figures included transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Ms Georgieva had credited the Gulf Co-operation Council's efforts to reroute energy supplies for preventing a larger shock to the global economy during a meeting with the bloc's finance ministers and central bankers in Bahrain last week. She also said the IMF anticipates the GCC economy will contract this year, adding that the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping. A separate report from the World Bank released on Tuesday said GCC economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. Meanwhile, continued supply disruptions in liquefied natural gas will hit buyers in Europe and Asia particularly hard, Ms Georgieva said, noting price pressures could further build with winter approaching and reserves dwindling. AI revolution is here In her address, the IMF chief also used her address to urge governments to embark on policies to unlock the productive gains under artificial intelligence . Ms Georgieva described the global economy as one being pulled in two directions, with the positive demand shock from AI partially offsetting the economic fallout from the US-Iran conflict. “Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy,” she said. Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva In the US, the AI buildout is shaping up to become the largest investment drive in the country's history. Analysts at Brookings anticipate AI investment in data centres, infrastructure, chips and other equipment will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032, or an average of 3.63 per cent of US GDP per year. The broad S&P 500 hit a fresh record-high of 7,800 on Tuesday driven by renewed AI enthusiasm. But with fears of an AI bubble also fomenting, Ms Georgieva said countries should adopt regulation and supervision as a “first line of defence” to prevent a far-reaching shock if AI earnings fall short. The Trump administration has recently adopted a defensive posture of AI amid a growing domestic backlash against the data centre buildout ahead of November’s midterm elections. US President Donald Trump has taken a light regulatory touch on AI advancement and repeatedly expressed his desire to beat China in the global AI race. Countries in the Gulf are seeking to advance large-scale acceleration of AI. The UAE targets to have AI contribute 20 per cent of its non-oil GDP by 2031. Ms Georgieva said AI could deliver up to a half percentage point of additional world growth – or “adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy” – annually. “Yet as this drives forward today’s AI economies, it largely bypasses most others, increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe,” she said.

events.title: Capital Group secures ADGM licence to expand Middle East operations
events.summary: Capital Group, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, has secured a licence from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Abu Dhabi's ADGM to operate as a regulated investment manager and expand operations across the region. The development comes after the company announced plans to set up its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi in May, with Capital Group relocating associates from North America, Europe and Asia to support clients in the region. The company will now be able to conduct trading, investment management and distribution activities within Abu Dhabi's financial centre, it said in a statement on Wednesday. “Establishing a regulated presence in Abu Dhabi brings us closer to our clients and to the investment opportunities across the Middle East, a region where we have been active for many years,” said Benno Klingenberg-Timm, head of Abu Dhabi office and head of institutional for Europe and Asia at Capital Group. “From day one, we will have a meaningful presence, with on-the-ground investment, operational and client-facing capabilities,” he added. The move reflects “our confidence in the region’s long-term growth”, Mr Klingenberg-Timm said. Capital Group’s expansion adds to the growing number of global investment firms setting up in Abu Dhabi. ADGM , the largest international financial centre in the Middle East and Africa by number of active licences, has continued to attract global institutions, despite the Iran war. New Mountain Capital, an alternative investment firm based in New York, said on Tuesday it was opening an office in ADGM to strengthen its presence in the Middle East. Founded in 1999, New Mountain has about $60 billion in assets under management across its private equity, credit and net lease investment strategies. “We have been privileged to work with many leading investors in the region for years and establishing a local presence will allow us to deepen those relationships while building new partnerships over time,” said Adam Weinstein, president and chief operating officer. Last week, Eurazeo, a European asset manager with €40 billion ($45.2 billion) in assets under management, opened an office in ADGM . Global private markets firm Pantheon last week opened its first Abu Dhabi office in ADGM to expand its presence in the Middle East and tap growing demand from investors across the Gulf. A base in Abu Dhabi provides global investors and money managers with opportunities to expand regional operations and work closely with some of the world's biggest sovereign wealth funds, as well as large family offices and institutional partners. Other high-profile companies that the UAE capital has attracted in recent months include private credit lender Blue Owl Capital, tech-focused US company Vista Equity Partners, the world’s largest listed hedge fund Man Group, Barings, Bain Capital, Cantor and Swiss derivative investment company Adapt Investment Managers. Collectively, asset managers that established operations in ADGM in the first half of the year oversee more than $2.1 trillion in global assets under management. Capital Group’s “decision reflects the strength of Abu Dhabi’s financial ecosystem and ADGM’s growing position as a leading international financial centre for global institutions seeking long-term opportunities across the region”, said Ahmed Al Zaabi, chairman of ADGM.

events.title: South Korean president calls for creation of tools that stop all cyber-attacks
events.summary: South Korean president Lee Jae Myung has told the nation’s cabinet that it’s time to develop AI-powered defensive tools to combat AI-wielding attackers. “Recently, a series of personal information leak incidents have been occurring at financial and public institutions,” he said yesterday – likely referring to incidents like the breach at e-tailer Coupang and last week’s raid on local banks that exposed customer data. “Circumstances indicate that artificial intelligence was utilized, causing great concern and anxiety among the public,” he claimed. “I request that the relevant authorities swiftly and clearly identify the circumstances of these incidents, and rapidly deploy and concentrate the necessary personnel and resources to minimize damage,” he added, before calling for South Korea’s government to “build security capabilities that can detect attacks in advance and preemptively block them.” “I urge the relevant ministries to quickly inspect the security systems across the entire national core infrastructure, as well as the private sector, and immediately implement any necessary security measures,” he continued. “I hope we can accelerate the development and distribution of AI technologies specifically tailored for cybersecurity.” President Lee thinks South Korea needs to “completely innovate our society's security paradigm to fit the AI era.” That work will involve public and private sector players collaborating “to transform our technology, systems, and awareness.” The remarks amount to a major policy statement, and a very public one at that. South Korean ministers and tech giants now get to turn the president’s words into action, a complex task given the broad scope of the leader’s demands and the fact that nobody thinks it's possible to defeat cybercrime. Meanwhile, Down Under Also yesterday, Australian politicians had their chance to grill OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon, who fronted a parliamentary committee to answer questions about how his company’s agents accessed a government medical records website. Kwon allowed that OpenAI should have done better than emailing the abuse reporting email address at the relevant Australian government agency but defended the company’s efforts to learn from the Hugging Face incident. The committee is sitting for another two days this week, with one topic of debate being how or if Australia should tweak its copyright laws to ensure AI companies pay content creators whose works they use when training their models. Australian law doesn’t include a fair use provision like those that AI companies in the USA relied on when sourcing content. Creators fear a rumored opt-in payments scheme will be too weak, but Australia’s government fears it may miss out on big datacenter investments and access to onshore frontier models if it doesn’t change copyright law to make it more AI-friendly. ®

events.title: Abu Dhabi to upgrade Tamm app as it pursues AI-native government goal
events.summary: Abu Dhabi plans to launch the latest version of the Tamm app in December as it pursues its goal of becoming the world’s first fully AI-native government, a senior executive has said. The refreshed Tamm 5.0 app, which would be introduced at the Gitex Global technology exhibition in Dubai, promises "increasingly intelligent" services, Department of Government Enablement director general Ruba Al Hassan told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Those services are to also be more "proactive and personalised", but they still have to remain "simple and trusted", said Ms Al Hassan, who oversees strategic affairs and future foresight at the department. Tamm currently has about 4.7 million users, having grown by more than 1.5 million in just a year. About 90 per cent of its transactions are finalised within a day, the latest data from the DGE shows. Tamm 5.0 would be "another step" in the evolution from a digital government to an AI-native government, "moving towards a model where government increasingly understands context ... anticipates needs and helps people achieve things more easily", Ms Al Hassan said. The DGE did not reveal the specific changes to Tamm or new services that are to be introduced. "It’s time for the next phase, which is about making the experience even more seamless and reducing the effort required from residents, businesses and visitors," she added. The DGE remains "focused" on its goal of transforming the capital's government services into a fully AI-native platform by next year, Ms Al Hassan said. The agency is "moving with urgency, but building responsibly", she added. "We are already seeing that tangible progress across government, not only through individual AI applications, but through the foundations that make AI-native government possible," she said, referring to data, infrastructure, digital services, workforce capability and governance. "The question is not whether we can deploy AI faster, it’s whether we can create lasting value at scale, so we believe we are on the right path to do that." Abu Dhabi is boosting tech use across the emirate under its digital strategy, which focuses on five key enablers – one of them being the use of AI across public services. Despite the persisting challenges – especially issues involving AI models going rogue and compromising other websites – the DGE is seeking to ensure the safety and reliability of such systems. "We’re seeing a lot of noise in the global AI conversation. New models are constantly coming out, capabilities are getting better quickly and everyone’s focused on what might happen in the future," Ms Al Hassan said. "Our focus is slightly different. We’re interested in where AI delivers practical value today ... we also believe trust is critical. People need confidence that AI is being used responsibly, transparently and with clear human accountability." Educating users is also a key part of the DGE's mandate, she said. "As AI improves, the value of human judgment actually also increases. People need to know how to work effectively with AI, challenge AI outputs and make better decisions," she said. "When it comes to AI, the skill won’t be coding, it will be maintaining judgment." 'Most powerful generation' Meanwhile, Omar Al Olama, Minister of State for AI, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, described the present generation as the "most powerful in human history", while calling for more responsible use of AI. "The reason ... is because you have the intelligence of every single generation, every single human that has lived, that has actually produced something that has lasted ... the content and knowledge are at your fingertips," he told the conference. "And you don't just have raw knowledge. You're actually able to leverage intelligence to do something with it through agentic AI," he added, referring to the class designed to make autonomous decisions and act with minimal human supervision. "This is the time for a new ambitious generation ... people might not believe in your ideas, to wield these tools to create something that others can't see or don't believe is possible. It's a calling."

events.title: Microsoft defines its Azure instance lifecycle, without any info about timing
events.summary: Microsoft has updated the lifecycle of an Azure instance, without offering any information on how long it takes for an instance type to expire. Redmond’s “enhanced lifecycle” landed in late September in a post that explains the four phases in the life of a cloudy VM: Current – VMs are recommended for new deployments, are available in many regions, and receive standard maintenance and support; Extended – Still supported, but may be subject to usage quotas and unspecified “changes to purchasing options and pricing.” Microsoft recommends planning a move to Current VMs. End of Life – VMs are still supported but are only available to existing customers and you may not be able to get more of the instances you want. Once VMs reach this stage, Microsoft wants you “actively” working to shift workloads onto Current or Extended VMs. Retired – Unsupported but not quite dead. Microsoft says VMs in this phase are no longer available and have been “deallocated” – Azure-speak for not having an IP address and being dormant, with data preserved. Customers can’t provision the instance types. Microsoft’s post explains that the company defined this lifecycle because it is “committed to helping you navigate these infrastructure transitions and take advantage of the next wave of innovation.” The post includes many mentions of “modernization” – the process of moving to Current Azure instance types. “As Azure continues to advance, our commitment is to make change predictable, transparent, and supported through clear lifecycle guidance, early visibility, and practical help to modernize with confidence,” the post states. The mention of “predictable” change led The Register to wonder if the lifecycle has a predictable cadence that means users can expect that instance types will remain in “Current” status for a certain number of years. We asked Microsoft if its Azure instance lifecycles are timed, and a spokesperson sent the following comment: “As Azure continues to innovate, we regularly evolve our infrastructure to give customers access to newer technologies and capabilities. As part of our updated Azure Virtual Machines lifecycle, we will continue to provide customers with advance notice when select older-generation VM series enter the End of Life stage. We’re giving customers time, guidance and resources to plan their transition to the current VM generations, while continuing to support Azure VMs through their lifecycle in alignment with the policies we published.” The spokesperson added that Microsoft customers are “notified directly about their specific VM retirements.” For what it’s worth, Microsoft publishes retirement announcements for Azure services. The company has also previously revealed it runs Azure servers for six years. It is unclear if the new Azure lifecycle is tied to that hardware retirement schedule. What is clear is that Microsoft wants Azure customers to regularly consider moving to its latest instance types. That’s a reasonable suggestion given that newer VMs will likely use more powerful processors. There’s also plenty of upside for Microsoft because more recent silicon typically offers more cores per die, and better performance-per-watt. Microsoft therefore gets greater processor density with lower energy consumption, which lowers its operating costs. Let’s see if Redmond’s lifecycle tweaks also see it pass on those savings. ®

events.title: Kenya confirms its first Ebola case and death in a man who traveled from Congo
events.summary: A Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi over the weekend has become Kenya’s first confirmed case of Ebola and the country’s first death from the disease in the fast-moving outbreak NAIROBI, Kenya -- A Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi over the weekend became Kenya’s first confirmed case of Ebola and the country’s first death from the disease in the fast-moving outbreak , authorities said Tuesday, sparking urgent contact-tracing efforts to try to contain the spread of the virus. The man had been residing in Congo for the past seven years and fell ill about a month ago. He was treated at various hospitals before traveling by road to Kampala, Uganda, where he boarded a flight to the Kenyan capital, arriving on Saturday afternoon, Health Minister Aden Duale said. Health authorities in Kenya have placed the country’s border points on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases. Duale said that the man had been isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for the Ebola virus and died late Monday. Ebola is highly contagious and spreads in the human population through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The current outbreak was declared in mid-May, months after it had been spreading in a remote part of eastern Congo. At least 8,400 cases have been recorded, including more than 4,000 deaths, according to government data, making it the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history. Kenya has never had an outbreak of Ebola, according to the Kenya Medical Research Institute. The country hosts a United States-funded isolation center for American citizens exposed to Ebola to quarantine for 21 days before traveling back to the U.S. The isolation facility faced legal battles and deadly protests by locals who feared it was exposing them to the virus. Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Uganda has recorded 20 cases and France one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August. Duale said that 28 contacts of the man who had returned on Saturday, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers on the flight and four crew members, who traveled on the same plane from Uganda, were being traced. The contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released after testing negative for the virus, said the ministry’s director-general, Dr. Patrick Amoth. After the man arrived in Nairobi, his relatives took him in a private vehicle to Nairobi Hospital, where he was immediately isolated. He was buried on Tuesday afternoon in accordance with recommended public safety protocols. The minister said that Kenya had tested 267 samples at five laboratories across the country since May before this first case was detected.
