events.title: Scoop: Senate GOP to send $5m to shore up Graham in South Carolina
events.summary: The main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates plans to inject $5 million into the South Carolina campaign as an "insurance policy" to help GOP nominee Darline Graham , a source familiar with the move tells Axios. Why it matters: The GOP's concern that a Senate seat in blood-red South Carolina could be in play shows just how bad the political environment is for Republicans, who face a rash of troubles in states long considered conservative strongholds. "It's an insurance policy. We're going to be there for Darline," said a Republican briefed on the plans for the Senate Leadership Fund. The shift to spending in conservative South Carolina comes after Senate Republicans announced they no longer were financing ads in swing-state North Carolina, where the GOP's Michael Whatley is lagging behind former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in polls. Democrats, meanwhile, are reallocating resources in a way that reflects their optimism four weeks before Election Day. Democrats' main Senate super PAC canceled roughly $1.1 million in ad reservations in North Carolina, Semafor reported, based on their belief Cooper is well-positioned to flip the seat now held by retiring Republican Thom Tillis. Zoom in: Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was appointed to her seat in July at the urging of President Trump , a friend of her brother's. Graham faces a host of challenges: She's a relatively poor fundraiser compared to her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who is outspending and outraising Graham, according to the South Carolina Post & Courier . Unlike her brother, Graham shields herself from the press and has shown a relative lack of mastery of foreign policy, which tripped her up during a GOP primary debate. Graham won that primary over Rep. Ralph Norman with 52% of the vote after getting help from Trump. It left some bad feelings with Norman, who endorsed her but briefly suggested he would mount a write-in campaign for the Nov. 3 general election. Zoom out: Voter anger over high prices and Trump's sagging popularity have helped to create a political landscape in which the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC is having to play defense across the country. It's trying to shore up GOP incumbents and challengers from Alaska to Ohio to Texas, where it recently plowed in $131 million over 17 days to boost Ken Paxton's campaign against Democrat James Talarico. "We're not taking anything for granted. We won't be caught flat-footed in any of these races," the source said. The money for Graham will be spent mainly on TV ads to "remind voters that Andrews is a Democrat." Democrats haven't won a statewide race in South Carolina since 2006. By the numbers: Closer-than-expected polling from two firms that typically survey for Republicans sparked concern last week in GOP circles. A survey from Trafalgar showed Graham pulling 43% and Andrews 42%, a statistical tie. InsiderAdvantage also produced a poll showing a 1-point race that's essentially tied, with Graham at 46% and Andrews at 45%. Earlier in September, GOP-leaning Rasmussen Reports showed Graham up by 5 points. Catch up quick: Andrews' campaign has been under the radar compared to that of Jaime Harrison, the Democrat who challenged Graham's brother for the seat in 2020. Harrison raised $100 million for that race, but because he was the state's former Democratic Party chair, it was easier for Republicans to make the race a partisan contest. In contrast, Andrews is running as a "mom and a doctor." Her campaign was largely financed with $3.6 million in campaign contributions bundled by 314 Action Fund, a political committee founded to elect Democratic candidates with STEM backgrounds. What they're saying: "South Carolinians don't know who Darline Graham is or what she believes — she avoids reporters, avoids voters, and lies about Annie rather than doing her job," an Andrews spokesperson told Axios. A Graham spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. Trump gave a preview Monday of the bare-knuckle attacks to come when he took to Truth Social and used a slur for transgender people to attack Andrews while accusing her of a host of liberal positions. "South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her," Trump wrote . The 314 Action Fund jabbed back at the president in a statement late Monday, calling Trump "perverted" and saying that he "has resorted to name-calling and juvenile insults because his candidate can't win on the issues." Axios' Hans Nichols contributed to this story.

events.title: Longevity guru Bryan Johnson: "People really want me to die"
events.summary: LOS ANGELES — Bryan Johnson , the face of the longevity movement who believes he may never die, announced recently that he had an incurable autoimmune disease — and his critics cheered, he told "The Axios Show" in an exclusive interview Monday. "I mean, I think people really want me to die. Now I get it. It's funny. It's ironic. I push a lot of buttons that people don't like," he said. The big picture : As Johnson himself acknowledged, there's an irony in the founder of the "Don't Die" movement watching people celebrate his diagnosis. But Johnson sees his diagnosis as rocket fuel for his mission to promote longevity, rather than a setback. Catch up quick: Johnson, 49, has autoimmune gastritis (AIG), a chronic condition in which the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach lining. Johnson said "there was joy all around the world" after he announced his diagnosis in July. He spends millions of dollars a year on extreme health interventions, documenting the experiments for an online following that has ballooned to roughly 8 million across platforms including YouTube . When asked if any of his interventions could have fueled his AIG diagnosis, he said: "No. I got diagnosed with hypothyroidism when I was 21 years old. The thyroid and the stomach are very closely linked in immunology. I probably have had this thing for about 30 years." The intrigue : Johnson views the diagnosis, which might appear to undermine his campaign against aging, as just another test of it. In his view, his efforts to do more than manage the disease can help prove the efficacy of his ambitions. "I like the challenge. I'm up for it. I think it's good timing. I'm going to get diagnosed with something at some point. Why not this?" Friction point: Johnson, who calls himself the "most measured person in the world," spends over $2 million a year on his personal health and longevity treatments. He has an entire medical concierge team and a makeshift doctor's office in his home. Experts say the cause of the disease is unknown, and that Johnson's proposed effort to reverse it is experimental. Zoom out: Johnson made his fortune founding Braintree, which bought Venmo and was later sold to PayPal for $800 million. He now runs longevity businesses including Blueprint and Immortals, alongside neurotechnology company Kernel and venture fund OS Fund. Between the lines: One common critique of intensive health tracking is that more testing can uncover more abnormalities, not all of them meaningful. Doctors warn that false positives and incidental findings can trigger a "cascade" of follow-up tests and treatments that can bring added cost, stress, and in some cases, harm. Johnson is a full-throated fan : "I personally appreciate information. I want to know because when you find things early, you're much more likely to be able to address them." He also said his process doesn't feel addictive to him, adding that "the biggest addiction in the world is to make money." The bottom line: The face of the longevity movement sees the hit to his public health record as another potential achievement in his quest to live forever.

events.title: Wall Street on track for record profits
events.summary: Data: NYSE/Intercontinental Exchange via the New York State Comptroller; Chart Emily Peck/Axios; Note: 2026 projected by the comptroller if first-half growth continues at current pace. First-half 2026 profits were $45.9 billion. Profits are for broker-dealer operations of NYSE member firms and are not adjusted for inflation. Wall Street profits are blowing past expectations this year, the New York State Comptroller's office finds in a new report. Why it matters: Profits are on track for an all-time record, a sign of how the AI boom is fueling dealmaking and how volatile markets are helping trading. By the numbers: In the first half of this year, Wall Street firms raked in $45.9 billion — that's 51.3% more than the same period last year, and already more than the $45.3 billion forecast for the entirety of 2026. If growth continues apace, annual profits could exceed $90 billion. Zoom out: That's far more than 2025's record $65.1 billion and rivals the 2009 record even after accounting for inflation, the report says. Stunning stat: The fees that firms earn from underwriting — helping companies sell new stocks and bonds — rose 68% in the first half of the year, compared with the first half of 2025. Zoom in: That tracks with a 76.5% increase in global equity issuance, a large chunk from the SpaceX initial public offering . Plus, there was also an 11.3% increase in debt issuance, with the AI hyperscalers among the biggest borrowers. Yes, but: It's anyone's guess as to whether the second half of the year looks like the first. There are plenty of market headwinds blowing: the Iran war, higher inflation and interest rates, the potential for the AI bubble to burst among them. The intrigue: Wall Street appears to be thriving despite fears over the city's democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani. The big picture: The securities industry makes up a big and growing share of the city and state's tax revenues, but local business and politics aren't significant profit engines. Those instead are driven by national and global markets — it's been a huge year for stocks, the SpaceX IPO was the biggest ever, M&A hit a record and war-driven volatility juiced trading. What to watch: The big Wall Street banks are set to release third-quarter earnings numbers next week — that's the first big test of whether the pace is holding up.

events.title: Latino group bets on bilingual AI to cut voter confusion before the midterms
events.summary: A national Latino civic engagement group is turning to an AI app to help voters cut through an increasingly complicated election system — in English or Spanish. Why it matters: Nearly 39 million Hispanics can vote in this year's midterms, and their political loyalties are increasingly up for grabs. Hispanics have added 5.25 million eligible voters since 2022, more than any other racial or ethnic group, according to Pew Research Center. The Latino electorate remains highly fluid: About 1 in 7 Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 now say they want Democrats to control Congress, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll . How it works: Mi Familia en Acción launched Nubi last week, a bilingual AI-powered app that answers questions about voting, voter registration, citizenship and Know Your Rights information. Users can ask questions in English or Spanish about where and when to vote, early voting, mail ballots and registration. Nubi operates in all 50 states and can tailor information to the local or district level. Unlike a general-purpose chatbot , Mi Familia en Acción president and CEO Héctor Sánchez Barba tells Axios that Nubi doesn't search the open internet for answers. The organization feeds it information from sources it considers reliable, with human review and guardrails around what the AI can answer. If Nubi doesn't have an answer, Sánchez said, it is designed to say so and direct the user to a trusted source or partner rather than invent a response. State of play: Nubi represents a five-year effort to marry Mi Familia en Acción's traditional organizing with technology. The organization launched a more basic chatbot about two years ago before developing the current AI version. Mi Familia en Acción financed development itself, Sánchez said, though he declined to disclose the cost, calling it a "very big investment." The organization says it plans to keep updating Nubi as voting rules, court decisions and government policies change. Zoom in: The goal is to turn a complicated search across election websites into a conversation. A voter could ask whether they're registered, whether they can vote by mail, where their polling place is or what early-voting options exist. Nubi then walks the user through basic questions before giving a locally specific answer. The tool is updated regularly and eventually could expand its answers on questions involving immigration enforcement or problems a voter encounters at a polling place. What they're saying: "People don't need to be a constitutional lawyer to find information about how they need to vote," said Sánchez, adding that the goal is to put reliable information in one place. He stressed that Nubi is nonpartisan and doesn't recommend candidates or causes. Sánchez also said the technology won't replace door-knocking and other traditional organizing, but could extend civic information into rural or overlooked communities that organizers rarely reach. Zoom out: Nubi arrives as Latino voters play an increasingly large — and less predictable — role in American elections. Pew projects Hispanics will account for 16% of eligible voters in 2026, nearly double their 9% share in 2006. Latino voters are also fragmenting into competing political identities rather than moving uniformly toward either party. In May, 52% of registered Latino voters surveyed in 17 competitive House districts said they were undecided or could change their minds.

events.title: Scoop: Gun safety groups jump into midterms with $10 million assist for Democrats
events.summary: Everytown for Gun Safety , a group that advocates for stricter gun laws, is teaming up with House Democrats on a $10 million ad campaign to boost former gun safety advocates now running for Congress, Axios has learned. Why it matters: That's a significant sum at a moment when Democrats are raising alarm bells about being outgunned financially in the midterm elections. The candidates boosted by the campaign are all former volunteers for Moms Demand Action, which is part of Everytown. The candidates include: JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, Pia Dandiya of Florida, Christina Bohannan, Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James of Iowa, Christina Hines and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, and Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania. "For nearly two years, a MAGA House has rubber-stamped the Trump administration as it tore up federal gun safety laws, and flipping these eight seats is how we put a stop to it," Everytown president John Feinblatt said in a statement first shared with Axios. "There's a Moms Demand Action volunteer on the ballot in every one of these districts, and we're partnering with House Majority PAC to turn them into majority makers." Mike Smith, the president of House Democrats' main super PAC, House Majority PAC, said in a statement: "Every seat on this map is a chance to put a check on a Trump administration and a MAGA House that have spent two years putting the gun lobby ahead of American families." Between the lines: The money will go to fund TV and digital ads focused broadly on "public safety," referencing not just gun control but drug trafficking, immigration, crime, and police funding. The Bohannan ad says she is "running for Congress to put public safety first. That means working with both parties to secure our border, hire more police officers and keep illegal guns and fentanyl off our streets." The Cognetti ad mostly focuses on her broader anti-corruption message but lauds how "she got millions for police and cut violent crime by 80%" as mayor of Scranton. The other side: "House Democrats have fully embraced the radical socialist agenda of abolishing prisons, releasing criminals back on the streets, and defunding the police," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement. "Voters won't buy their lies about Republicans who have fought to protect our communities." Editor's note: This article has been corrected to clarify that Moms Demand Action is part of Everytown.

events.title: Inside Trump's new AI playbook
events.summary: President Trump's newly minted "super intelligence" task force faces a daunting mandate: Reconcile fiercely divided Cabinet factions to create a tech policy that keeps pace with the blistering AI race. Why it matters: The task force brings the administration's scattered AI work under one roof, but it also makes it likely that any new rules will be forged in the crossfire of competing internal camps. In an interview, task force co-chair Scott Kupor rejected the assertion that the administration is asleep at the wheel on AI policy, arguing that rigid, static legislation would risk becoming instantly obsolete. What they're saying: "The worst thing for us to do would be to assume a static set of knowledge that allows us to put a regulatory schema in place that then has unintended consequences," said Kupor, a Silicon Valley veteran who is currently serving as director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, akin to an HR director for the federal government. "Look, we live in D.C.," he said. "There's nothing that's not political in this town. People have different views and that's totally fine. Our obligation is to demonstrate to the American people that this is good and also that we take the anxieties and the concerns seriously." "At the end of the day there is no daylight between the president and anyone else ... we need to win," he said. Between the lines: The group's makeup highlights the competing fiefdoms driving Trump's AI strategy , with some working on model approval and coordination and others continuing to voice deep skepticism about pro-regulation forces in the industry. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trump Chief of Staff Susie Wiles have worked behind the scenes to encourage some oversight, including through the voluntary model-review process that already exists. Managed within the Commerce Department, the reviews have already been used for top models at Anthropic, OpenAI and now Google, sources tell Axios. On the other end of the spectrum, figures like David Sacks and the Pentagon's Emil Michael represent an approach that is wary of the potential for a slowdown in model development or new regulation to reduce competition for frontier companies. Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and the new AI czar , is expected to bring cohesion to the group's collective work, much as he does with the myriad intelligence agencies. The entire committee is set to operate under Trump's explicit marching orders: Innovation cannot be bottlenecked, and America must stay ahead while finding a safe path forward, Kupor said. Kupor suggested one outcome may be that AI regulation is divided among different federal agencies, although it is too early to know what the group — which will do its work over 120 days — will ultimately recommend to the president. His primary area of focus initially will be to seek input from stakeholders in the energy, manufacturing, security and financial services industries. Kupor said he expects Clayton will keep close tabs on the intelligence community and the committee will continue to stay in close touch with the AI companies. Zoom in: The administration is leaning hard into corporate self-policing to manage the risks. Kupor and other officials believe that third-party audits and direct reporting to corporate boards carry severe securities law implications that rival traditional government oversight. The bottom line: The task force's goal isn't to draft a bureaucratic "Ph.D. dissertation," in Kupor's words. But it remains to be seen whether streamlining existing efforts without new legislation will satisfy Americans who are increasingly anxious about AI safety.

events.title: The most-watched election in U.S. history
events.summary: The 2026 midterms are shaping up to be the most intensely observed, recorded, dissected and challenged election in American history. Why it matters: A small army of partisan and nonpartisan observers will show up. So will a surge of Justice Department monitors, organizers looking for signs of ICE and citizen journalists broadcasting their search for illegal voting in real time. Between the lines: More nonpartisan observation can bolster confidence in elections, studies show . But officials worry that activists expecting to find wrongdoing could misread routine events. Election officials have been raising concerns that "vigilante citizen journalists" could interfere with the election, said Andrew Walchuck of Common Cause, a nonprofit organization that's also recruiting nonpartisan election observers. "I worry that people are going to go in and claim they're seeing things that they aren't," said Andrew Garber of the Brennan Center. "Just minor, innocuous things that are going to happen as millions and millions of ballots get cast and counted, then it gets spun into something nefarious or untrue," Garber said. The intrigue: After the 2020 election, claims from observers and activist sleuths helped fuel challenges to the results. It was then channeled into numerous lawsuits from the Trump campaign. The cases were almost all dismissed or denied relief in court. Influencers and online activists can turn real-time claims about wrongdoing into national controversy before officials can weigh in or push back — including while votes are being cast or counted. "What gives me concern is that we have an administration that is trying to spread conspiracy theories and spread lies about our elections and... [then] having more people out there with that purpose behind their work troubles me," Walchuck said. The other side: "Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of voter fraud continues to pile up. Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable," Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement. This year there have been more than two dozen federal charges against people for voting when they're not eligible and about 160 arrests, according to the Justice Department . A review from the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonpartisan organization, says instances of illegal voting are "extremely small." Zoom in: The DOJ plans to train 1,000 election monitors to deploy across the country, one of the largest-ever efforts from the agency. It builds on a significant increase in observers in 2024 . The Senate Democrats have spun up their own arm of election observers, using office staff to monitor the polls. That's in addition to a new 50-state-plus-territories recruitment program by a coalition of Democratic state parties, aiming to recruit at least 10,000 election watchers. The Republican National Committee is building on its election watch network set up in 2020 to counter perceived voter fraud. GOP partisans have signed up in record numbers to be poll workers and the party is hosting virtual and in-person trainings for observers and challengers. A network of anti-ICE activists is transitioning ICE watch trainings into poll watching trainings, responding in part to the Trump administration saying ICE could make arrests at the polls. When asked in September about deploying agents, Trump told TIME magazine he hadn't thought of it. Zoom out: These efforts will coexist with a slew of nonpartisan observing efforts, ranging from voter protection groups to international election observers. There will also be state party and campaign staffers who regularly monitor the polls for concerns. These are typically more mundane, including monitoring accurate opening and closing times for polling locations that can be remedied with quick litigation. The rules and terminology for observers vary by state laws , which also govern how close an observer can be to voting machines or tabulation processes and how to document concerns about malpractice. The bottom line: "Having questions and wanting to understand more about the election process as a sort of curious citizen is a good thing," said Avery Davis-Roberts of the Carter Center, which monitors elections internationally and will have volunteers in five states in November. "And we hope that people will use observation and the findings of our observation as a way to better understand how the process works and maybe have some of those questions answered."

events.title: Our Reporter Spent 10 Weeks Gambling on DraftKings. Here Are 5 Things He Learned.
events.summary: Bankrolled by ProPublica, reporter Jake Pearson tested online gambling guardrails by mimicking the betting patterns of a problem gambler for 10 weeks. Photo illustration by ProPublica. Source images: Jake Pearson/ProPublica, Chris Alcantara/ProPublica. Online gambling has surged in the U.S. since the Supreme Court allowed states to legalize sports betting in 2018, prompting public health concerns about gambling addiction and calls for stricter consumer protections. Online sportsbooks such as DraftKings and FanDuel have touted “responsible gaming” features as evidence that they are taking appropriate steps to protect consumers from spiraling out of control. Reporter Jake Pearson put these safeguards to the test. Bankrolled by ProPublica, he mimicked the betting patterns of a problem gambler for 10 weeks, consulting a panel of addiction specialists, recovering gambling addicts and professional sports bettors for advice. He found that the safety features were overpowered by the app’s product design and promotions that pushed him to continue gambling. Pearson detailed his entire journey, which you can read here . Here are five takeaways from his investigation. 1. Sports betting is ubiquitous. The industry relies on very active losers. Today, nearly a quarter of all Americans , and half of men ages 18 to 49, say they have an active sportsbook account, according to the Siena Research Institute. But that rapid growth has come with consequences: About a quarter of active sportsbook account holders surveyed by the organization this year said that they’d lost enough on a bet that they’d have trouble meeting their financial obligations. Gamblers who lose frequently are the bettors sportsbooks are most interested in, Matthew Gaskell, a British psychologist and expert on gambling addiction, said. Gaskell noted that a relatively small number of active losers account for a substantial amount of sportsbooks’ revenue. A 2024 study out of Connecticut found that 1.8% of problem gamblers in the state accounted for 51% of sports betting revenue . What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files. Share Your Experience DraftKings says its responsible gaming system provides adequate safeguards to protect customers from spiraling out of control. “I think as a business, as an industry, we’re doing a good job of educating people, of raising awareness, of making tools and resources available, of monitoring accounts,” Lori Kalani, DraftKings’ chief responsible gaming officer, told Pearson. But policymakers aren’t so sure. Lawmakers from Colorado to Massachusetts are now proposing stricter consumer protections. 2. DraftKings has adopted responsible gaming tools. They require users to opt in, limiting their effectiveness. DraftKings’ responsible gambling safeguards include in-app notifications that encourage gamblers to take a break after they’ve lost money and “time reminders” that tell users how long they’ve been on the app. The app also features a responsible gaming center that allows users to set a budget, track their spending or opt into tools like those that allow them to limit the amount of time and money they spend in a 24-hour period or enact more severe restrictions such as a multiday “cool off.” But this system largely relies on users to have the wherewithal to opt into the tools — something that experts say can be difficult for someone struggling with gambling addiction. DraftKings told Pearson that if a customer’s behavior raises too many red flags, the company will proactively close an account. Yet it wouldn’t specify how often this actually happens. Screenshot by Jake Pearson/ProPublica Pearson’s experiment mimicked the behavior of a problem gambler to see when — and if — the company’s safeguards would stop him. The first in-app responsible gaming prompt Pearson received came more than a week after he began gambling on the NBA playoffs, when he’d already lost roughly what a minimum-wage worker in New York City earns in a month. It told him that he’d hit $2,500 or more in deposits and said to “visit our Responsible Gaming Center anytime to set limits for yourself and access tools for safer play.” But the app’s warning wasn’t triggered by Pearson’s reckless betting. It was legally required. When New York legalized mobile sports betting in 2023, lawmakers required the apps to notify users when they hit $2,500 in total deposits. The pop-up gave Pearson two options: set limits or “I understand.” He clicked the latter and was back in action. Even as Pearson exhibited red flag after red flag, according to our panel of experts, his subsequent warnings from the app followed the same pattern. DraftKings says millions of customers have visited its responsible gaming center, but the little data available publicly suggests only a small percentage opt into these tools. Just over 8% of active DraftKings users in Massachusetts were using them as of April, a company official told state regulators this summer. The official added the number was trending up. Kalani says her 51-person team manually reviews user accounts suspected of problem gambling. Yet even after Pearson deposited $21,600 into his account in less than eight weeks and exhibited just about every sign of compulsive gambling, he didn’t register for a manual review under the company’s criteria. 3. The design of online sports betting platforms can encourage users to gamble more.  Online gambling companies have created sophisticated technology products designed to squeeze maximum engagement out of users, just as social media companies like Meta did years earlier with users of Facebook and Instagram, according to Darragh McGee, a researcher at the University of Bath. Indeed, Pearson found that the app’s design encouraged him to keep betting. Pearson found the app’s quick-tap deposit buttons increased automatically. Screenshot by Jake Pearson/ProPublica. Debit card number redacted by ProPublica. As he gambled more, he found that the app’s quick-tap deposit buttons increased automatically, making it even easier to mindlessly transfer large sums from his bank into his DraftKings account. And while DraftKings’ safety warnings were sporadic, he was getting up to six push notifications a day notifying him of rewards and betting opportunities. DraftKings told Pearson it sent him 32 responsible gambling prompts over 10 weeks of gambling, including emails that every DraftKings customer gets. Pearson counted in-app notifications about his betting 14 out of the 71 days he gambled on the app. 4. Perks can also help encourage users to bet more. events.title: Crypto PACs’ House targets raise eyebrows
events.summary: The News The cryptocurrency industry’s leading network of super PACs is under scrutiny after revealing it will back 19 House Republicans but only 13 House Democrats. Fairshake, which emerged as a kingmaker last election cycle, said three members from each party would receive $1 million ahead of November. But it did not provide a breakdown for the rest of its spending, even as skeptics pointed out that its list contained more Republicans than Democrats in tough races. “The absence of [North Carolina Democratic Rep.] Don Davis is the most dangerous thing, because that’s a Dem who’s in a swing seat who’s not getting love,” despite backing the industry’s top legislative priority, one cryptocurrency executive told Semafor. Last cycle, “there was at least the argument that Dems had driven them to this; this time, it’s been two years of going hard in on [President Donald] Trump.” Know More Hill Democrats privately grumbled about Monday’s announcement and the group’s decision not to support Democratic backers of cryptocurrency legislation like Davis and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., who represent swing districts and stood to benefit from outside spending. The vast majority of lawmakers on Fairshake’s list represent safe districts, facing only token opposition in their general elections. And the three Democrats named by Fairshake as receiving $1 million represented districts that have been competitive in previous elections but who are expected to win re-election this year. Fairshake, which a spokesperson noted “has always been and always will be an issue-focused organization,” spent more in Democratic primaries than Republican ones this cycle. But Monday’s announcement is nevertheless fueling speculation that it could give the GOP a boost in Senate races by not spending against Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, despite her vote against the cryptocurrency bill. “It’s completely full of sh*t,” another cryptocurrency executive told Semafor after Fairshake announced plans to spend against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, last month. “The fig leaf of bipartisanship is no longer fooling anybody.”

events.title: Polls show how AI is changing the workplace
events.summary: As AI adoption spreads across the US workforce, new polling suggests that its benefits have so far been concentrated among those likely to hold upper-level positions. Twenty-eight percent of US employees say they use AI at least weekly, according to a two-year study from Jobs for the Future, The Families & Workers Fund, and Gallup, while 54% say they haven’t used it at work. Use of the technology on the job is much more common among those with college degrees and those in managerial roles. Speed is the most common benefit that AI users point to, with 63% saying the technology helps them do their jobs faster. Among those in the highest paid positions — people earning $10,000 or more a month — seven in 10 say it’s accelerating their work, while fewer Americans who earn less say the same. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Democrats press White House on still-secret AI framework
events.summary: Two Democratic senators want answers from Trump administration officials on industry influence on the still-unreleased AI regulatory framework, part of the AI executive order President Donald Trump signed earlier this year, according to a letter shared first with Semafor. “We are concerned that the Trump administration is accommodating the interests of Big Tech CEOs rather than addressing the safety and security risks posed by increasingly sophisticated AI systems,” Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., wrote in the letter addressed to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House cyber adviser Sean Cairncross, and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, among others. The letter cites reported industry influence over what eventually became the executive order. It also highlights Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s central role in shaping the more recent White House AI accord, pointing to the administration’s “cozy relationship” with and “deference to industry executives.” The letter is the latest indication that Democrats are not giving up on a sustained push for answers from the administration on what is still a mysterious, voluntary framework for AI companies to submit their highest-level AI models to the government before release. Should the party gain power back in Congress, its demands will have more teeth. “The American people deserve strong guardrails set by democratically elected officials, not a toothless framework shaped in secret by a handful of billionaires,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote Monday, pressing for answers to five questions by Oct. 19. They asked for details on meetings and correspondence between industry and government officials leading up to the release of the executive order in June. They also want to know whether independent evaluators or other stakeholders beyond industry were consulted, and demanded a description of the pre-deployment testing process established under the framework.

events.title: Trump administration presses Congress for anti-fraud legislation
events.summary: The Scoop The White House has formally sent Congress proposed legislation that would impose mandatory minimum sentences on those convicted of fraud involving federal benefit programs, according to a copy of it seen by Semafor. The proposal, sent to House and Senate leadership on Sunday night, follows President Donald Trump’s call over the weekend for lawmakers to crack down on “fraud in Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security programs.” The administration’s language would establish a range of mandatory minimum sentences based on the amount of loss involved in fraud schemes, according to the document. The proposal would also bar courts from placing those sentenced under the provision on probation or suspending their sentences. People found responsible for less than $40,000 in losses would face at least one year in prison; those responsible for between $40,000 and $250,000 in losses would face at least two years in prison; and violations involving $100 million in losses or more would result in at least 20 years in prison. All violations would carry a maximum sentence of life in prison. It’s unlikely that Congress would be able to take up and pass the legislation during its post-election session after the midterms. With Democrats poised to take the House majority next month and the Senate also in play, the proposal also faces a steep climb in 2027. Also included in the administration’s legislative proposal is language that would hold “any officer or employee of the state” personally liable if they knew about alleged fraud and “willfully, intentionally, or recklessly” ignored it. Such officials could also be financially liable for damages up to the “amount of all loss resulting” from the fraud, or if that loss exceeds $1 million, up to three times the amount. Know More Trump in recent months has empowered Vice President JD Vance to pursue fraud across the US, as he and other Republicans have sought to campaign on a familiar message of stopping waste, fraud, and abuse. The administration has pursued a number of high-profile fraud claims, most notably in Democratic-led states such as Minnesota and California. This is the latest crime-related push from Trump, who won his presidential election in part on a law-and-order message. The proposal now sits with Congress, where lawmakers will have to decide whether to take it up.

events.title: While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution | Charlotte Hill
events.summary: Food businesses and the government must make redistribution a key policy to address food insecurity. We know the surplus food is out there Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix How often does this happen? You open the fridge and find some ingredient you meant to use but didn’t get round to, and even though it’s still edible you think perhaps it’s just easier to throw it away. In the UK it’s estimated that an average household wastes about three meals a week , or 156 meals a year. Household fridges are one thing. But across the food sector, more than 1bn meals’ worth of easily accessible surplus food is wasted each year in the UK for the same reason: because it is easier to throw it away. That equates to 470,000 tonnes – enough to feed every child in the UK three meals a day for a month. When so many people are struggling to afford food, that is a staggering amount – and what’s even more shocking is that it is good quality and nutritious. events.title: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
events.summary: It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff? Temperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter Shop this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 15th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.” I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues. Continue reading...

events.title: Arizona welcomes new Taiwan representative office, rejecting warning from China
events.summary: Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an office in Phoenix to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region PHOENIX -- Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an economic and cultural office Monday to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region, despite pressure from the Chinese government to block it. Taiwanese authorities have said the new Phoenix office — their 14th in the United States — will promote collaboration in technology, especially in semiconductor manufacturing, and better serve a growing number of Taiwanese migrants in the city. After the plans for the office were announced in July, Hobbs received two letters from China’s consulate general in Los Angeles asking her to object to the proposal, according to documents the governor’s office shared with The Associated Press. In a July 3 letter, the Chinese authority called the governor to “refute such an attempt by the Taiwan authorities and stop any political gimmicks to harm the friendship and cooperation between China and the State of Arizona.” The stance was reiterated in an Aug. 21 letter. The letters were first reported by Phoenix radio station KJZZ. Hobbs highlighted Arizona’s ties with Taiwan at Monday’s opening. “Every Arizona elected official should show the courage necessary to support the partnership between Arizona and Taiwan,” Hobbs said. “As our economic partnership grows, we are mobilizing every available resource to support Taiwanese companies expanding here in Arizona.” Beijing claims the island as a breakaway province inseparable from China, while Taiwan considers itself separate from the Chinese mainland and has its own government. Scholars say that local-level collaborations with the Chinese government and Taiwan have become more politicized as U.S.-China relations have deteriorated over the years. events.title: Ukraine claims to have taken out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity
events.summary: Ukraine said long-range strikes have put more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity out of action KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine says its long-range strikes have neutralized more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow's ability to supply its forces during its 4 1/2-year-old invasion. The Defense Ministry said late Sunday that recent strikes on refineries in cities, including Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov and Syzran, had disabled 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity. The claim could not be independently verified. Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their aerial assaults as progress along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line has largely ground to a halt. Ukraine has launched repeated attacks on refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict gasoline sales. Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country’s oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes’ economic impact, President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 1 that they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. “They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” Putin told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said analysts from Ukraine’s intelligence services, the General Staff and the Defense Ministry had assessed the strikes' effects. “Fifty-one percent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings. Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory,” he said. Russia has historically been the world’s third-largest producer of refined fuel products from crude, after the U.S. and China. Some of Russia’s 32 refineries have been hit as many as 15 times since the start of the war, and one refinery has been hit every three days in recent months, creating a cycle of damage and emergency repairs that could degrade units long term, according to the International Energy Agency. Ukrainian strikes have also increasingly targeted the more complex equipment that removes impurities from fuel, which takes months to repair. The IEA says diesel output has fallen by about 30%, and drivers have had to wait up to 40 hours to fill up at gasoline stations. Russian refiners have tried to compensate by delaying scheduled maintenance and bringing mothballed units back online. Another response has been to lower fuel quality standards to maintain gasoline supplies, which risks damage to engines and pollution control equipment. The Kremlin has also banned diesel exports, pushing global prices higher and prompting U.S. President Donald Trump on Sept. 13 to urge Ukraine to stop hitting refineries. A Russian attack with a guided aerial bomb killed at least three people and wounded 39 others, including three children, in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv on Monday, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said. “There may be people under the rubble of the residential building that was hit. A search and rescue operation is underway,” Terekhov wrote on his Telegram channel. An earlier Russian drone attack on the city's Industrialnyi district also killed one person, Terekhov said late Sunday. Vehicles and an administrative building were set alight and apartment buildings were damaged, he said. Another person was also killed in a separate Russian attack on the Sloviansk community in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, said Vadym Liakh, head of the Sloviansk city military administration. He urged residents not to wait for a mandatory evacuation order but to leave the area. Russia’s Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that it had struck an electrical substation in the Kharkiv region, in addition to energy and port infrastructure and maritime vessels used by Ukraine's military elsewhere in the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone attack caused a fire on board a commercial vessel that later sank in the Black Sea . Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said. In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy described the attack as “a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel” in neutral waters. He said the vessel was Turkish-owned and carrying corn. Russia did not immediately comment on the incident. Ukraine has struggled in recent weeks to fend off Russia’s intensified aerial attacks on cities that include ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones .

events.title: Inside the transgender rights fight injecting chaos into Democrats' midterm efforts
events.summary: An intra-party debate over how best to deflect Republican attacks on transgender issues has Democrats angrily sniping at each other just weeks out from the midterm elections. Why it matters: This is not the position Democrats hoped to be in two years after their 2024 election loss , which many in the party attributed to being outflanked by GOP messaging on trans issues. "People feel you need to respond in some way to some of these attacks because people didn't do it two years ago," Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a co-chair of the Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus, told Axios. "But you also need to realize what we're winning on right now," Pocan added, saying Democratic candidates need to strike "a balance." "Silence is deadly, and I think we played that out in 2024," said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at the centrist think tank Third Way, citing polling that found most voters believed Democrats "thought there should be no rules in sports, no rules around health care." Driving the news: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) set off a firestorm in her district and on Capitol Hill in September by stating in a direct-to-camera ad that she "voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools." "Parents know what's best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls' sports," Kaptur said in the spot — a response to an ad from Republican Derek Merrin that said she "voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports." Multiple county parties condemned the ad — particularly the reference to transgender girls as "boys" — and urged Kaptur to take it down. One LGBTQ+ group, the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, said in a statement there is "no difference" between Kaptur and Merrin because they are "both united against the LBTQIA+ community." What they're saying: "The ads were deeply offensive to the Equality Caucus and the broader LGBTQ community that we represent," said Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.), who co-chairs the caucus' political arm, Equality PAC. He told Axios: "The Equality Caucus is not going to stand by passively and allow anyone to scapegoat the trans community. It is a red line for us." Equality PAC "is absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time," the group said in a separate statement to Axios, calling Kaptur's language "unacceptable." What we're hearing: Kaptur's colleagues also privately communicated their disgust with the ad to her office, multiple House Democrats familiar with the matter told Axios. The lawmakers predicted there will be in-person conversations with Kaptur when the House returns in November, especially if she wins her election. "Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls' sports stay fair," said Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer. "She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor." Zoom out: It's not just Kaptur. Democratic House candidates Blake Gendebien of New York and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa, and Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, have put out ads featuring similar rhetoric. Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) released an ad last week in which he said there are "real concerns about fairness and safety" and that "states should decide what's right for protecting women and girls." That ad, like Kaptur's, raised eyebrows privately among LGBTQ+ House Democrats, though none have called him out publicly for it. The other side: Centrist groups and lawmakers say the party has to be realistic about districts like Kaptur's, which President Trump carried by 11 percentage points in 2024. "Marcy Kaptur and Don Davis are doing the most important work in Democratic politics: winning Trump districts," said Liam Kerr, cofounder of centrist group Welcome PAC. Kerr argued attacks from LGBTQ+ groups will only help swing-district Democrats: "Taking the 20% side of an 80/20 issue may be bad politics, but elevating the big winners repudiating you is even worse advocacy." Between the lines: "Our latest [research] showed that anti-trans attacks take about 8 points off of the Democratic vote if you just let it sit out there," Erickson, the Third Way official, told Axios. "But there are ways to respond that get you back up 10 to 12 to 14 points," she continued. "There are a bunch of different ways to say it ... just being clear that there need to be rules. Not laws, but rules." "When it comes to health care, that parents, not politicians, should be in charge of decisions about their kids' health care." The bottom line: Centrists and LGBTQ+ Democrats alike say a careful balance can and should be struck. Several lawmakers pointed to Senate hopefuls James Talarico and Sherrod Brown as examples for deftly maneuvering on this issue. Erickson said "calling transgender girls 'boys' ... is not respectful" and that candidates "don't have to do it. There's better ways to talk about this."

events.title: MCP for agent-to-agent comms may be the riskiest protocol you've never heard of
events.summary: The adoption of AI agents in millions of organizations is creating new opportunities for attackers to make them take malicious actions, such as exfiltrating database contents and sensitive business and personal information. In the past five months, Google and four other organizations—with little in common except for their use of AI agents—have acknowledged vulnerabilities that exploit one agent inside a targeted network to spread harmful instructions to other internal agents. The technique is a special form of prompt injection that targets not the LLM but a particular agent, such as one for translation or data analysis. Guardrails inside such agents, if they exist at all, are often lax and will send the instructions to other agents down the chain. Because the latter agent explicitly trusts the first one, it follows the directions. Unexpected and hard to mitigate Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin tested agents from organizations including Google, JP Morgan Chase, Weviate, Rapid7, the French government's interministerial digital directorate, and the US federal government. His proof-of-concept attacks exploit trust gaps in MCP, short for Model Context Protocol . The standard is one way AI apps and agents communicate with each other inside an internal network. events.title: Envision to end operations and stop product development if it can't find partner
events.summary: Envision , a Netherlands-based start-up that made hardware and software tools for the visually impaired , will be stopping product development at the end of the year unless it can find a partner. In a statement posted to the company's website on Monday, founder Karthik Mahadevan and Karthik Kannan said that despite efforts towards a successful business model, the company has been unable to yield profitable results. "We reached the conclusion that we have given it our all and brought Envision as far as we could with our nimble efforts," they wrote. "There’s still so much potential for this product and business to grow, but realising it needs someone who can take it in a new direction, whether that's a new audience or a different business model." Mr Mahadevan and Mr Kannan said they were in talks with a few possible partners who might be able to keep the company going. They were also open to speaking with others who may have ideas as to how to keep it alive. In 2024, Envision's founders spoke with The National about the company's aspirations. Its journey to selling smart glasses for the visually impaired started in 2017, when the start-up's smartphone app, Envision AI, began to gain popularity. The app uses a phone camera to identify and read signs, objects, menus, books or other material in real time, making life easier for visually impaired users. The popularity of the app's free version, according to Mr Kannan at the time, fuelled Envision's desire to improve the user experience based on feedback from customers. “If you're a low-vision person and you have to have a phone in one hand and a cane in the other, that can be cumbersome,” he said. “So we started looking for something that might be sleek and modern-looking to implement.” Part of enhancing the experience, Mr Kannan said, was to take the best aspects of the Envision app and use it in the glasses. Envision's app won a Google Play Award in 2019 in the category of “best accessibility experience”, and Mr Kannan said it could come to an agreement with Google and eventually use the company's largely defunct Google Glass technology for its product. The glasses, priced from $1,899 to $3,499, were introduced in 2020 and underwent various improvements amid the AI boom. In the announcement on Monday, the founders outlined plans to wind down operations and promised there would be a final update, with hopes of keeping the app and some offerings operational for as long as possible "offline”. Mr Mahadevan and Mr Kannan said the ultimate problem was scaling Envision's business model to something sustainable given the competition from Apple and Meta , and the current economy. "On paper, 300 million blind and low-vision people is a big market, but for the majority of them, the problems that come first are ones technology can't solve yet: poverty, lack of basic access, unemployment," Envision’s founders wrote. "That's why even products that are cheap or free struggle to get past that million mark, and paying users are a much much smaller slice of that." In 2024, Envision told The National of the intention to turn the company's focus to Arabic . "As our user base in the Middle East grew and we built up a community of users, we've started to bring a lot more of those efforts in-house,” Mr Kannan said. “As a result, we now have more control over how the AI works when translating documents that are scanned and how it works if there's written text on a blackboard.”

events.title: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base because of threat of Iranian drone attack
events.summary: The U.S. military evacuated a dozen B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the UK over the weekend as a result of intelligence suggesting an Iranian drone attack, U.S. officials said. Why it matters: Such an Iranian drone attack from British soil against the base could have led to the killing of U.S. service members and destroyed the strategic bombers. It would have been an unprecedented and brazen attack by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential for dramatic escalation in the war in the Middle East. When asked by reporters on Monday if Iran planned to launch a drone attack against the base from British soil, Trump said: "I can't tell you that. If they did they will suffer greatly." Driving the news: The dozen B-1 bombers were evacuated from the base in the UK only several weeks after being deployed there. The Pentagon said on Sunday that "all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States." It added that the U.S. military bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, "remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States." Between the lines: The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base. U.S. officials say it is unclear whether the people who were arrested are connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack. Behind the scenes: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel gave the UK intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack. On Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Netanyahu from the plane on his way to Iceland, the State Department said. What they're saying: Rubio told reporters earlier that the movement of the bombers was part of "regular rotations" of U.S. Air Force assets around the world and was not directly tied to an Iranian threat. But several hours later, President Trump contradicted Rubio and told reporters the bombers were moved because of a security threat from Iran. "They didn't fly out by accident ... there was a threat. We moved them around a little bit," he said. Trump added that the U.S. knows who was behind the threat and their links to Iran. Trump was then asked about the attempted terrorist attack on the Fly Dubai flight and said he thinks Iran was responsible.

events.title: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
events.summary: President Trump said Monday that the United States will help Russia amid a potential case of pneumonic plague , though he hasn't spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it. Why it matters: International concern spiked over the weekend over the news that a Russian lab worker had died from a possible case of pneumonic plague, reminding some of how the COVID-19 epidemic began. Trump's comments came after a question about the reported death of Darya Shipilova, who was potentially exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. There has been no official confirmation that Shipilova's death was due to pneumonic plague, but five hospitals in the area and dozens of institute workers have been quarantined out of precaution. Russian health authorities say Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing showed no pathogen tied to her work. No additional deaths or sicknesses tied to the incident have been reported. What they're saying: "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." Trump said the disease used to be more controllable, but "microbes and the germs have gotten stronger." The president appeared to be referring to antimicrobial resistance , but pneumonic plague itself remains treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early Between the lines: The White House is monitoring the outbreak, Axios scooped, with the Department of Health and Human Services and State Department also on alert. The European Commission is also "very closely" monitoring the suspected outbreak. Go deeper: How pneumonic plague spreads, and how it is and isn't like COVID
